Let the whole wide world despise me,
'Tis for her alone I live.
Grant me yet this one poor favour,
With this one request comply;
Let us each go on for ever,
I to ask, and you deny.
Since, my Strephon, you so kind are,
All pretensions to resign;
Trust Chlorinda. — You may find her

Less severe than you divine.
Strephon struck with joy beholds her,
Wou'd have spoke but knew not how;
But he look'd such things as told her
More than all his speech cou'd do.
To CHLORINDA.
By the Same.
SEE, Strephon, what unhappy fate
Does on thy fruitless passion wait,
Adding to flame fresh fuel:
Rather than thou should'st favour find;
The kindest soul on earth's unkind,
And the best nature cruel.
The goodness, which Chlorinda shews,
From mildness and good breeding flows,
But must not love be stil'd:

Or else 'tis such as mothers try,
When wearied with incessant cry,
They still a froward child.
She with a graceful mien and air,
Genteely civil, yet severe,
Bids thee all hopes give o'er.
Friendship she offers, pure and free;
And who, with such a friend as she,
Cou'd want, or wish for more?
The cur that swam along the flood,
His mouth well fill'd with morsel good,
(Too good for common cur!)
By visionary hopes betray'd,
Gaping to catch a fleeting shade,
Lost what he held before.
Mark, Strephon, and apply this tale,

Lest love and friendship both should fail;
Where then wou'd be thy hope?
Of hope, quoth Strephon, talk not, friend;
And for applying — know, the end
Of ev'ry cur's a rope.
The Fable of IXION.
To CHLORINDA.
By the Same.
IXION, as the poets tell us,
Was one of those pragmatic fellows,
Who claim a right to kiss the hand
Of the best lady in the land;
Demonstrating by dint of reason,
That impudence in love's no treason.
He let his fancy soar much higher;
And ventur'd boldly to aspire

To Juno's high and mighty grace,
And woo'd the goddess face to face.
What mortal e'er had whims so odd,
To think of cuckolding a God?
For she was both Jove's wife and sister,
And yet the rascal wou'd have kiss'd her.
How he got up to heav'n's high palace,
Not one of all the poets tell us;
It must be therefore understood,
That he got up which way he cou'd.
Nor is it, that I know, recorded,
How bows were made, and speeches worded;
So, leaving this to each one's guess,
I'll only tell you the success.
But first I stop awhile to shew
What happen'd lately here below.

Chlorinda, who beyond compare
Of all the fair ones is most fair;
Chlorinda, by the Gods design'd
To be the pattern of her kind,
With every charm of face and mind;
Glanc'd light'ning from her eyes so blue,
And shot poor Strephon through and through.
He, over head and ears her lover,
Try'd all the ways he cou'd to move her;
He sigh'd, and vow'd, and pray'd, and cry'd,
And did a thousand things beside:
She let him sigh, and pray, and cry on —
But now hear more about Ixion.
The Goddess, proud, (as folks report her)
Disdain'd that mortal wight shou'd court her,
And yet she chose the fool to flatter,

To make him fancy some great matter,
And hope in time he might get at her;
Grac'd him with now and then a smile,
But inly scorn'd him all the while;
Resolv'd at last a trick to shew him,
Seeming to yield and so undo him.
Now which way, do you think, she took?
(For do't she wou'd by hook or crook)
Why, thus I find it in my book.
She call'd a pretty painted cloud,
The brightest of the wand'ring crowd,
For she you know is queen o' th' air,
And all the clouds and vapours there
Governs at will, by nod or summons,
As Walpole does the house of commons.
This cloud which came to her stark naked,

She dress'd as fine as hands could make it.
From her own wardrobe out she brought
Whate'er was dainty, wove or wrought.
A smock which Pallas spun and gave her
Once on a time to gain her favour;
A gown that ha'n't on earth its fellow,
Of finest blue and lined with yellow,
Fit for a Goddess to appear in,
And not a pin the worse for wearing.
A quilted petticoat beside,
With whalebone hoop six fathom wide.
With these she deck'd the cloud, d'ye see?
As like herself, as like cou'd be:
So like, that cou'd not I or you know
Which was the cloud, and which was Juno.
Thus dress'd she sent it to the villain,

To let him act his wicked will on:
Then laugh'd at the poor fool aloud,
Who for a Goddess grasp'd a cloud.
This you will say was well done on her
T' expose the tempter of her honour —
But more of him you need not hear;
Only to Strephon lend an ear.
He never entertain'd one thought
With which a Goddess could find fault;
His spotless love might be forgiven
By ev'ry saint in earth and heav'n.
Juno herself, though nice and haughty,
Wou'd not have judg'd his passion naughty.
All this Chlorinda's self confess'd,
And own'd his flame was pure and chaste,
Read what his teeming Muse brought forth,

And prais'd it far beyond its worth:
Mildly receiv'd his fond address,
And only blam'd his love's excess:
Yet she, so good, so sweet, so smiling,
So full of truth, so unbeguiling,
One way or other still devis'd
To let him see he was despis'd:
And when he plum'd, and grew most proud,
All was a vapour, all a cloud.
A TALE.
To CHLORINDA.
By the Same.
DAME Venus, a daughter of Jove's,
And amongst all his daughters most fair,
Lost, it seems, t' other day the two doves,
That wafted her car thro' the air.

The dame made a heavy sad rout,
Ran about heav'n and earth to condole 'em;
And sought high and low to find out,
Where the biddyes were stray'd, or who stole 'em.
To the God, who the stragglers shou'd meet,
She promis'd most tempting fine pay,
Six kisses than honey more sweet,
And a seventh far sweeter than they.
The proposal no sooner was made,
But it put all the Gods in a flame;
For who would not give all he had
To be kiss'd by so dainty a dame?
To Cyprus, to Paphos they run,
Where the Goddess oft us'd to retire;
Some rode round the world with the sun,
And search'd every country and shire.

But with all their hard running and riding,
Not a God of 'em claim'd the reward;
For no one could tell tale or tiding,
If the doves were alive or were starv'd.
At last the sly shooter of men
Young Cupid, (I beg the God's pardon)
Mamma, your blue birds I have seen
In a certain terrestrial garden.
Where, where, my dear child, quickly shew,
Quoth the dame, almost out of her wits:
Do but go to Chlorinda's, says Cu,
And you'll find 'em in shape of pewits.
Is it she that hath done me this wrong?
Full well I know her, and her arts;
She has follow'd the thieving trade long,
But I thought she dealt only in hearts.

I shall soon make her know, so I shall —
And with that to Jove's palace she run,
And began like a bedlam to bawl,
I am cheated, I'm robb'd, I'm undone.
Chlorinda, whom none can approach
Without losing his heart or his senses,
Has stol'n the two doves from my coach,
And now flaunts it at Venus' expences.
She has chang'd the poor things to pewits,
And keeps 'em like ord'nary fowls:
So when she robs men of their wits,
She turns 'em to asses or owls.
I cou'd tell you of many a hundred
Of figure, high station, and means,
Whom she without mercy has plunder'd,
Ever since she came into her teens.

But her thefts upon earth I'd have borne,
Or have let 'em all pass for mere fable;
But nothing will now serve her turn,
But the doves out of Venus's stable.
Is it fit, let your mighty ship say,
That I, like some pitiful flirt,
Shou'd tarry within doors all day,
Or else trudge it afoot in the dirt?
Is it fit that a mortal shou'd trample
On me, who am styl'd queen of beauty?
O make her, great Jove, an example,
And teach Nimble-fingers her duty.
Sir Jove when he heard her thus rage,
For all his great gravity, smil'd;
And then, like a judge wise and sage,
He began in terms sober and mild.

Learn, daughter, to bridle your tongue,
Forbear to traduce with your prattle
The fair, who has done you no wrong,
And scorns to purloin goods and chattel.
She needs neither gewgaw nor trinket,
To carry the world all before her;
Her deserts, I wou'd have you to think it,
Are enough to make all men adore her.
Your doves are elop'd, I confess,
And chuse with Chlorinda to dwell;
But blame not the lady for this;
For sure 'tis no crime to excel.
As for them, I applaud their high aims;
Having serv'd from the time of their birth
The fairest of heavenly dames,
They would now serve the fairest on earth.

FLOWERS.
By ANTHONY WHISTLER, Esq;
LET sages, with superfluous pains,
The learned page devour;
While Florio better knowledge drains
From each instructive flow'r.
His fav'rite Rose his fear alarms,
All opening to the sun;
Like vain coquettes, who spread their charms,
And shine, to be undone.
The Tulip, gaudy in its dress,
And made for nought but show,
In every sense, may well express
The glittering, empty beau!
The Snow-drop first but peeps to light,
And fearful shews its head;

Thus modest merit shines more bright,
By self-distrust misled.
Th' Auric'la, which thro' labour rose,
Yet shines compleat by art,
The force of education shows;
How much it can impart.
He marks the Sensitive's nice fit;
Nor fears he to proclaim,
If each man's darling vice were hit,
That he would act the same.
Beneath each common hedge, he views
The Violet, with care;
Hinting we should not worth refuse,
Altho' we find it there.
The Tuberose that lofty springs,
Nor can support its height,

Well represents imperious kings,
Grown impotent by might.
Fragrant, tho' pale, the Lily blows;
To teach the female breast,
How virtue can its sweets disclose
In all complexions drest.
To every bloom that crowns the year,
Nature some charm decrees;
Learn hence, ye nymphs, her face to wear,
Ye cannot fail to please.
SONG.
By the Same.
WHILE, Strephon, thus you teize one,
To say, what won my heart;
It cannot sure be treason,
If I the truth impart.

'Tis the reverse of what you love,
And all the men of sense approve.
None of the Nine e'er gave it birth;
The offspring first of foolish mirth,
The nurs'ry's study, children's play,
Inferior far to Namby's lay.
What vacant Folly first admir'd,
And then with emulation fir'd,
Gravely to imitate, aspir'd.
'Tis opposite to all good writing,
In each defect of this delighting.
Obscurity its charms displays,
And inconsistency, its praise.
No gleam of sense to wake the soul,
While clouds of nonsense round it roll.
No smooth description to delight;

No fire the passions to excite;
Not joke enough to shake the pit:
A jest obscene wou'd here be wit.
What train of thought, tho' e'er so mean,
Of black-shoe-boy or cynder-quean,
But far out-shines Sir Fopling's mind
While bent this secret charm to find!
The greatest charm as yet remains,
Best suited to the searcher's brains,
That when he seems on it to fall,
He finds there is no charm at all.
Th' appearance, first, of Nothing's fine,
To find it Nothing is divine!
But Batho is the flow'r, to sink
Below what mortal man can think —
Well, now what is't? — what is't — a fiddle! —

Yes, do be angry — 'tis a Riddle.
SONG.
By the Same.
LET wisdom boast her mighty pow'r,
With passion still at strife,
Yet love is sure the sov'reign flow'r,
The sweet perfume of life.
The happy breeze that swells the sail,
When quite becalm'd we lie;
The drop, that will the heart regale,
And sparkle in thy eye.
The sun that wakes us to delight,
And drives the shades away;
The dream that chears our dreary night,
And makes a brighter day.
But if, alas! it wrongly seize,

Delia comes often to you, Tucca; but to see her
is not allowed: she is hidden, shut behind a husband's threshold.
To you Delia comes often, but to me she has not yet come: for
if she is hidden, it is far to touch what you cannot.
She will have come: I have heard it. But what use to me now
is that messenger? Tell it to him to whom she returned.
That lover of Corinthian words,
that fellow, that rhetorician! For inasmuch as he is wholly
Thucydides, a tyrant, an Attic fever,
the Gallic "tau," the "min" and the "psin," and "ill befall him"—
all those words he mixed up for his brother.
Behold him whom glory, upheld by a mighty realm,
had lifted higher even than the seats of heaven:
this man had shaken the great globe of the earth with war,
this man had broken the kings of Asia, this man its peoples;

this man was bringing grievous slavery to you, now to you, Rome,
(for the rest had fallen by the hero's spear-point):
when suddenly, in the midst of the contest of affairs, headlong
he collapsed, driven from his fatherland into exile.
Such is the power of the goddess; by such a nod the deceitful
hour, in a moment of time, wears away mortal things.
Wherever the seasons of our varied life bid us go,
whatever lands to touch, whatever men to see,
may I perish, if any other shall be dearer to me than you.
For what other can be sweeter than you,
to whom, a youth before others, the gods and the gods' sisters,
the Muse too, gave all good things, and not undeservedly,
all things in which the chorus of Phoebus and Phoebus himself rejoice?
O who could have been more learned than you, Muse?

O who on earth speaks more pleasantly than you alone?
For surely bright Clio herself does not so speak.
Wherefore it is enough, if you permit yourself to be loved;
for that the love be mutual in return—whence is that to come to me?
Away from here, you empty bombasts of the rhetoricians, away,
words puffed up with no Achaean dew,
and you, Selius and Tarquitius and Varro,
the race of schoolmen, dripping with grease,
away from here, you cymbal of empty youth.
And you, O Sextus, the care of my cares,
farewell, Sabinus; now farewell, fair ones.
We are setting our sails for the blessed harbours,
seeking the learned sayings of great Siro,
and we will free our life from all care.
Away from here, Camenae; you too, away—and yet farewell,
sweet Camenae, for we will confess the truth,

sweet you were, and yet revisit my pages,
but modestly and seldom.
Father-in-law, blessed neither to yourself nor to another,
and son-in-law Noctuinus, you rotten head,
has such a girl, then, by your stupor and by yours,
been crushed and gone off to the country? Ah me,
how that verse fits, on every side:
"Father-in-law and son-in-law, you have ruined everything."
This indeed without offence, sweetest Varius, I will say:
may I perish, if that pretty boy has not undone me.
But if the precepts forbid me to say it, then truly
I will not say it, but that boy has undone me.
Little farm, that were Siro's, and you, poor little field,
yet to that master you too were riches,
I commend to you myself and these, along with me, whom I have ever loved,
if I shall hear anything sadder of my fatherland,

and first of all my father. You will now be to him
what Mantua had been, and what Cremona was before.
A few things to me, but to snowy Phoebus not unknown,
a few things to me say, you learned daughters of Pegasus.
The victor is at hand—behold, the great glory of a great triumph,
the victor, wherever the lands and wherever the seas lie open,
bearing the bristling tokens of barbarian battle,
like great Oeneus' son and like proud Eryx;
nor any the less for that worthy to pour forth your songs,
greatest, and to enter the holy choruses.
And so by these unwonted cares I am the more tossed, best one,
as to what I can write of you, or what to you.
For (I will confess it) that which ought to have been the greatest cause
of deterring became the greatest cause of urging me on.
A few of your songs have come into our pages,

songs both for their tongue and for their Cecropian wit,
songs that, welcome to ages to come, deserve to surpass
the Phrygian, the Pylian elder.
Softly here, beneath the green covering of a spreading oak,
were the shepherds Moeris and Meliboeus,
tossing sweet songs in alternate verse,
such as the learned youth of Trinacria loves.
In rivalry all the gods adorned the heroine,
in rivalry the goddesses too, each with her own gift.
O you, happy beyond others with such a writer for your maiden!
No other shall be called prior in fame:
not she who, had she not been caught by the gift of the Hesperides,
had outrun winged Hippomenes in the race;
not the bright daughter of Tyndareus, brought forth from the swan's egg,
not Cassiopeia gleaming in the upper sky,
not she long defended in the great contest of horses,

which each suitor's pregnant hand desired for itself,
for whom the impious father often drained a son-in-law's life-blood,
often, like ruddy ground, the earth flowed with blood;
not royal Semele, not the Inachian daughter of Acrisius,
who tested Jove with pitiless lightning and rain;
not she by whose rape, driven out, the Tarquinii
left their household gods, son and father alike,
at that time when Rome first changed its proud
masters for placid consuls.
Many rewards too she gave to deserving nurslings,
rewards greatest to the Messallae, the Publicolae.
For why should I record those zeals of measureless labour?
why the bristling seasons of hard soldiering?
the camp set so often before the forum, the camp before the city,
this so far from your son, this so far from your fatherland?

to endure now the unmeasured stars, now the heats?
to be able to stretch yourself even upon the hard flint?
often to glide across the fierce sea under a hostile star?
often by daring to conquer the sea, often the storm?
often too to hurl your body among the dense foe,
and not to remember the god common to war?
now the swift Africans, the thousands of a perjured race,
now to approach the golden streams of swift Tagus?
now by warfare to seek one nation after another,
to conquer and pass beyond the bounds of Ocean?
It is not ours, no, I say, to touch upon such great praises—
nay, I will even dare to say this: it is scarcely within man's power.
These very deeds, these will bear their own memorials of things through the world,
they will of themselves win for themselves a glorious renown.

We, those songs which the gods fashioned with you,
the Cynthian and the Muses, Bacchus and Aglaia,
if we, lowly, can aspire to praise and approach Cyrene,
if in our father's song we can approach the Greek wit,
we already advance beyond our very wishes.
This is enough; I have nothing to do with the gross crowd.
That Sabinus whom you see, strangers,
says he was the swiftest mule-driver,
and that he could not fail to pass the onrush
of any flying gig, whether to Mantua
he must fly, or to Brixia.
And he denies that the house of his rival Trypho
denies this noble fact, or the island of Caerulus,
where that man, Sabinus after, before Quintio,
says he cropped with the two-pronged forceps
their long-maned necks, lest, the Cytorian yoke

pressing, the harsh mane should breed a wound.
Cold Cremona and muddy Gaul,
that to you these things were and are most well known
Sabinus says: from his ultimate origin
he says he stood in your morass,
in your marsh laid down his packs,
and thence through so many rutted miles
bore the yoke, whether to left or right
the mule had begun to balk, or both,
and that no vows were made by him to the wayside gods,
save this latest one:
his father's reins and the nearest comb.
But these things were of old: now of ivory
he sits, and sits on his seat, and dedicates himself to you,
twin Castor and twin of Castor.
What god, Octavius, has snatched you from us? or was it,

as they say—ah!—the cups too harsh with unmixed wine?
"With you, if it is a fault, I drank. Each man's own fates
follow him: what guilt have the undeserving wine-cups?"
Your writings indeed we shall greatly marvel at, and you,
snatched away, and Roman history we shall weep,
but you will be nothing. Speak, you perverse shades,
what envy was it that this man should outlive his father?
Proud Noctuinus, you rotten head,
the girl is given to you whom you seek, she is given;
she is given, proud Noctuinus, whom you seek.
But, O proud Noctuinus, do you not see
that Atilius has two daughters,
two, and that this one and the other are given to you?
Be present now, be present: behold, as is fitting,
proud Noctuinus leads home his wine-jug.
Talasius, Talasius, Talasius!

You think me cast down, because I cannot, as before,
be borne over the deep seas,
nor endure the hard cold, nor suffer the heat,
nor follow a victor's arms?
They are strong, strong in me, my wrath and ancient frenzy
and the tongue by which I am a man to you,
and the foul fellowship of your prostituted
sister. O why do you provoke me?
Why, you shameless one, you who must be reproved to Caesar,
if your thefts be told,
and your late thrift over a squandered patrimony
toward your brother,
or the banquets held as a boy with grown men,
and your buttocks wet through your sleep,
and, you unaware, the sudden shout besides
of "Talasius, Talasius"?

Why did you turn pale, woman? Do the jokes hurt?
Or do you recognize your own deeds?
You shall not summon me through the fair Cotyttia
to your festival phalli,
nor afterward shall I see you wag your loins in your little gown,
clutching the altars,
nor, by the yellow Tiber, the reeking sailor
to call, where the beached rafts
stand in the shallows, held by foul mud,
and, struggling, in the meagre water;
nor into the kitchen and the greasy crossroads-feasts
shall you lead the squalid banquets,
filled with which, as if with slobbering waters,
you go back to your fat wife,
and, seething, you loose your bowels at the price of her dowry,
and lick mouth and shin with your kisses.

Now wound me, now provoke, if you have any strength!
And I write down your name.
Lucius, you catamite, have your riches now left you,
and do your back teeth chatter with hunger?
I shall see you holding nothing besides your cowardly
brothers and an angry Jove,
and your split belly, and the feet of your ruptured
uncle, swollen with starvation.
13a.
Beneath this citadel of Pallas lies the wrong done to the Italian age,
a guest not less than the men of ancient genius,
and one in whom Rome might vie with learned Athens;
but to no man is it given to conquer the iron fates.
If the task I have undertaken shall be allowed to run its course,
O Paphos, O you who dwell in the Idalian seats,
that Trojan Aeneas through the Roman towns at last

may go, borne in a song worthy of you, with you:
not only with incense, or with a painted tablet, shall I
adorn your temples and bear garlands with pure hands;
a horned ram, a bull—humble these, but greatest—a victim
shall sprinkle with honour your consecrated hearths,
and in marble, his head and his fire-coloured wings
fashioned, after the manner of a painted quiver, Love shall stand.
Be present, O Cytherea: your own Caesar from Olympus
and the altar of the Surrentine shore calls you.
14a.
Of him who was sweeter than the Syracusan bard, and than Hesiod
greater, and not less than the lips of Homer,
these too are the rudiments of that divine poet,
and Calliope unpolished in his varied song.

I have played, Octavius, while slender Thalia gave the measure,
and like little spiders have spun a delicate thread.
I have played: let these be the songs spoken on behalf of the Gnat,
so that the whole course of the tale may chime in sport
for the learned, and let learned men approve, though the envious be present.
Whoever stands ready to blame these jests and the Muse,
will be carried lighter than the weight of a gnat, and lighter in fame.
Hereafter my Muse will speak to you in a graver strain,
when the seasons grant me their unanxious fruits,
that songs worthy of your judgment may be polished for you.
Glory of Latona and of great Jove, golden offspring,
Phoebus shall be the prince and author of my song,
and its patron with answering lyre, whether
Arna nurtures him, drenched with the Chimaerean stream of Xanthus,

or the glory of Asteria, or where the Parnassian rock
spreads forth its horns on this side and that with broad brow,
and the sounding wave of Castalia glides on its liquid foot.
Wherefore, glory of the Pierian spring, come, sisters,
Naiads, and celebrate the god with the chorus's applause.
And you, holy Pales, to whom the rustics' coming
returns, may their care be secure that holds
the airy tendance of the groves and the greening woods:
with you as my guardian I am borne, a wanderer, among glades and caverns.
And you, for whom assurance arises from deserving pages,
venerable Octavius, glide to my undertakings,
holy boy; for not for you does my page sing of war,
the grim war of Jove, and it lays aside . . . Phlegra, the land sprinkled with Giant-blood,
nor does it drive the Centaurs against the swords of the Lapiths,

nor does the East scorch the Erichthonian citadels with fires,
nor will Athos pierced through, nor the chains cast upon the great sea
now seek belated fame in my volume,
nor the Hellespont beaten by the hooves of horses,
when Greece feared the Persians coming from every side,
but soft songs, ranging in slender verse,
driven by their own strength, rejoice to play with Phoebus as their guide.
These things, holy boy, we will record for you; for you may this
glory remain, shining, abiding through perpetual ages.
And may a place await you in the holy abode, and for you, safe,
may the life you are owed be remembered through happy years,
welcome, shining for the good. But let us be borne to our beginning.
The fiery Sun had now pierced the ethereal heights
and was shaking his bright light from his gilded chariot,

and Aurora with her rosy locks had put the shadows to flight:
the shepherd drove the she-goats from the stalls to the glad pastures,
and sought the topmost ridges of the lofty mountain,
where flowering grass clothed the open hills.
Now wandering through woods and thickets, now in the valleys
they hide their bodies, and now, swift, straying everywhere,
they cropped the greening grass with tender bite.
They clung to the rocky hollows on the lonely banks,
and the hanging arbutus is plucked from the outstretched branches,
and the dense wild-vine is eagerly sought among the thickets.
This one snatches at the high tips with cropping bite,
or of the pliant willow, or of the alder newly springing;
this one searches the tender briars of the bushes, but that one
leans over toward the shadow of its image cast in the stream.

O blessings of the shepherd, if any, with mind first taught,
disdain not the way of life of the poor man, and approve for him
dreams of luxury, unknown, his cares spurned—
cares that rend greedy minds with hostile breast.
If the fleeces, twice washed and seething with Assyrian dye,
given with Attalic wealth, do not seethe for him; if the gleam of gold
beneath the panelled ceiling of a house wrings not his greedy soul,
nor the glory of paintings, nor the gleam of gems is kept
in any service known, nor do Grecian cups

After this, when this son was born to us, to me, forsooth, and to my excellent wife, we squabbled then about the name: for she was for adding hippos to the name, Xanthippus, or Charippus, or Callipides;

dancing-tune
with bubble-bursting plashings.
FROGS
Brekekekex koax koax!
CHORUS
Iacchus, O Iacchus!
Iacchus, O Iacchus!
CHORUS
Iacchus, O greatly-honoured, dwelling here in your seats,
Iacchus, O Iacchus,
come dance across this meadow
to your holy worshippers,
shaking about your head

the fruit-laden, blossoming
wreath of myrtle, and with bold
foot beating out
the unbridled, frolic-loving rite,
that holds the greatest share of grace, the pure and sacred
dance for the holy initiates.
CHORUS
Wake the blazing torches, for in your hands he comes brandishing,
Iacchus, O Iacchus,
the light-bringing star of the nocturnal rite.
The meadow shines with flame;
the old men's knees leap up;
they shake off their griefs
and the long years of ancient time,
beneath the sacred worship.
And you, blazing with your torch,

lead forth, stepping on, to the flowery marshy floor,
the dance-rousing, blessed throng of youth.
CHORUS
Go now, every man, boldly
into the flowery folds
of the meadows, stamping
and joking
and playing and mocking;
and a sufficient breakfast has been eaten.
CHORUS
But come on, and see that you nobly extol
the Saviour-goddess
with your voice in song,
who declares she'll keep
the land safe through the seasons,
even if Thorycion doesn't want it.

CHORUS
Come now, raise another kind of hymn, the fruit-bearing queen,
the goddess Demeter, adorning her, and sing in sacred strains.
CHORUS
Demeter, mistress of the pure rites,
queen, stand by us,
and keep your own chorus safe,
and let me safely all day long
play and dance;
CHORUS
and let me, having said
many funny things and many serious,
and having played and mocked
worthily of your feast,
win and be crowned with the ribbon.
CHORUS

Come, on now,
call hither too the comely god
with songs, the fellow-traveller of this dancing.
CHORUS
Iacchus, greatly honoured, who found the sweetest
song of the feast, come along with us
to the goddess,
and show how without toil
you make your way over the long road.
Iacchus, lover of the dance, escort me.
CHORUS
For you it was who tore, for laughter
and for cheapness' sake, this little sandal
and this rag,
and found a way for us to play
and dance unpunished.

Iacchus, lover of the dance, escort me.
CHORUS
For just now I caught sight, with a sidelong glance,
of the lovely-faced face of a young girl,
a playmate of mine,
with her little tunic torn,
and a little breast peeping out.
Iacchus, lover of the dance, escort me.
CHORUS
Go now
round the sacred circle of the goddess, through the flowery grove,
sporting, you who share in the god-loved feast;
and I'll go with the girls and women,
to where they keep the all-night vigil for the goddess, to bear the holy light.
CHORUS
Let us go to the rosy

meadows, full of flowers,
in our own manner,
the loveliest in the dance,
sporting — the manner the blessed
Fates bring together.
CHORUS
For on us alone the sun
and the cheerful light shine,
all of us who've been initiated
and led a pious
life toward strangers
and ordinary folk.
DIONYSUS
"Apollo — who hold Delos or Pytho somewhere—"
DIONYSUS
"—who rule the Aegean headlands or the depths of the grey sea."

CHORUS
Muse of the sacred dances, step here and come for the delight of my song,
to see the great crowd of people, where wits
beyond number are sitting,
greedier for fame than Cleophon, on whose ever-babbling lips
there roars terribly
a Thracian swallow,
perched on a barbarous leaf,
and shrills a tearful nightingale-tune, that he'll perish,
even if the votes come out equal.
CHORUS
And if I'm right in judging the life or character of a man
who'll yet be sorry,
not for long will this ape who now troubles us,
little Cleigenes,
the most rascally bath-attendant of all who rule over the cinder-mixing

adulterated lye-ash
and Cimolian earth,
linger out his time; and seeing this, he's
not peaceful, for fear he might some day be stripped, drunk,
walking without a stick.
CHORUS
Surely the loud-thunderer will feel a dreadful anger within,
when he sees his sharp-tongued rival
whetting his tooth; then, under a dreadful madness,
his eyes will roll.
CHORUS
There will be helmet-tossing strife of horse-plumed words,
and splinterings of axle-pegs and chisel-work of deeds,
as a man wards off the horse-prancing
phrases of a mind-building man.
CHORUS

Bristling the shaggy-necked mane of his self-grown crest,
knitting a dreadful frown, roaring, he'll hurl
bolt-fastened phrases, tearing them off plank by plank
with earth-born blast;
CHORUS
and from there the mouth-working, word-testing, smooth
tongue, unrolling itself, moving its envious reins,
splitting hairs over the phrases, will whittle down
a great labour of the lungs.
CHORUS
O nine holy maiden
Muses of Zeus, who look upon the subtle, shrewd minds
of sentence-coining men, when into strife with sharp-witted
twisting wrestling-tricks they come, contending,
come and behold the power
of two most dreadful mouths to furnish

phrases and shavings of words.
For now the great contest of wisdom moves to its work at last.
CHORUS
And indeed we long
to hear from these two clever men
what eloquence of words
you'll set on its hostile road.
For the tongue is wild,
and the spirit of both not without daring,
nor are their minds unmoved.
So it's reasonable to expect
the one will say something witty
and finely polished,
the other, tearing up his arguments roots and all,
falling on him,
will scatter many

tumbling-grounds of words.
CHORUS
You see all this, glorious Achilles;
but come, what will you say to it?
Only see . . .
that your spirit doesn't snatch you
and carry you outside the olives;
for he's accused you dreadfully.
But see, noble sir,
that you don't answer in anger,
but reefing your sails, using
only the tips of them,
and then gradually bear on
and watch,
when you find the breeze
smooth and steady.

CHORUS
Great is the matter, much the strife, mighty the war that comes.
A hard task, then, to decide,
when one strains violently,
and the other can turn round and bear down keenly.
But don't stay sitting in the same spot;
for there are many openings, and other clever tricks besides.
Whatever, then, you have to wrangle over,
speak, go at it, lay bare
the old and the new,
and risk saying something subtle and clever.
EURIPIDES
"Phthian Achilles, why, hearing the man-slaying
— alas, the blow! — do you not draw near to the rescue?
Hermes our ancestor we honour, we of the lake.
Alas, the blow! Do you not draw near to the rescue?"

EURIPIDES
"Most glorious of the Achaeans, far-ruling son of Atreus, learn from me.
Alas, the blow! Do you not draw near to the rescue?"
EURIPIDES
"Keep holy silence; the bee-keepers are near to open the house of Artemis.
Alas, the blow! Do you not draw near to the rescue?
I have authority to proclaim the auspicious power of men on the road.
Alas, the blow! Do you not draw near to the rescue?"
EURIPIDES
"How the twin-throned power of the Achaeans, of the youth of Hellas,
tophlattothrat, tophlattothrat,
sends the Sphinx, presiding bitch of evil days,
tophlattothrat, tophlattothrat,
with spear and avenging hand, a rushing bird,
tophlattothrat, tophlattothrat,
granting it to meet the bold air-roving hounds,

tophlattothrat, tophlattothrat,
and the host that leans against Ajax,
tophlattothrat, tophlattothrat."
AESCHYLUS
"Halcyons, who beside the ever-flowing waves
of the sea babble on,
wetting the skin of your wings
with watery drops, dewed with spray;
and you spiders under the roof, along the corners,
twirl-i-i-irl with your fingers
the loom-wrought weavings,
the labours of the singing shuttle,
where the flute-loving dolphin leaped
about the dark-prowed beaks,
oracles and race-courses,
the gladness of the vine-blossom,

the pain-stilling tendril of the grape.
Throw your arms about me, child."
You see this foot?
AESCHYLUS
And you, doing such stuff,
dare to find fault with my songs,
you who make your songs
in the twelve-postured manner of Cyrene?
Those are your lyric songs. But I still want
to go through the manner of your solo-songs.
"O dark-gleaming gloom
of the night, what
ill-starred dream
do you send me from the unseen,
a servant of Hades,
having a lifeless life,

child of black Night,
a shuddering, dreadful sight,
clad in black corpse-shrouds,
glaring murder, murder,
with great talons.
But, handmaids, light me a lamp,
and in pitchers draw dew from the rivers, and heat water,
that I may wash away the god-sent dream.
Ho, sea-spirit!
There it is! Ho, housemates,
behold these portents!
Glyce has snatched my cock
and is gone.
O mountain-born Nymphs!
O Mania, seize her!
And I, poor wretch, happened to be busy

at my own work,
twirl-i-i-irling in my hands
a spindle full of flax,
making a thread, so that
in the dim dawn to the market
I might carry it and sell it;
but he flew up, flew up to the aether
on the lightest tips of his wings,
and to me left woes, woes,
and tears, tears from my eyes
I shed, I shed, the wretched one.
But O Cretans, children of Ida,
take up your bows and come to my aid,
and ply your limbs, circling the house.
And together let Dictynna, the fair child Artemis,
come with her hound-bitches all through the house, everywhere;

and you, daughter of Zeus, holding aloft
the double-fired torches, sharpest in your hands, Hecate, light my way
to Glyce's, so that
going in I may search out the theft."
EURIPIDES
"Would that the Argo's hull had not winged its way across—"
AESCHYLUS
"River Spercheius, and you cattle-grazing haunts—"
EURIPIDES
"There is no other shrine of Persuasion but Speech."
AESCHYLUS
"For Death alone of the gods loves not gifts."
EURIPIDES
"And in his right hand he took the iron-laden club."
AESCHYLUS
"For chariot upon chariot, and corpse on corpse."

CHORUS
Blessed is the man who has
keen understanding perfected.
There's much to learn from many cases.
For this man, thought to have good sense,
goes back home again,
for the good of his fellow-citizens,
and for the good of his own
kinsmen and friends,
through his being shrewd.
CHORUS
So it's a fine thing not to sit
beside Socrates and chatter,
casting off music
and neglecting the greatest things
of the tragic art.

And to idle away one's time
on solemn-seeming words
and the scratchings of trifles,
is the part of a man out of his wits.
CHORUS

rising into the light, you gods beneath the earth,
and to the city good thoughts of great blessings.

and from grievous armed encounters. And let Cleophon do the fighting,
and any other of these who wishes, in his ancestral fields.

CHORUS OF OLD MEN

CHORUS OF OLD MEN

CHORUS OF OLD MEN
How fiercely, lord Heracles, this smoke leaps at me from the pot and bites my two eyes like a mad dog! CHORUS OF OLD MEN
By the gods' grace this fire is awake and alive. Which of the generals at Samos will lend a hand with the log? There—it's stopped crushing my back at last. Now it's your job, pot, to wake up the coal, so you may first bring me the lit torch. I think I see smoke and a haze, women, as of a fire burning. We must hurry faster.

CHORUS OF WOMEN

CHORUS OF WOMEN
For I heard that some doddering old men were on the move, carrying logs to the citadel as if to heat a bath—a three-talent weight—uttering the most dreadful threats, that the loathsome women must be reduced to charcoal by fire. O goddess, may I never see them burning—but rather see them rescuing Greece and the citizens from war and madness! That is why, O gold-crested guardian of the city, they have taken their seats in your shrine. And I call you to my aid, Tritogeneia: if any man sets those women alight, help us carry water!

CHORUS OF WOMEN
For I would never grow weary of dancing, nor would weariness seize my knees with toil. I'm willing to go to any length on behalf of these women, for the sake of virtue—women in whom there is nature, there is grace, there is daring, there is wisdom, and a virtue both prudent and patriotic.
CHORUS OF WOMEN
O most manly of grandmothers and nettle-mothers, advance in anger and don't be softened; for still you run before a fair wind.

CHORUS OF WOMEN
And I want to tell you a tale in answer to your Melanion. There was a certain Timon, a roamer with no fixed home, his face fenced about with impassable thorns, an offshoot of the Furies. So this Timon went off out of hatred, hurling many curses at wicked men. So that man hated your wicked men forever, in return, but to the women he was dearest.

In dreadful misery, poor wretch, your soul wears away, deceived. And I pity you—alas! For what kidney could hold out, what soul, what testicles, what loins, what backside, stretched taut and getting no screwing at dawn?

CHORUS OF OLD MEN
In dreadful misery, poor wretch, your soul wears away, deceived. I pity you too, alas! For what kidney could hold out, what soul, what testicles, what loins, what backside, stretched taut and getting no screwing at dawn?
CHORUS OF SPARTANS
Stir up the youths, Mnemosyne, and my Muse, who knows us and the Athenians, when at Artemisium they charged like gods against the ships and conquered the Medes, while Leonidas led us like boars whetting their tusks, I think; and much foam blossomed about our jaws, and much foam streamed down our legs as well. For the Persian men were no fewer than the sands. O Huntress, slayer of beasts, come hither, maiden goddess, to our treaties, that you may keep us together a long while. And now again may friendship ever be abundant by these compacts, and may we cease from the cunning foxes. O come here, come, huntress maiden!

CHORUS OF ATHENIANS
Bring on the dance, summon the Graces, call upon Artemis, and her twin, the chorus-leading Healer, gracious, and the Nysian one, who flashes Bacchic fire among his maenads, and Zeus blazing with fire, and the blessed queen his consort; and then the divinities whom we'll call as witnesses, not forgetful, of gentle-minded Peace, which the goddess Cypris made. Alalai! Hurrah for the Healer! Leap up high—hurrah!—as for victory—hurrah! Euoi, euoi, euai, euai!
CHORUS OF SPARTANS
Leaving lovely Taygetus once more, Laconian Muse, come, and fittingly hymn for us the god of Amyclae, and Athena of the Brazen House, and the noble sons of Tyndareus, who sport beside the Eurotas. Come, step lively! O step, lightly leaping, that we may hymn Sparta, which delights in choruses of the gods and the beat of feet, where the maidens like fillies beside the Eurotas leap, kicking up dust thick with their feet, and their locks toss like Bacchants brandishing the thyrsus and sporting. And the daughter of Leda leads them, the holy, comely chorus-leader. Come, bind up your hair with your hand, and leap with your feet like a deer; and make a clapping at once to aid the dance. And hymn again the goddess most mighty, of the Brazen House, the all-conquering one.

LITTLE GIRL

CHORUS
Come here, everyone, eagerly, straight for our salvation. O all you Greeks, let's help, if ever, now—freed from the battle-lines and the scarlet evils. For this day has dawned that hates Lamachus. So tell us what we must do, and direct the work; for there's no way I'd consent to give up today, before, with crowbars and machines, we've hauled up into the light the greatest of all the goddesses and the lover of the vine.
CHORUS
If only it might fall to me to see this day! For I've put up with many hardships and the pallet-beds that fell to Phormio's lot. And you'd no longer find me a sharp and peevish juror, nor harsh in my ways, as before, but you'd see me soft and much younger, freed from troubles. But come, tell us what we can do that will please you most; for some good fortune has chosen you as our commander with full authority.

CHORUS
O day longed for by the just and by the farmers, gladly seeing you, I want to greet my vines, and the fig-trees which I planted when I was younger—my heart longs to embrace them after so long a time.
CHORUS
Hail, hail, how welcome your coming, O dearest! For I was overcome with longing for you, wishing fervently to creep away into the country. For you were our greatest gain, O longed-for one, to all of us who wore out a farmer's life. For you alone helped us. For we used to enjoy many sweet and cheap and dear things in your time. For to the country folk you were barley-gruel and salvation. So the vines and the young little fig-trees and all the other plants there are will laugh and welcome you gladly.
CHORUS
O Muse, having thrust away wars, dance with me, your friend, celebrating the marriages of gods and the feasts of men and the festivities of the blessed; for these have been your care from the beginning. And if Carcinus comes and begs you to dance with his sons, neither obey nor go as their fellow-laborer, but consider them all home-bred quails, dancers with thin necks, dwarfish creatures, parings of goat-droppings, contrivance-mongers. CHORUS
Such songs of the fair-haired Graces should the wise poet sing, when in spring the swallow sits and warbles, and Morsimus has no chorus, nor Melanthius—whose most bitter voice I once heard, when he and his brother held the tragic chorus, both of them gluttonous Gorgons, ray-fish-watching Harpies, foul old-hag-chasers, goat-armpit-smelling fish-spoilers; on whom, spitting greatly and broadly, O Muse, goddess, join with me in sporting at the festival.

HIEROCLES

HIEROCLES

The finest one, surely, that Homer ever made: "So they, having thrust away the hateful cloud of war, chose Peace and set her up with a sacrifice. TRYGAEUS
But the wise Homer, by Zeus, spoke cleverly: "Clanless, lawless, hearthless is that man who loves chilling civil war."

HIEROCLES
Take care, lest somehow a kite, deceiving your wits by guile, snatch—
CHORUS

CHORUS
For there's nothing sweeter than for the seed to be already sown, and the god to drizzle upon it, and for some neighbor to say: "Tell me, what shall we do at this hour, Comarchides?" "I'd like a drink, since the god is doing well by us. Come, wife, parboil three quarts of beans, and mix in some of the wheat, and bring out some of the figs; and let Syra call Manes in from the field. For there's no way at all to dress the vine-shoots today or break up the clods, since the ground is sodden. And let someone bring out from my place the thrush and the two finches; and there was some beestings-curd inside too, and four hares—unless the weasel carried off any of them in the evening; for something was thumping and clattering inside, I don't know what. CHORUS
And when the cricket sings its sweet tune, I delight to look over my Lemnian vines, whether they're ripening yet—for the plant is early by nature—and to see the wild fig swelling; and then, when it's ripe, I eat and keep eating, and at the same time I say, "Dear seasons!" and, pounding some thyme, I mix a draught; and then I grow fat at that time of the summer.
CHORUS
—rather than looking at a god-detested captain with three crests and a very sharp scarlet cloak, which he says is a Sardian dye; but if ever he has to fight wearing the scarlet cloak, then he himself gets dyed a Cyzicene dye; and then he flees first, like a tawny horse-cock, shaking his crests, while I stand there watching the nets. And when they get home, they do unbearable things: enrolling some of us and rubbing others out, up and down, twice or three times. And tomorrow is the march-out; but so-and-so has bought no provisions, for he didn't know he was marching out; and then, standing before the statue of Pandion, he sees his name, and at a loss runs off, looking sour at his trouble. Such things they do to us country folk, but to the city folk less—these throwers-away-of-shields, hateful to gods and men. For all which they'll yet render me an account, if god wills.

CHORUS
For they've wronged me much, being lions at home but foxes in battle.

LAMACHUS'S SON

LAMACHUS'S SON

Come here, wife, to the country, and see that, lovely as you are, you lie lovely beside me. Hymen, Hymenaeus, oh!

SECOND SEMICHORUS

AGATHON (singing as both leader and chorus)
"Take up, girls, the sacred torch in honor of the goddesses below, and with free fatherland raise the festal cry of the dance."
"To which of the divinities is the revel? Tell me now. My spirit is ready to reverence the gods."
"Come now, glorify, O Muse, Phoebus, drawer of the golden bow, who founded the hollows of the land in the Simoïs country."
"Hail, Phoebus, in the fair contests of the Muses bearing the sacred prize of fairest song!"
"And sing too the maiden in the oak-bearing mountains, Artemis of the wilds."
"I follow, hymning and glorifying the holy child of Leto, Artemis who knows no bed."
"And Leto, and the strains of the Asian lyre that move the foot to the dance, beat out of measure yet in measure to the Phrygian sway of the Graces."

"I revere queen Leto, and the cithara, mother of hymns, famed for its manly cry, by which the light flashed forth in the god's divine eyes, and through our sudden song. Wherefore glorify lord Phoebus with honor. Hail, blessed child of Leto!"
AGATHON
You once wrote, "You rejoice to see the light; do you think your father does not rejoice?"
CHORUS
We accept it, and we entreat the race of the gods to appear, rejoicing in these prayers. O Zeus of mighty name, and you of the golden lyre who hold holy Delos, and you, all-conquering grey-eyed Maiden of the golden spear who dwell in our embattled city — come hither. And you of many names, slayer of beasts, child of golden-faced Leto, scion of her; and you, holy Poseidon of the sea, ruler of the deep, leaving the fish-haunted depths stirred by the gadfly; and you daughters of Nereus of the sea, and you Nymphs that wander on the hills. And may the golden lyre ring out upon our prayers; and may we, the noble women of the Athenians, hold our assembly to good effect.

CHORUS
We join in praying that these prayers may be fulfilled, fulfilled for the city and for the people; and that the best things may go to those whose part it is to win by speaking well. But all those who deceive and transgress the established oaths, for gain, to do harm; or seek to overturn decrees and the law; or tell our secrets to our enemies; or bring the Medes against the land for gain, to do harm — these are impious and wrong the city. But, O all-powerful Zeus, ratify these things, so that the gods may stand by us, women though we are.
CHORUS
Come now, let us sport in the ways that are the custom here for women, whenever we hold up the holy mysteries of the two goddesses at the sacred seasons — those which Pauson too reveres and fasts at, often praying to them, from season to season, that such things may often be his care. On, advance; lead off lightly with your feet into the ring; join hand to hand; take up, every one, the rhythm of the dance; step with nimble feet. And one must watch on every side, wheeling the eye round to keep the chorus in order. And at the same time hymn and honor the race of the Olympian gods, every one, with voice, in dance-maddened style. And if anyone expects me, being a woman, to speak ill of men in the holy place, he is not right-minded. But we ought, as if at some new work, first to set the well-formed footing of the fair-ringed dance.

CHORUS
Step forward with your feet, hymning the lyre-player and Artemis the archer-queen, the chaste. Hail, far-darter, and grant victory. And let us hymn Hera the goddess of fulfillment, as is fitting, who joins in all the dances and keeps the keys of marriage. And I entreat Hermes the god of the pastures, and Pan, and the dear Nymphs, to smile graciously on our dances, taking delight in them. Lift up eagerly the double grace of the dance. Let us sport, O women, as is the custom, and let us by all means fast. But come, leap and turn about with rhythmic foot, work out the whole song; and you yourself, lead the way thus, ivy-bearing Bacchus, lord; and I with revel-songs that love the dance will hymn you. Euhoe, O Dionysus, Bromius, child of Semele, delighting in dances on the mountains amid the lovely hymns of the Nymphs — euhoe, euhoe, euhoi! — dancing in answer. About you echoes the Cithaeronian sound; and the dark-leaved mountains, thick with shade, and the rocky glens, resound; and round about you the ivy, fair with leaves, flourishes with its tendrils.

MNESILOCHUS
Pitiless was he who bound me, most groaning of mortals. Hardly having escaped a rotten old woman, I have perished all the same. For this Scythian here, set to guard me this long while, has hung me up, friendless and forlorn, a feast for crows. Do you see? Not amid dances, nor standing with girls of my own age holding the voting-urn, but tangled in tight bonds I am set out as fodder for the monster Glaucetes — not with a marriage hymn but with a bondage-song. Wail for me, O women, since I have suffered wretched things, wretch that I am — O wretched, wretched me! — and from my kinsmen lawless sufferings, while I implored a man, weeping the much-wept dirge of Hades, — alas, alas, eh, eh! — the man who first shaved me, who clothed me in the saffron gown, and besides this sent me up to this holy place where women are. O cruel power of my doom! O accursed me! Who will not look upon my unenviable suffering amid the presence of evils? Would that a fire-bearing star of the sky might destroy the barbarian! For it is no longer dear to me to behold the immortal flame, since I was hung up, my throat-cut anguish, the wavering grief of the divinities, to journey among the dead.

MNESILOCHUS
"O holy night, how long a course you drive, riding over the star-spangled back of the sacred sky, through most majestic Olympus!"
MNESILOCHUS
"Why ever has Andromeda got, beyond all others, her share of evils —"
CHORUS
Pallas, the lover of the dance, it is our custom to call hither to the chorus, the unwedded virgin maiden, who holds our city and alone has manifest power, and is called the key-holder. Appear, you who hate tyrants, as is fitting. The people of the women call you; come to me, holding peace that loves festivals. And come, gracious and kindly, ladies, to your grove, where it is not lawful for men to behold the holy mysteries of the two goddesses, where you reveal by torchlight your immortal face. Come, come, we entreat you, O most lady Thesmophoroi; if ever before you came to hear us, come now, we beseech you, here to us.

I mark, and grief lies deep within my heart,
as I behold the eldest land of Ionia
sinking down;
But you, who have driven on to a surfeit of many good things,
calm the strong heart within your breasts,
and set your proud minds upon moderate things. For neither shall we
submit, nor will these things be fitting for you.
Anthemion son of Diphilus dedicated this to the gods,
having exchanged the labourer's class for the knight's.
To the people I gave such privilege as is sufficient,
neither taking from their honour nor reaching out for more;
and as for those who had power and were admired for their wealth,
for these too I took thought that they should suffer nothing unseemly.
I stood casting my strong shield about both,
and allowed neither to win an unjust victory.
The people would best follow its leaders thus,

if it were neither too much relaxed nor constrained by force.
For surfeit breeds insolence, whenever great prosperity follows
upon men whose minds are not sound.
Those who came for plunder had abundant hope,
and each of them supposed he would find great wealth,
and that I, though speaking smoothly, would reveal a harsh purpose.
Vain were their imaginings then; and now, angry with me,
they all look askance at me, as at an enemy.
Yet without cause; for what I said, with the gods I accomplished,
and the rest I did not work in vain, nor does it please me
to do anything by the violence of tyranny, nor that the noble
should have an equal share with the base of the rich land of the fatherland.
But I—of the things for which I gathered the people together,
which of them did I cease from before I had achieved?

To this, in the court of Time, might bear me witness
the greatest mother of the Olympian gods,
the best, the black Earth, from whom I once
tore up the boundary-stones fixed in many places;
before enslaved, she is now free.
And to Athens, their god-built fatherland, I brought back
many who had been sold, one unjustly,
another justly, and those who through forced necessity
had fled, no longer speaking the Attic tongue,
as men who had wandered far and wide;
and those who here at home endured a shameful slavery,
trembling at their masters' moods,
I set free. These things by the power of law,
fitting together force and justice,
I wrought, and carried through as I had promised.
Ordinances alike for the base and the noble,

fitting a straight justice to each man,
I wrote. Had another taken the goad as I,
a man ill-counseled and greedy of gain,
he would not have restrained the people. For had I been willing
to do what then pleased the opposing side,
and again whatever the others devised for them,
this city would have been bereft of many men.
For these reasons, drawing strength from every side,
I turned about like a wolf among many hounds.
If I must openly reproach the people,
what they now have they never could have seen,
even in their dreams.
And those who are greater and stronger in power
would praise me and make me their friend.
For if any other, he says, had gained this honour,
he would not have restrained the people, nor ceased

until he had stirred up the milk and taken out the cream.
But I stood, as it were in the no-man's-land between them,
a boundary-stone.
Alas, Leipsydrion, betrayer of comrades,
what manner of men you destroyed, good fighters
and of noble birth,
who then showed of what fathers they were sprung.
Pour for Cedon too, servant, and do not forget,
if one must pour wine for good men.

True RESIGNATION.
By Mr. H****
WHEN Colin's good dame, who long held him a tug,
And defeated his hopes by the help of the jug,
Had taken too freely the cheeruping cup,
And repeated the dose till it laid her quite up;
Colin sent for the doctor: with sorrowful face
He gave him his fee, and he told him her case.
Quoth Galen, I'll do what I can for your wife;
But indeed she's so bad, that I fear, for her life.
In counsel there's safety — e'en send for another;
For if she shou'd die, folks will make a strange pother,
And say that I lost her for want of good skill —
Or of better advice — or, in short, what they will.
Says Colin, your judgment there's none can dispute;
And if physic can cure her — I know yours will do't.

Nature's chief spring had broke, and all been lost.
Nor less destructive would this license prove,
Tho' thy breast flam'd with universal love.
In vain were thy benevolence of soul;
Soon would thy folly disconcert the whole.
No rains, or snows, should discompose the air;
But flow'rs and sun-shine drain the weary year:
No clouds should sully the clear face of day;
No tempests rise, — to blow a plague away.
Mercy should reign untir'd, unstain'd with blood;
Spare the frail guilty, — to eat up the good:
In their defence, rise, sacred Justice, rise!
Awake the thunder sleeping in the skies,
Sink a corrupted city in a minute:
— Wo! to the righteous ten who may be in it.
Pick out the bad, and sweep them all away!

The POET's IMPORTANCE.

Why, when Life's tedious March was almost o'er,
Was I brought back, to suffer on the Shore?
My cruel Father, worse than Death destroys,
Death is a Good, when Life's bereft of Joys.
Cease my lov'd Lord, the fair Florella cry'd,
Wou'd I had ne'er been born, or born, that Moment dy'd.
All things to your kind Family I owe,
And in return, Curses alone bestow:
I'll go where you shall ne'er behold me more,
And with my Absence, former Peace restore.
Peace without thee! the doting Youth reply'd,
No Griefs will all my Days and Nights devide:
Dispair and Sorrows, all my restless Hours betide.
Since from what my Soul desires I'm debarr'd,
Forgive my earnest Suit, nor think it hard:
I beg you ne'er will yield to a new Lovers Charms,

Those eyes no longer can divine

What pleases now, or grieves my mind,
What makes me sad, or gay,
It is not in thy power to give,
Nor canst thou take away:
Each pleasant spot without thee charms,
The wood, the mead, the hill;
And scenes of dullness, even with thee,
Are scenes of dullness still.
Judge, if I speak with tongue sincere;
Thou still art wond'rous fair;
Great are the beauties of thy form,
But not beyond compare:
And, let not truth offend thine ear,

WITHOUT preamble, to my friend,
These hasty lines I'm bid to send,
Or give, if I am able;
I dare not hesitate to say,
Tho' I have trembled all the day —
It looks so like a fable.
Last night's adventure is my theme,

Must make you own the matter such,

The moon did shine serenely bright,

"Wilt thou? —

I, who with more than manly strength have bore
The various ills impos'd by cruel Fate,
Sustain the firmness of my soul no more,
But sink beneath the weight:
Just Heaven (I cry'd) from Memory's earliest day
No comfort has thy wretched suppliant known,
Misfortune still with unrelenting sway
Has claim'd me for her own.
But O — in pity to my grief, restore
This only source of bliss; I ask — I ask no more —
Vain hope — th' irrevocable doom is past,
Ev'n now she looks — she sighs her last —
Vainly I strive to stay her fleeting breath,

TO THE RIGHT HONOURABLE THE EARL OF CHESTERFIELD. ON HIS LATE RECOVERY FROM A DANGEROUS ILLNESS.
BY THE REV. WALTER HARTE.
AT length, in pity to a nation's prayer,
Thou liv'st, O STANHOPE, Providence's care:
"Life's sun, we read, when heaven a respite lends,
" Ten degrees back against the shade descends. "
By wisdom purify'd, by age inspir'd;
For twice nine years in Greenwich groves retir'd;
Rapt like Elijah in the aërial car,
Thou wisely mark'st this busy world from far:
Where Avarice and Ambition vainly run,
This to undo, and that to be undone. —
Considerate truths are now thy favourite themes;
Age may see visions, tho' our youth dream'd dreams:
Hail truly wise, and good! O happier thou
Than if state diadems had grac'd thy brow!

Lallet.
Ah what are Flowers or Spring to me:
Oh good! how fair my LAD would lay!
How loose we lean'd the livelong Day!
How wont I with his Bosom play!
Her dainty CHEEK, with that same Word,
From off the Green she pertly rear'd.
But as gan think what she had done,
Poor HEART down flapped it agen.
The dabling DEW fell all emong,
Her buding Breasts so fair and young;
Her buding Breasts, that bloomie grew,
Soft shrinked at the dabling DEW.
At lenth, howe're, the tender Twey
Won her to rise from off the LEA.
Quoth Cubbin, Prethee to my COTT,

That helps himself as timely as he can,
When able. But if there is an Hereafter,
And that there is, Conscience, uninfluenc'd
And suffer'd to speak out, tells ev'ry Man;
Then must it be an awful Thing to die:
More horrid yet, to die by one's own Hand.
Self-Murther! name it not: Our Island's Shame!
That makes her the Reproach of neighbouring States.
Shall Nature, swerving from her earliest Dictate
Self-Preservation, fall by her own Act?
Forbid it Heav'n! Let not upon Disgust
The shameless Hand be foully crimson'd o'er
With Blood of its own Lord. Dreadful Attempt!
Just reeking from Self-slaughter, in a Rage
To rush into the Presence of our Judge!
As if we challeng'd him to do his worst,

Thus fools and bravoes kindred pranks pursue;
As savage quite, and oft as fatal too.
Happy the man that foils an envious elf,
Using the darts of spleen to serve himself.
As when by turns the strolling Swine engage
The utmost efforts of the bully's rage,
Whose nibbling warfare on the grunter's side
Is welcome pleasure to his bristly hide;
Gently he stoops, or lays himself along,
Endures the insults of the gabbling throng,
That march exulting round his fallen head,
As human victors trample on their dead.
Still TWILIGHT, welcome! Rest, how sweet art thou!
Now eve o'erhangs the western cloud's thick brow;
The far-stretch'd curtain of retiring light,
With fiery treasures fraught, that on the sight

The trembling hopes, the anxious fears,
The pleasing pains which love inspires,
Each trouble past the bliss indears,
And helps to fan the guiltless fires.
Long as the hand of this machine
Marks, as they pass, the fleeting hours;
As long as life itself is mine,
Engaging wit and beauty yours:
This well-wrought heart shall e'er retain
The name to love and friendship dear;
While in my own your charms remain
In glowing colours painted there.
TO THE SAME, WITH SHENSTONE'S WORKS, AFTER HAVING VISITED THE LEASOWES TOGETHER.
BY THE SAME.
TO speed the sad moments away,
Which by absence seem tedious and slow,

I'm asham'd to repeat what he said in the Sequel,
Aspersions so cruel as nothing can equal!
I declare I am shock'd such a Fellow should vex,
And spread all these Lyes of the innocent Sex,
For whom, while I live, I will make Protestation
I've the highest Esteem and profound Veneration;
I never so strange an Opinion will harbour,
That they buy all the Hair they have got of a Barber:
Nor ever believe that such beautiful Creatures

One Thing tho' I wonder at much, I confess, is
Th'Appearance they make in their different Dresses,
For indeed they look very much like Apparitions
When they come in the Morning to hear the Musicians,
And some I am apt to mistake, at first Sight,
For the Mothers of those I have seen over Night;

I would not thus have barter'd ease for care,
Spight of the keys that move our fear and hope,
I ne'er would quit such penance to be Pope.
Let him who Rome's stern tyrant stoop'd to praise,
The tuneful chanter of sweet georgic lays,
Let Maro boast of streams that Nature pours
To lave proud villas on Italia's shores;
Superior far the streams that court my song,
Superior far the shores they wind along:
Blest shores! the dwelling of that sacred power
Who rules each joyful, and each glorious hour,
Queen of whate'er the good or great desire,
The patriot's eloquence, the hero's fire,
Shrin'd in each breast, and near the tyrant's sword
Invok'd in whispers, and in sighs ador'd,
Immortal Liberty, whose generous mind

Would dread thy Praise, and shun the dubious Strife.
Be it thy Choice, when Summer-Heats annoy,
To sit beneath her leafy Canopy,
Quaffing rich Liquids: Oh! how sweet t' enjoy,
At once her Fruits, and hospitable Shade!
But how with equal Numbers shall we match
The Musk's surpassing Worth! that earliest gives
Sure hopes of racy Wine, and in its Youth,
Its tender Nonage, loads the spreading Boughs
With large and juicy Off-spring, that defies
The Vernal Nippings, and cold Syderal Blasts!
Yet let her to the Read-streak yield, that once
Was of the Sylvan Kind, unciviliz'd,
Of no Regard, 'till Scudamore's skilful Hand
Improv'd her, and by courtly Discipline
Taught her the savage Nature to forget:

And when it came, borne to our peaceful grave
By the plain villager; what tho' no tomb
Of sculptur'd marble call'd the passing eye
To read our story, yet the cottage tear
Should on our ashes fall, and the good heart
O'erflow sincerely for a neighbour lost:
Upon our bier the virgin troop would hang
Fresh-woven chaplets of the sweetest flowers:
Green turf should deck our grave; and every year
In spring-time would some friendly hand with care
Bind the fresh briar around, to guard the place
From the rude insult of the careless step;
And faithful Memory to late time record,
We were the happiest pair of human kind.

A TALE.

That Europe ripens, and that Asia hides.

Nor thankless he; for to the god he rear'd
