THE WISH.
SHOULD I e'er become parson (for so I'm inclin'd)
May I get a snug benefice pat to my mind,
Large enough to allow of a wife at my table,
A cow in my yard, and a nag in my stable.
May my flock n'er embroil me in quarrels and strife,
In good humour I'd live all the days of my life,
And die before tir'd of myself or my wife.
With a friend or two near me of equal degree,

And leave me life to plain, as I do now.
Abdallah.
Alas, my son, I doubt not of thy prowess,
It is thy fondness which I fear; that weakness,
Which only brave men know; and while it sinks
Their spirit as a vain presumptuous man,
Exalts it to the softness of a seraph.
Nouradin.
Were but my life, my happiness, at stake,
Well might'st thou doubt the weakness of my virtue,
Against Amana's charms — But where her safety
Becomes the question, I can turn a stoic;
Scarcely indulge my ravished eyes to gaze,
Or raptured hand to feast upon her touch,
'Till I restore her to her father's arms,
Abdallah.

Yet is the sweet retirement ours.
For here, when as the pallid moon
"Riding near her highest noon,"
Edging the clouds with silver white,
Darts thro' these shades a checquer'd light,
Here, when we cease our airy sport,
We range our bands and fix our court.
My royal throne, exalted high,
Unseen by feeble, mortal eye,
Tho' spangled with ten thousand dews,
Tho' colour'd with ten thousand hues,
(Approach not with unhallow'd hands)
Beneath yon tall Laburnum stands.
Then enter here with guiltless mind,
Spurn each vile passion far behind.
Hence Envy with her pining train,

May the divine Waters be auspicious to us for our succour, auspicious for us to drink; may they flow about us bringing well-being and ease.
O Waters, fill me full of healing medicine, a shelter for my body; and may I long behold the sun.
Soma declared to me that within the Waters are all remedies, and Agni who brings well-being to all.
Ruling over precious things, dwelling among the peoples — from the Waters I beg healing medicine.
The mothers — kinswomen who minister at the sacrifice — travel along their paths, mingling the milk with honey.
Those yonder that are near the sun, and those with whom the sun moves together — may they speed our sacrifice.
I call upon the divine Waters where our cows drink; an oblation is to be made to the rivers.
Within the Waters is immortality, within the Waters is medicine; and in the praises of the Waters, O horses, you become vigorous steeds.

He whom the three — gods, men, and all cattle — follow in their going: may the divine mind speak on our behalf for him; may good guidance lead us; may we not fall prey to the enemy.
Splendorous art thou among the gods, splendorous among the plants. Now make splendorous the one upon whom, O Aśvattha, thou dost climb.
The Aśvattha has ascended over him who is king of the human folk. Like Indra he smites down foes; may the kingship not be dislodged from him.
Āroha by name thou art; thou hast arisen with might. May this man carry thee, O Aśvattha, crusher of rivals.
Thou art king of all beings, the bull, the lord of plants. O Aśvattha, scatter our rivals asunder in all directions.
Looking upon one another they came for immortality, pure ones being born forth from their wombs. Making auspicious augury, smell this one here; place this hero among heroes.

That which is born from the north, the madhugha plant, born from the madhugha — in it I know the remedy. My tongue is full of sweetness.
Sweet is your leaf, O plant, sweet your horns and your blossom. Sweet was the mountain from which you were born, O herb.
You are the embryo of the plants, and you were the embryo of the waters. Moreover, you are the brother of Soma — O madhugha, promote my speech.
For good fortune I have grasped the name of the madhugha plant as one grasps a father's name — may it make me brilliant as gold, beloved of men.
Make me dear among the gods, make me dear among kings. Make me dear in the sight of all who look — both the Śūdra and the Ārya.
Be pleased with the udder, be pleased with the heart, be pleased with the mouth and the tongue. Be pleased, O cow swollen full with milk.

This Agni has bewildered all the thoughts that are in your hearts; he blows you away from your dwelling, he blows you forth from every side.
O Indra, confound their minds — draw their very intent hither; with the rushing blast of Agni and of Wind scatter them in all directions and destroy them.
Let their intentions scatter hence, and let their minds be bewildered; and whatever is today within their hearts — that, strike out and expel from them utterly.
Seizing their minds in utter bewilderment, O Apvā, go forth and grasp their limbs; advance, burn them inwardly with grief in their hearts, pierce our foes — those enemies fit to be seized — with darkness.
That army yonder of our adversaries, O Maruts, which advances against us contending with its might — hide it away with darkness and by the hostile rite, so that not one of them may know another.

Soma, the demon-slayer [sharp, sharp-horned, the seer of seers, the poet most poetic — let him thrust away the evil-sayer, overwhelm hostility; back with the counter-stroke: upon the one who works harm, harm we hurl back].
Varuṇa, the demon-slayer [sharp, sharp-horned, the seer of seers, the poet most poetic — let him thrust away the evil-sayer, overwhelm hostility; back with the counter-stroke: upon the one who works harm, harm we hurl back].
Vāyu, the demon-slayer [sharp, sharp-horned, the seer of seers, the poet most poetic — let him thrust away the evil-sayer, overwhelm hostility; back with the counter-stroke: upon the one who works harm, harm we hurl back].
Tvaṣṭā, the demon-slayer [sharp, sharp-horned, the seer of seers, the poet most poetic — let him thrust away the evil-sayer, overwhelm hostility; back with the counter-stroke: upon the one who works harm, harm we hurl back].

Agni, united with the bodies of the waters, who became the lord of the plants — may Jātavedas, the All-knower, win rain for us, the breath of life, the immortal drink, from heaven, for our offspring.
Let lightning flash in every direction; let the winds blow from all quarters. Let the clouds, set in motion by the Maruts, rain down upon the earth.
Prajāpati, stirring up the waters from the primordial flood, from the ocean, agitates the sea. Let the seed of the virile horse swell forth; come hither, our father, the mighty Asura, pouring down the waters with this thunder.
Let the gurgling whirlpools of the waters breathe; send down the waters below. Let the frogs with their speckled arms speak out along the pools.
Having lain dormant for a year, like Brāhmaṇas who observe their vow, the frogs have spoken forth, quickened into voice by Parjanya.

He whose heat poured forth from thy body, dripping gold, pure, following their own nature — here thou dost hold the immortal names; the robes, O master, are set in motion for us.
When these have proclaimed the ancient foremost thing, standing seat by seat on that which ages not — the Sage, as the two Mothers of vitality lick him, has measured the kinsman-bride's form as counterpart.
That great and broad ruling power — the Sage has fashioned it with his wisdom, O Yama, in reverence; when the converging ones press toward the earth, then the great wheel of obstruction has grown.
The seven sages have fashioned the seven bounds; towards one of them the sinful one has gone; yet thou who art immortal in breath, encompassed, advancing, O Asura, attained, goest along by thine own power.

Those who plunge headlong into rivers, clinging together like maidens — of those dog-companied ones, Indra has cut off the head.
Those who wade into fords, hissing like inviolable cows — of those dog-companied ones, Indra has cut off the head.
Those who rise up out of the ocean, uttering loud cries, chattering and clamorous — of those dog-companied ones, Indra has cut off the head.
Those who go from person to person desiring many by the myriad — of those dog-companied ones, Indra has cut off the head.
Agni is long-lived; long-lived is he together with the forest-trees. May he make me long-lived and make this one long-lived.
Vāyu is long-lived; long-lived is he together with the mid-air. May he make me long-lived and make this one long-lived.
Sūrya is long-lived; long-lived is he together with the sky. May he make me long-lived and make this one long-lived.

The Brāhmaṇa was his mouth; the Rājanya became his arms; that which is his middle is the Vaiśya; from his feet the Śūdra was born.
Virāj first came into being; from Virāj the Puruṣa arose; having been born he spread beyond, backward across the earth and also forward.
When the gods performed the sacrifice with the Puruṣa as the oblation, spring was its clarified butter, summer its firewood, autumn its oblation.
They sprinkled with the rains that sacrifice, that Puruṣa born in the beginning; with him the gods sacrificed — the Sādhyas and the Vasus.
From him horses were born, and all those that have teeth on both jaws; from him cattle were born, and from him goats and sheep were born.
From that sacrifice offered entire, the Ṛc verses and the Sāman chants were born; the meters were born from it; the Yajus was born from it.

This udumbara amulet, heroic, is bound on for the hero. May it make our acquisition sweet and honeyed, and may it bestow upon us wealth with all its heroes.
May we attain the favour of Bhaga the king, whom human beings invoke in many ways. He who acts in accordance with dharma wins Bhaga as his own — may He make us fortunate among the people.
Awakening to the east, may we behold the divine Dawn shining forth. The bright one facing toward us, bringing Bhaga together with wealth — may Aditi come to us bearing good fortune.
May Bhaga today, at dawn, bestow upon us favour and lead us here along the path of the gods. May auspicious benevolence come toward us; and then may our kindling-fire glow bright with Bhaga.
By Bhaga's impulsion, splendid in lustre, may I speak a speech directed by Sarasvatī, honeyed. May what is given by Bhaga come to me in abundance, so that radiant with lustre I may speak in the assembly.

The sprinkling-water that fell around the sacred grass, south of the altar, charged with vital power — the vaśā-cow lowed above it in full presence; her marrow became her armor-garment.
Homage to your greatness and to your eye, O Vaśā and Ṛṣabha — this I do with the mind. Go together to the gods by auspicious paths; harm us not with divine wrath.
The bull mounted the vaśā-cow as she stood upon the threads of fate. Who today knows that embryo — in what manner he has disposed it?
One encompassed form entire; one is called King by name; one is lord of form, its very form; one is the form of those who act aright.
Prajāpati, Parameṣṭhin, Mṛtyu, Viśvānara, and Svarga — from this sacrifice, from this vaśā, were they born.
In whose house the vaśā were received as an oblation fashioned by the gods — the treasure to be sought of her is like a daughter's to her husband.

O divine Añjana, O Traikakuda, protect me on all sides. Neither the external herbs nor the mountain ones surpass you.
He released the strong middle portion — the destroyer of demons, the disperser of disease. Driving away all diseases, destroying them, the overpowering one expelled them from here.
Much falsehood, O King Varuṇa, has a man spoken. From that, O you of a thousand powers, free us from transgression on every side.
What we have said — \"O inviolable waters,\" \"O Varuṇa\" — from that, O you of a thousand powers, free us from transgression on every side.
May Mitra and Varuṇa follow after you, O Añjana. Having followed you far, may it grow again for enjoyment.
As one debt is discharged by another debt, carry the sorcery back to the house of its maker. O collyrium, O evil-hearted one of the eye-spell, shatter even the ribs.

The divine waters are foremost among the healing herbs. They have driven out the sin-laden yakṣma from your limb by limb.
I address the spreading plants, the clumping ones, the single-stemmed, the creeping herbs. I call you — the filamentous, the jointed, those with spreading branches — those plants that belong to all the gods, the potent, the life-sustaining for man.
By that power of yours, O herbs, which overpowers, by the virile force and strength that is in you — with that, release this man from this yakṣma disease.
I invoke Jīvalā, Naghāriṣā, the living herb, and Arundhatī the uplifting, the flowering one, the honey-sweet one.
May the wise, the knowing ones come here at my word, so that we may carry this man across, beyond misfortune.
The food of Agni, the embryo of the waters — those that grow anew as punarṇavās: may those steadfast, thousand-named healing plants be gathered and brought here.

You are the Low One and you are the Upturned One; in your mouth are Growth and Abundant-Growth. To those two of yours we are subject; to those two be our bow; by those two be gracious to us, speak over us, breathe upon us. As a mother to a son, as a father to a son — this one here am I; release him not, O Seizer; lead this man forth, freed from the bonds of possession.
You are Rohiṇī and you are Surohiṇī; in your mouth are Food and the Eating-of-Food. To those two of yours we are subject; to those two be our bow; by those two be gracious to us, speak over us, breathe upon us. As a mother to a son, as a father to a son — this one here am I; release him not, O Seizer; lead this man forth, freed from the bonds of possession.
You are Sarā and you are Sarasvatī; in your mouth are Sacred-Power and Lordly-Might. To those two of yours we are subject; to those two be our bow; by those two be gracious to us, speak over us, breathe upon us. As a mother to a son, as a father to a son — this one here am I; release him not, O Seizer; lead this man forth, freed from the bonds of possession.

Those auspicious, gracious forms of thine, O Kāma, by which that which one chooses comes to be true — with those enter into us fully; drive the evil thoughts elsewhere away.
Those two limb-marks which your mother wiped off you at birth — the pativedanau auspices — let not the Evil-Named one covet them there, neither the aliṃśa nor the vatsapa.
The palāla, the anupalāla, the śarkuṇa, the koka, the malimruca, the palījaka, the āśleṣa, the vavrivāsasa, the ṛkṣagrīva, the pramīlina — we smite them away from her pudenda.
Let him not press close, let him not creep up against her thighs, let him not glide between them. I prepare for her this remedy, the baja-plant, banisher of the Evil-Named.
Both the Evil-Named and the Fair-Named desire a woman who is enclosed; we smite away the arāya — the Fair-Named desires what belongs to women.

These indeed — both the beloved and the unloved — are the officiating priests who lead one to the heavenly world, namely the guests (atithis).
When he summons the doorkeeper and causes him to be called, and when he responds and causes the response to be heard in return.
When the servers enter the lodging-places, they are in truth the cup-bearing adhvaryus for those guests — not a single one of them is without the function of an hotṛ.
What one brings forth in the morning — that is verily the morning pressing (prātaḥsavana).
What one brings forth at midday — that is verily the midday pressing (mādhyaṃdina savana).
What one brings forth in the evening — that is verily the third pressing (tṛtīya savana).
When the lord of the guests, having served the guests all round, asks leave of his seat — he thereby approaches the avabhṛtha (the concluding ablution of the sacrifice).

She on whom the gathering waters flow in their rounds, pouring day and night without ceasing — may that Earth, abundant-streamed, milk nourishment for us, and also sprinkle us with vital radiance.
She whom the gods guard, ever-wakeful, at all times, the Earth, the wide one, without negligence — may she milk sweet, dear nourishment for us, and also sprinkle us with vital radiance.
She who was the primordial waters above the ocean; whom the wise have traced through their visionary powers; she whose heart, in the highest sky, is wrapped in truth, the immortal essence of Earth — may that Earth place brilliance and strength in my realm for me.
She whom the two Aśvins measured out, upon whom Viṣṇu strode; she whom Indra, lord of power, made enemy-free for himself — may that Earth release milk for us as a mother for her son.

These living ones have turned away from the dead; auspicious has been our invocation of the gods today. We have gone forward to dance and to laugh; endowed with good heroes, may we speak in the assembly.
I set this barrier for the living; let no other cross over to this purpose of theirs. May they, living long, traverse many autumns, setting Death aside as if by a mountain.
Just as the days come in succession, just as the seasons go together with the seasons, just as the earlier does not abandon the later — so, O Tvaṣṭṛ, arrange the life-spans of these.
Mount up in life, choosing old age, striving forward in succession wherever you go. May Tvaṣṭṛ of good birth, in harmony with them, lead all their life-span onward to full living.
The stony river flows — take hold, be vigorous, cross over, O friends. Leave behind here those who were of ill will; free from disease, may we rise above to the prizes.

And behold — the rays carry yonder god Jātavedas, the sun, for all the world to see.
Away they go like thieves, as the stars depart through the nights, before the Sun, the all-seeing.
His beams, his rays, have become visible spreading among the peoples, blazing like fires.
Swift, visible to all, maker of light, O Sun — you illuminate all things, shining brilliantly.
Facing the host of gods, facing the races of men, you rise; facing all things you rise to be seen in the sky.
With that purifying eye, O Varuṇa, you behold the bustling peoples moving about.
You traverse the broad sky and the wide atmosphere, measuring out the day with the nights, beholding all created beings, O Sun.
The seven tawny mares carry you on your chariot, O divine Sun — you who have flames for hair, you the far-seeing.

When thou hast matured him, O Jātavedas, then hand him over to the Fathers all around. When this one goes to the guidance of the breath, then he shall become subject to the will of the gods.
Let the eye go to the sun, the breath to the wind; go to heaven and to the earth according to the sacred law. Or go to the waters, if that is thy destiny — take thy stand in the plants with thy bodily parts.
O unborn portion of ascetic heat, blaze upon him; let your flame scorch him, let your fire-ray sear him. O Jātavedas, with those gracious forms of yours, carry him to the world of the well-doers.
Those swift, fierce forms of yours, O Jātavedas, that rush swirling around — let them gather and follow the goat as it goes; then with those other, most benign forms, render him well-cooked and fit.

Whatever vigor is within your hearts, whatever intention has entered your minds — that I attune with oblation and clarified butter; may your delight, O kinsmen, rest in me.
Come to my thought, all of you, at the moment of departure and departure, as to the invocation of Indra and Agni. May Bṛhaspati yoke you to me; be of one mind and follow my speech.
I seize your minds with my mind; come to my thought with your thoughts. I make your hearts subject to my will; come following in my path, come to me.
Let your eye come to me, let your breath come to me; may the Dhātṛ make your path follow my footstep. Whether your elders or your young ones — come, following in my path, come with those who follow.
You were born above the gods; you are placed as a friend of Soma. As such, be gracious for the in-breath, the out-breath, and the sight of this one.

To every being here, and to every one who sees — to all of them I am indeed glorious.
Push away, uncover whatever this is or is not; make the sight blind and impaired — do this to the eyes.
Having made the golden limb, the plow-handle, and the cataract — gods, take that away.
May my mind be possessed of sight, may my heart be possessed of sight; may my consciousness be possessed of sight, may my eye be possessed of sight — place sight in my two eyes.
Soma is king, and Savitā is king, Bhava is king, and the world is king; Śarva is king and Śarman is king — may those gods grant us shelter.
Bṛhaspati with the Ādityas, Bhaga together with Soma, the All-Gods, the wide atmosphere — may those gods grant us shelter.
Strike out the un-pierced one and also loosen the taut one; O All-Gods, O Maruts, do not direct your missile at us.

You are the one that points the way and the one that points it forth. [Prajāpati... may the students of sacred knowledge] come to me. Svāhā!
You are approval and you are the one who grants approval. [Prajāpati... may the students of sacred knowledge] come to me. Svāhā!
You are conquest and you are victory. [Prajāpati... may the students of sacred knowledge] come to me. Svāhā!
You are complete conquest and you are what is won by joining together. [Prajāpati... may the students of sacred knowledge] come to me. Svāhā!
Agni is the lord of the earth; may Soma protect you. We know you; know us. You are the overlord — make me the overlord of cattle, horses, men, students of sacred knowledge, of prosperity and the eating of food.
Vāyu is the lord of the atmosphere; [may Soma protect you. We know you; know us. You are the overlord — make me the overlord of cattle, horses, men, students of sacred knowledge, of prosperity and the eating] of food.

Cry out favourably to us, O owl, and lead away from here the one we hate. In the house of King Yama, your gaming with sand shall be your portion, and a mouse shall nibble it away.
Speak of the plentiful cow-pen, the calf-seeking cow, the cow not lost. Speak of two-footed beings to the crow; speak of four-footed beings to the dog.
May King Varuṇa give back to me again, may Indra give back again, may Bhaga give back again; may all the gods give back to me again life and the means of living.
Rise up, run forward toward us; do not stand gazing here. Having taken the radiance away from the rival wife, then you shall be together with us.
Rise up, run out; there is no descending for you here. I press toward you the wealth of that man yonder — follow it, O fair-toothed ones; the serpent has shed that.

It is a peculiar kind of wine; and it is neither sweet nor thick, but dry and
hard, and of extraordinary strength; and Aristophanes says that the Athenians did
not like it, for that the Athenian people did not like hard and sour poets,
nor hard Pramnian wines, which contract the eyebrows and the stomach; but they
prefer a fragrant wine, ripe, and flavoured like nectar. For Semus says
that there is in Icarus a rock called the Pramnian rock; and near it is a great
mountain, from which the Pramnian wine has its name, and some call it a medicinal
wine. Now Icarus used formerly to be called the Fishy Icarus, from the number of
fish around it; just as the Echinades had their name from the sea-urchins, and the
promontory Sepias from the number of cuttle-fish which are taken near it. And in

skin, promotes the secretions of the body, and is full of agreeable and wholesome
juice; but it is still more juicy when cooked. Its alterative qualities are
increased when it is eaten with mustard, but it is more digestible, and it
promotes the secretions more, when boiled.
Mnesitheus too says, "All the vegetables and fruits which are easily affected by
the action of fire, such as the cucumber, and the gourd, and the quince, and the
small quince, and everything else of the same sort, when they are eaten after
having been roasted, afford nutriment to the body, in no great quantity indeed,
but still such as is pleasant and promotes moisture. However all these vegetables
and fruits have a tendency to produce constipation, and they ought to be eaten
boiled rather than raw. But the Attic writers call the gourd by no other name but

The dish much loved by widows.
And Cratinus also speaks of the pinna in his Archilochi—
She indeed like pinnas and sea oysters.
And Philyllius, or Eunicus, or Aristophanes, in the Cities, says—
A little polypus, or a small cuttle-fish,
A crab, a crawfish, oysters, cockles,
Limpets and solens, mussels and pinnas;
Periwinkles too, from Mitylene take;
Let us have two sprats, and mullet, ling,
And conger-eel, and perch, and black fish.

like a trumpet.

was carried round, Leonidas said, Euthydemus the Athenian, my friends, in

Some sorrily-clad fishermen did seek
To catch a lamprey; men who love to haunt
The Bosporus's narrow strait, well stored
With fish for pickling fit. They cut their prey
In large square portions, and then plunge them deep
Into the briny tub: nor is the oxyrhyncus

And the flutes called lotus flutes are the same which are called
photinges by the Alexandrians; and they are made of the plant called the lotus;
and this is a wood which grows in Libya. But Juba says that the flute which is ma
e out of the leg bones of the kid is an invention of the Thebans; and Tryphon says

corn; the construction of one of which I will describe. For the wood, he caused
such a number of trees to be cut down on Mount Aetna as would have been sufficient
for sixty triremes, and when this was done he prepared nails, and planks for the
sides and for the inside, and wood for every other purpose that could be required,
some from Italy and some from Sicily. And for ropes he provided cordage from
Spain, and hemp, and pitch from the river Rhone; and he collected great quantities
of useful things from all quarters. And he collected also shipwrights and other
artisans. And having appointed Archias the Corinthian the superintendent of them
all, and the principal architect, he bade them labour at the construction with
zeal and earnestness, he himself also devoting his days to watching its progress.

By the whole flattering band,
And listen ye, and learn
How well-bred we all are.
For first of all a boy,
Another person's slave,
Attends us; and we are
Content with very little.
I have two well-made garments,
And always have one on;
I hie me to the forum,
And when I see a man,
A foolish man but rich,
I make my way to him,
And if he says a word
I praise his wit and laugh,
Delighted at his jests.

But Chrysippus says that there is a difference between a δοῦλος and οἰκέτης; and he draws the
distinction in the second book of his treatise on Similarity of Meaning, because
he says that those who have been emancipated are still δοῦλοι, but that the term οἰκέτης is
confined to those who are not discharged from servitude; for the οἰκέτης, says he is a δοῦλος, being actually at the time the property of a mast the

Etrurians, and was the only person unwounded in that naval battle; and that by he
will of Jupiter he appeared in the depths of the sea, and so became a sea deity,
but was seen by Jason alone. But Nicanor the Cyrenæan, in his Changes of Names,
says that Melicerta changed his name and assumed the name of Glaucus.
Alexander the Aetolian also mentions him in his poem entitled the Fisherman,
saying that he
First tasted grass,
(and then was immersed in the sea and drowned,)
The herb which in the islands of the blest,
When first the spring doth beam upon the earth,
The untill'd land shows to the genial sun.
And the sun gives it to his weary steeds,
A most refreshing food, raised in the shade.
So that they come in vigour back renew'd
Unto their daily task, and no fatigue
Or pain can stop their course.

But Nausicrates, the comic poet, praises the mullets from Aexona, in his
Captains of Ships, saying—
Those yellow fleshed fish, which the high wave
That beats Aexona brings towards the shore,
The best of fish; with which we venerate
The light-bestowing daughter of great Jove;
When sailors offer gifts of feasts to heaven.
B. You mean the mullet.
There is, too, the tænia; and this is mentioned by Epicharmus:—
The most belovèd tænia, which are thin,
But highly flavour'd, and need little fire.
And Mithæcus, in his Cookery Book, says— Having taken out the
entrails of the tænia, and cut off its head, and washed it, and having cut it
into slices, sprinkle over it cheese and oil. But this fish is found in
the greatest number and in the finest condition off Canopus, which is near

digestible, apt to bind the bowels, especially when it is broiled; but when it is
fried in a frying-pan, then it is heavy and indigestible; and, as a general rule,
the whole tribe of mullets has the property of causing secretions of blood. The

“Pharamond! Pharamond! we have fought with the sword.
“We have hurled the battle-axe with two blades; sweat ran from the brow of the warriors, and trickled down their arms. The eagles and birds with yellow feet uttered screams of joy; the crows swam in the blood of the dead; all ocean was but a wound. The virgins have long wept.
“Pharamond! Pharamond! we have fought with the sword.
“Our fathers fell in battle, all the vultures moaned at it: our fathers satiated them with carnage. Let us choose wives whose milk shall be blood, and shall fill with valour the hearts of our sons. Pharamond, the song of the bard is ended, the hours of life are passing away; we will smile when we must die.
“O virgin, whom I admire, and whom thy husband will adore, Brunehilda, more brilliant, more radiant than the ethereal lamp, the light of precious stones is dimmed by the splendour of thy countenance; thou art another Venus, and thy dowry is the empire of beauty! Among the Nereids who swim in the seas of Iberia, in the springs of the ocean, there is none who can call herself thy equal; none of the Napææ are more beautiful, and the river-nymphs bow down their heads before thee. The whiteness of milk and the brightest red are the colours of thy complexion; lilies and roses, purple woven with gold, present nothing comparable to it. Sapphires, diamonds, crystals, emeralds, and jasper are vanquished; Spain has produced a new pearl.”

“I have seen women carried into slavery, with bound hands and flowing hair; one walked barefooted in the blood of her husband, the other passed over the corpse of her brother. Each one has had cause for tears, and I, I have wept for all. I have wept for my relations who have died, and I must weep for those who remain alive. When my tears cease to flow, when my sighs are hushed, my sorrow is not silent. When the wind murmurs, I listen if it brings me any news; but no shadow of my relations presents itself to me. A whole world divides me from what I love most. Where are they? I ask it of the wind that whistles; I ask it of the clouds that float by: I wish some bird would come and tell me of them. Ah! if I was not withheld by the sacred walls of this convent, they would see me arrive at the moment when they least expected me. I would set out in bad weather; I would sail joyfully through the tempest. The sailors might tremble, but I should have no fear. If the vessel split, I would fasten myself to a plank, and continue my voyage; and if I could seize no fragment, I would swim to them.”

pr. Prologue
I never wet my lips at the nag's spring,
nor do I remember dreaming on two-peaked Parnassus,
that I should step forth all at once a poet so.
The Heliconian Muses and pale Pirene
I leave to those whose portraits the clinging
ivy licks: I myself, half a rustic outsider,
bring my own song to the holy rites of the bards.
Who taught the parrot his "good morning,"
and schooled the magpie to attempt our speech?
That master of skill, that lavisher of talent,
the belly, an artist at chasing voices once denied;
for let the hope of treacherous coin glitter,
and you would believe that raven-poets and magpie-poetesses

1. PREFACE. Receive these things in your minds, and turn your glad thoughts hither, both excellent in spirit, both distinguished in surpassing arms; both flourishing, a race unconquerable in war. And you first — for that you go over the deep under greater auspices is clear faith — than whom no other was more just in piety, nor greater in war and arms; and you, and your boy, the second hope of great Rome, the flower of men of old and the valour of heroes, my greatest care, recalling his grandsire in name, his parent in spirit and in hand. Not unbidden do I sing. To each his own undertakings will bring toil and fortune: for me it is right to take up what is commanded.
2. THE WEDDING FEAST. The awaited day was at hand, and for the worthy wedding the mothers and the men, the young before the faces of their parents, gather, and they recline on the spread purple. The servants give water for the hands and load with baskets the gifts of laboured Ceres, and bring the roasted flesh of fat game: a most long succession of courses. The kinds of birds and of beasts and the swift-following roe-deer are not absent there, nor sheep and the butting kids, and the sea-born kind, and the does and the fleeing stags: before the eyes and amid the hands are the mellow fruits. After hunger was banished and the desire of eating restrained, they set out great mixing-bowls and serve the wine of Bacchus. They sing sacred songs, beat out the dances, and recite poems. And the Thracian priest too, in his long robe, accompanies with measures the seven distinct notes of the voice; while from another quarter the flute gives its double-mouthed song. There is one rest from labours for all, and all, leaving the tables, rise up: through the glad thresholds, thronging, they run to and fro and change their turns — the people and the elders, the matrons, the boys — and roll their voices through the spacious halls: the lamps hang from the gilded ceilings.

3. DESCRIPTION OF THE BRIDE COMING FORTH. At last she comes forth, the most just care of Venus, now ripe for a husband, now marriageable in her full years, bearing a maiden's face and bearing, on whom a deep blush has set fire and run over her heated face, turning her intent eyes, and she burns men by being seen. Her all the youth, pouring out from houses and fields, and the throng of mothers, admire. The first traces of her foot were white, and she had given her hair to be spread to the winds. She wears garments embroidered with the woof of gold, the adornments of Argive Helen; and such as golden Venus is wont to appear to the heaven-dwellers, and how great, such was her aspect, such, glad, she bore herself toward her parents-in-law, and, raised high, she sat down on a lofty throne.

4. DESCRIPTION OF THE BRIDEGROOM COMING FORTH. But from another quarter the boy bore himself in through the lofty doors, marking his face with the unshorn down of earliest youth, his golden cloak embroidered with the needle, around which ran much Meliboean purple in a double maeander, and a tunic which his mother had woven with soft gold: in face and shoulders like a god, and with the light of youth. As, when Lucifer, bathed in the wave of Ocean, has lifted his sacred face to the sky: so he bore his face, so his eyes, and, frantic in his course, he hastens to the threshold. Love troubles him, and he fixes his looks upon the maiden; he tasted her kisses and, embracing, clung to her right hand.
5. THE OFFERING OF GIFTS. The boys advance, and together before the faces of the parents bear gifts: a mantle stiff with figures and gold, carrying gifts and talents of gold and of ivory, and a chair and a covering embroidered with saffron acanthus, vast silver for the tables, and a necklace of pearls for the neck, and a double crown of gems and gold. To her is given a handmaid and twin children at the breast; to him four young men and as many unwed maidens: for all, by custom, the hair is cut; on the top of the breast a flexible circle of twisted gold about the neck.

6. THE EPITHALAMIUM TO BOTH. Then the mothers, pouring out in eagerness, lead them to the threshold; but the chorus of equals, boys and unwed maidens, sport with unpolished verses and recite their songs: "O joined to a worthy man, most welcome bride, may you be happy, having known the first labours of Lucina and become a mother — take up the goblets of Maeonian Bacchus. Scatter the nuts, bridegroom; gird these altars with a fillet, you flower of men of old and valour of heroes: for you a wife is led, that with you, for such deserts, she may pass all her years and make you a parent by fair offspring. Fortunate both, if pious powers can avail anything, live happy." "Run," said the Parcae, harmonious, with the steadfast power of the fates, to their spindles.
7. THE ENTERING INTO THE CHAMBER. After they have come to the chamber, its roof hanging in pumice, at last they enjoy permitted converse. Coming together, they join right hands and lay themselves upon the couch. But Cytherea, with new arts, and Juno the bride's attendant, urge and counsel them to provoke unknown wars. He, when in soft embrace he cherishes her, and suddenly has received the wonted flame and the marriage-bed: "O maiden, a new face to me, most welcome bride, you have come at last, my only and late delight. O sweet wife, these things do not come to pass without the will of the gods: will you fight even against a love that pleases you?" Him, speaking such things, she, long since turned away, beholds, and hesitates in fear, and trembles that the weapon presses near, and, between hope and fear, pours forth these speeches from her mouth: "By you, by the parents who begot you such, O comely boy, this one night and no more, I pray, console my helplessness, and pity me as I entreat. We sink down: my tongue avails not, the wonted strength does not suffice my body, nor do voice or words follow." But he: "In vain you weave empty causes," and he hurries on all delays and looses her modesty.

8. The Consummation. After they had come together alone in the night through the darkness, and Venus herself had given the will, they attempt new battles. He raises himself up, eager; her, attempting much in vain, he seizes — her mouth and her face — and, ardent, he presses foot with foot, treacherous, making for the heights: the branch which lay hidden in his garment, ruddy with the blood-red berries of the danewort and with vermilion, his head bared and their feet entwined, a thing dreadful, shapeless, huge, from which the light has been taken away — he snatches it from his thigh and, ardent, presses upon her as she trembles. There is in a recess, where a narrow path leads, a fiery cleft, gleaming; the shadowed place breathes out a vapour. For none who is chaste is it lawful to set foot on that guilty threshold. Here is a dreadful cave: such a breath, pouring itself from its dark jaws, touches the nostrils with its odour. Hither the youth is borne by the known region of the ways, and, bending over, leaning with the topmost strength, he hurls his spear, with its knots and rough bark. It clung, and, driven home, drank deep the maiden's blood. The hollow caverns resounded and gave a groan. She, dying, draws the weapon with her hand; but the point, by the wound, settled the deeper, into the living flesh among the bones. Thrice raising herself and propped on her elbow she lifted herself, thrice she fell back upon the bed. He remains undismayed. There is no delay, no rest: fastened and clinging to his peg, he nowhere let go, and kept his eyes beneath the stars. He goes and comes back along the way again and again, and, the womb being shaken, he drives through her ribs and beats with his ivory comb. And now, well-nigh at the last lap, and wearied, they were drawing near the very end: then a frequent panting shakes his limbs and his dry mouth, the sweat flows everywhere in streams; he sinks down, bloodless, the fluid distils from the groin. — Be content, my Paulus, my Paulus, with the wanton page: to laugh, nothing beyond, is what I ask. But when you have read it, stand by me against those who, as Juvenal says, "feign to be Curii and live as Bacchanals," lest perchance they should judge my character from the poem. "Wanton is our page, our life is upright," as Martial says. But let them remember — learned as they are — that in the most upright man Pliny there was wantonness in his little poems and censoriousness in his conduct; that the little work of Sulpicia is wanton, while her brow was knit; that Apuleius was a philosopher in his life and a lover in his epigrams; that in the precepts of Cicero severity stands forth, while in the letters to Caerellia a wantonness lurks beneath; that Plato's Symposium contains little epyllia composed upon youths. For why should I speak of the Fescennines of Annianus, or of the books of Erotopaegnion of the most ancient poet Laevius? Why of Evenus, whom Menander called wise? Why of Menander himself? Why of all the comic poets, whose life is austere and their matter merry? Why even of Maro, called Parthenias for modesty's sake, who in the eighth book of the Aeneid, when he described the union of Venus and Vulcan, decently mingled in the "shameful-solemn"? And in the third book of the Georgics, on the males set among the herd, did he not veil an obscene meaning by an honourable transference of words? And if the severity of some men, dressed up, condemns anything in our jest, let it know that it was fetched from Vergil. So, whoever does not like this game of ours, let him not read it; or, when he has read it, let him forget it; or, not forgetting, let him pardon: for the tale is of a wedding, and, like it or not, these rites are not otherwise constituted.

praef. Preface. You too, whom no kinship joined to me, but the fame and the sacred bond of my dear homeland, and your devotion to books and your diligent care in teaching — I shall commemorate you, men renowned now that death has been met. It may chance that one day someone, wishing to be dutiful by my example, will so vindicate my own shade.
1. TIBERIUS VICTOR MINERVIUS, ORATOR. First to be named, pillar of Bordeaux, are you, Minervius, a second Quintilian of the rhetorical gown. By you as teacher there were once made illustrious Constantinople, Rome, and thereafter your native city — not indeed contending with the majesty of the other two, but more powerful in this name alone, that it is your homeland. Though Calagurris claim Fabius as ever its nursling, yet let the chair of Bordeaux be no lower for that. A thousand young men this man gave to the forum, twice a thousand he added to the senate's number and to the purple gowns; me too — but since the toga praetexta is much, I shall keep silent, and sing of you from yourself, not from my own honour. Whether one pleased to contend in panegyric books, you must be reckoned among the Panathenaics; or whether one liked to unroll the feigned disputes of the schools, Quintilian holds a doubtful palm. You had a torrent of fluent speech, which yet rolled gold, not also muddy filth. And that Demosthenic quality, which he called thrice first, so flourished in you that he himself would yield to you. Or shall I add the natural goods of the divine gift — how retentive of mind you were, so that you held things heard or read but once as if fixed, and there was one fidelity between your ears and books? We saw too once, in a long contest of the gaming-board, how you counted all the throws that had been made — at alternate turns, how many the cut-out steps pour forth through the hollow boxwood in their headlong roll — recounting through each several point with faithful recall what was given, what recalled through long delays. Your mind had no gall of malice; then your wit was much-salted, your tongue ready with kindly jests and without quarrel; your table neat, such as the censor's rule would not blame, nor Piso the Thrifty refuse to call his own; sometimes well-furnished for a birthday and a festal banquet, yet not so as to thin your slender means. Though wanting an heir, you, having completed twice six lustra, were wept by us as both father and young man. And now, whether anything survives after the last fates, you live still, remembering the age that has perished; or whether nothing survives, and the long repose has no perceptions, you have lived for yourself: us your fame delights.

2. LATINUS ALCIMUS ALETHIUS, RHETOR. Nor shall the descendants summon me, Alcimus, as guilty of impious silence, nor shall they bear me as less worthy, nor as having forgotten you, the minister of your memory — you whom this recent age sets forth, one man, against the men of old, glory of the forensic palm and of the Muses, a single model in letters, whether learned Greece cultivated them at Athens, or Rome cultivates them through Latium. Shall I speak of your character and the steadiness of your rule of life right to its term? That, famous for your praise, busied with letters, you fled all ambition? No one was graver or more courteous than you, or more liberal to the needy — granting safety, if the affair demanded the forum; with zeal for teaching, if the school. They shall live through all the memory of posterity whom you gave to sacred fame; and Julian you will give more to fame than the sceptres which he held for a short time. To Sallust your books will confer more than the consulship added. Of your character, of your dignity and eloquence, you gave the model to your sons. Forgive me, wounded by the homage of my pen: this is the fault of love for you, that, unable to bring forth things worthy, I do honour, injuriously diligent. Rest in peace, and repay the loss of your fallen body with glory.

3. LUCIOLUS, RHETOR. Recall, O mournful dirge, the rhetor Luciolus, my fellow-pupil and master and thereafter colleague — an eloquent and learned man, whether he composed his beginnings by the law of metres or loosened them into the measures of prose — whom Lachesis snatched from his father by a bitter death, leaving behind two children of each sex; whose heir, obscure, has by no means answered to his merits, though now your fame gives me aid. Gentle friend, good brother, most faithful husband, dutiful son, and father: one is sorry, since you were such. Courteous to your guests, never to cry out against your clients, never to speak harsh words to your servants — as you cultivated peaceful ways, so cultivate tranquil shades; and take from Ausonius this gift. Farewell, friend.

4. ATTIUS PATERA, THE ELDER, RHETOR. Although in age you have surpassed those named before, Patera, noble in eloquence, yet, because you flourished in the age nearest mine, and I, a young man, saw you old, you shall not lack the honour of a mournful dirge, O teacher of powerful rhetors. You, sprung of the Druid stock of the Baiocasses — if fame does not cheat belief — draw your consecrated race from the temple of Belenus, and thence are your names: yours, Patera; for so the Apollinarian mystics call their ministers. To your brother and father a name was given from Phoebus, and to your son from Delphi. No man in that time had so great learning, and so many turns and rounds of speaking: retentive, eloquent, of lucid fluency, endowed with melodious voice and refinement, modest in your wit, never smeared with gall, abstemious of wine and food, cheerful, chaste, handsome — even in old age, like the old age of an eagle or a horse.

5. ATTIUS TIRO DELPHIDIUS, RHETOR. Eloquent, learned, swift in tongue and wit, pleasant in jests, Delphidius — be woven into the tearful threnody of your father, as you followed close, his rival in praise. You, beginning almost from the very cradle, a noble poet of the god, bearing the garland of the Olympic crown, as a boy celebrated Jove; soon thereafter, swiftly, in the manner of a rushing sea, you bound metric epic, so that no book of song wove out an oration with equal law. Your eloquence, variously celebrated, shone bright at home and abroad: whether you cultivated the prefect of the praetorian cohort or the judges of the provinces, devoted to the protection of clients wounded in fame and safety. Happy, if you had remained in quiet letters, cultivating the work of the Muses, and no avenging impulse had armed the hatreds stirred up in great lawsuits, nor had you raised yourself in the restless palace of a tyrannical time. While you ever summon to yourself a remote hope, disdainful of what lay before you, and prefer the good to be your own rather than fortune's, you longed for very many things, ranging through all the formulas of dignities, and deserving more than you held. Whence, when a grave movement of charges followed, given over to your father's afflictions, soon thereafter a rhetor, and not persistent in teaching, you cheated the cares of fathers — having experienced less of evils, by the gift of god, in that you were snatched away in the midst of your age, and were not wounded by the error of a not-erring daughter and the punishment of a wife.

6. TO ALETHIUS MINERVIUS, THE SON, RHETOR. O flower of the young, glad hope of your father, a possession given to your homeland but not assured — rhetor Alethius: you, a teacher in your earliest years; at the time when, were you a grown man learning, it would be no shame, you, still wearing the boy's gown, were already compared to your father, and after Patera a teacher too. He increased the walls of proud Rome, renowned for fame and merits; greater than both, you, the glad joy of your homeland Bordeaux, ruling the bright standards of the cohort, had all the goods of fate, not without the bite of grievous envy: all things did precocious fortune give you and snatch away — both rhetoric, while still wanting the fruit of grown years, and a noble marriage with your father-in-law without your father's peace, and the riches of either house without an heir. As the solstitial grass is wont, shown forth and snatched away at once, in the bloom of youth you deserted the prayers of your own, adorned with goods not destined to abide. How truly, with fate-speaking utterance, the verse of Horace was spoken: “Nothing is in every part blessed.”

7. LEONTIUS, GRAMMARIAN, SURNAMED THE PLAYFUL. You who cultivate glad and merry ways, who love feast-days, jests, vows, and play, recall in the yearly threnody the name of Leontius, now that he has died. He, content to be called Lascivus (the Playful), never refused that name, unworthy of the uprightness of his life, because it was pleasing to friendly ears. He gained only so great a title in letters as is enough for a humble chair, that he might seem inserted into the number of the grammarians. You, ever the companion of my youth, though heaped with more years, even now grow warm again in my marrow, charming Leontius! And it gladdens me to celebrate with sad care the tearful song of a mindful complaint: a gift unwelcome to you, yet owed, in our verse.
8. TO THE GREEK GRAMMARIANS OF BORDEAUX. After these, shall I record first Romulus, or the Attic Muses of Corinthus, or of Spercheus, and likewise of his son Menestheus, the grammarians? Diligent was the zeal of all in teaching, slender the fruit and thin the discourse; but, because they taught in our age, they are to be commemorated. The third of these was not my master; the rest taught me in my first years, that I might not be ignorant of words or so without cultivation in speaking — because, I believe, the slower sense of my mind hindered, and the harmful error of boyish age did not drive me to Greek disciplines. May the light turf cover you, and the coverings of the tomb protect the hidden ashes, and the inscription of my voice render the last honour.

9. TO JUCUNDUS, GRAMMARIAN OF BORDEAUX, BROTHER OF LEONTIUS. You too, whom they say usurped the chair rashly and think did not deserve the name of grammarian, I shall yet summon by voice, simple, good, friendly comrade, Jucundus, the dearer for this very pursuit: because, though unequal, you loved so noble a name, you are to be commemorated among the deserving men.
10. TO THE LATIN GRAMMARIANS AND PHILOLOGISTS OF BORDEAUX — MACRINUS, SUCURO, CONCORDIUS, PHOEBICIUS; (and) to Ammonius and Anastasius, grammarian of Poitiers. Now, as the devout honour of a tearful duty suggests each to me, I shall set forth those who, though of humble stock, station, and merit, yet introduced the study of grammar to the untrained minds of Bordeaux. Let Macrinus be among these: to him at the start my boyhood was entrusted; and Sucuro, of freedman descent, sober and useful to the minds of boys; and you, Concordius, who, exiled from your homeland, exchanged your barren chair for another city. Nor shall I keep silent about the old man named Phoebicius, who, sacristan of Belenus, drew no aid from that; but yet, as was pleasing, sprung from the stock of the Druids of the Armorican race, obtained a chair at Bordeaux by his son's effort: let the series continue. Ammonius too I shall sing again — for it is devout to commemorate a grammarian of my homeland — who gave the first elements to untrained boys, slight in learning, of unquiet manners: accordingly, as was deserved, he had a slender fame. Compose, O Muse, a tearful melody for Anastasius too, and recall in a dirge the slender grammarian. Ambition transferred this man, born at Bordeaux, and gave him to the Pictones; poor there, cultivating a slender living and habit, he lost in old age his slight little glory, both of homeland and of chair; but yet our honour has commemorated him, lest the tomb cover alike his name and his bones.

11. TO HERCULANUS, SISTER'S SON, GRAMMARIAN OF BORDEAUX. Herculanus, who, set forth from my own bosom and school, gave your uncle hope rather than a thing to be enjoyed; sharer of my school and chair, and almost my successor — had not the swerve of slippery youth cast you headlong, you who held not the straight way of the Pythagorean path: be at peace, and cherish your seat with quiet shades, now long since commemorated by me among kindred names.
12. TO THALASSUS, LATIN GRAMMARIAN OF BORDEAUX. Your office and your name, Thalassus of an earlier time, I heard as a tiny child, and scarcely even remember; of what form or merit you were, of what stock of parents, no later age celebrates aught of you. Fame bore you only as a young grammarian, then too as slight as now no fame remains. But whoever you were, since you lived as a teacher in our age, take this our gift. Farewell.

13. TO CITARIUS, A SICILIAN OF SYRACUSE, GREEK GRAMMARIAN OF BORDEAUX. And you, beloved Citarius, shall be commemorated by me, worthy to be celebrated among the good grammarians. Yours would be the glory of Aristarchus and of Zenodotus among the Greeks, if the ancient honour followed; to the songs which were composed in your first years the Muse of Cean Simonides yields. Born in a Sicilian city, you came, a stranger, to our city, which you had so quickly made famed, refined by your studies. Having soon obtained a noble and wealthy marriage, by the envy of fate you die no father. But us we celebrate you, deceased, with mindful honour, as we cherished you living with the gift of friendship.
14. TO CENSORIUS ATTICUS AGRICIUS, RHETOR. Equal in the merit of eloquence to the first, you were, Agricius, placed in a later position: who, since you were born and died in a recent age, were deferred by me, not also omitted. In whatever number, you shall be commemorated with a sad threnody: there is one honour of the tomb, given late as well as early. As lofty was the peak of your lineage as the glory of your speaking, the glory known in the seat of the Athenaeum, which, granted once to Nazarius and to famous Patera, excellently refined many young men. Now, with your wife and surviving sons and son-in-law, you cherish the shades and monuments of your forefathers.

15. TO NEPOTIANUS, GRAMMARIAN AND ALSO RHETOR. Witty, courteous, an old man of youthful spirit, whose mind, dripping with no gall but much honey, mingled nothing bitter through all his age — medicine of my heart, Nepotianus, sharer alike of serious things and of jests; silent man, who would have outdone Amyclae in keeping silence: as you told your tales, Ulysses would not have left you, who left the singing melodious maidens. Upright and chaste, sparing, thrifty, abstemious, eloquent, yielding to no rhetor's pen, and a disputant up to Cleanthes the Stoic; knowing Scaurus and Probus in your inmost heart, and more mindful of Cineas of Epirus; comrade and table-companion, ever a guest — too little to say a guest: a stirrer of my mind. No one gave counsels with so pure a mind, or hid what was given in a deeper concealment. Renowned for the honour of a governorship you held, having completed ten times nine turns of years, leaving two children, you meet death, with much grief, of your own as of mine.

16. AEMILIUS MAGNUS ARBORIUS, RHETOR AT TOULOUSE. Among kindred shades already wept, my uncle, now you shall be commemorated among the rhetors; let that be the work of piety, this the reverend names of men for the sacred bond of my homeland. Let us celebrate with a twofold honour a father twice deserving — Arborius, son of Arborius and grandson of Argicius. Yours was the pedigree of an Aeduan father, the Tarbellic origin of Maura your mother: both of the race of nobles. A noble and dowered wife, a home and a school, the cultivated friendships of princes fell to you as a young man, while wealthy Toulouse held the brothers of Constantine, set apart under the show of exile. Thence the fame of you drove you to the citadel of Byzantium and the city of the Thracian Propontis, Constantinople. There rich in wealth, and honoured there by the learned Caesar, you die, Magnus, with the fathers surviving you. But the piety of the Augustan prince restored you to your native seat and the monuments of your own; hence the yearly day renews the cause for tears and the tearful gift, with thankless devotion.

17. EXUPERIUS, RHETOR AT TOULOUSE. Exuperius, to be remembered by me, eloquent without art, grave in gait and with mighty words, fair of face and, in sum, graceful in movement and bearing; whose fluency of speech was by far most beautiful, which, if you received it only by hearing, would please when puffed up, but, examined, you would know to bring forth nothing of solid sense. The gown of Palladian Toulouse first revered you, then with like fickleness drove you off. Narbo thereafter received you; there you formed, as rhetor, the sons born of Dalmatius, the fatal names of kings — then boys — teaching for a great fee, almost to the goal of grown age. They, having soon obtained the Caesarean name, assigned to you the honour of a governor and the Spanish tribunal; departing, very rich, you ended your peaceful ways and the tranquil times of your life in your Cadurcan seat. But the laws of your homeland and the origin of your parents call you, that you may render again to Bordeaux the name derived from the rhetor.

18. TO MARCELLUS, SON OF MARCELLUS, GRAMMARIAN OF NARBONNE. Nor shall I keep silent of you, Marcellus, born of Marcellus, whom a harsh mother drove from city and home; but powerful fortune quickly restored all and increased it: Narbo first gave you the homeland you had lost; here the noble host Clarentius, moved by your excellent disposition, gave you his daughter in marriage. Soon a school and many a hearer and the gown-clad youth gave you the name and riches of a grammarian; but fortune never makes the course perpetually favourable, especially when it has found a man of crooked disposition. But I must not pile up his fates, having undertaken to commemorate them; it is enough to have said that all perished at once: yet not also the name, of which I do not defraud you, received among the grammarians of very slight merit.

19. SEDATUS, RHETOR OF TOULOUSE. It is a sacred duty, if I should leave you, Sedatus, unmentioned, though you obtained your teaching-office abroad. Your homeland is common with mine: by the lot of powerful fate you obtained Toulouse as the seat of your school. There marriage and sons and a wealthy old age and fame, such as is equal to a great rhetor. Yet, though from a foreign region, your homeland brings you back and, death being met, reclaims you as its citizen; and though you spent your wandering toil on a separated city, your origin takes its own judgement of you. And your offspring now, following the manner of their parent, ennobles Narbo and Rome with their studies; but why do I complain? After a long time fame, willing or unwilling, will bring even them back to Bordeaux.

20. STAPHYLIUS, RHETOR, A CITIZEN OF AUSCH. Thus far I have observed for myself the law of commemorating fellow-citizens, whether they taught at home or abroad; but it is right to join to the citizens one foreigner — you, Staphylius, born of the stock of the Nine Peoples. You were to me both as a father and as an uncle — one man, both: the one as Ausonius, the other as Arborius. A grammarian equal to Scaurus and Probus, a most ready rhetor, skilled in the history of Livy and Herodotus. The whole method of all learning was known to you, as much as Varro packs into six hundred volumes. A golden mind, a persuasive voice, and quiet discourse: he was neither a delayer nor a hastener. A fair old age, a neat habit, anger and grief far off; and the goal of his peaceful life was fitting.

21. CRISPUS AND URBICUS, LATIN AND GREEK GRAMMARIANS. You too, into the age to come, Crispus, shall come, commemorated by the gift of a sad threnody; you who taught the first of the new signs of the elements to the youngest and to those untrained in speech; believed once to glow with wine, so that you bore matter to rival the passages of Vergil and of Flaccus. And to you, Urbicus, ranked after in Latin beginnings, but renowned among the Greeks, thus may my song raise the cry. For you, joined with your Crispus, were wont to speak prose and verse with the same impulse, so that, as in song, you might soon recount the ancient heroes once commemorated in the song of Homer: the sweet son of Plisthenes (Agamemnon) among the few, and, like the torrent's, the snowy words of the man of Dulichium (Ulysses), and King Nestor, singing words sweet to utter with the nectar of his honeyed voice. Both ready of speech, both learned in all songs, skilled in the fictions of myth and in history; both freedmen by birth, but such as it would befit to gain what they deserved, that they might have renown from freeborn fathers.

22. TO VICTORIUS, ASSISTANT-MASTER OR USHER. Victorius, studious, mindful, swift, assiduously reading in unknown books and nothing but what was obscure, having greater care to unroll pages eaten by moths and barbarous than for studies ready to hand: what the law of the pontiffs was, what treaties, what pedigree of the sacrificer once was at Cures before Numa; what Castor set forth of all the doubtful kings, what Rhodope from her husband's books; what the law of the pontiffs, what the decrees of the ancient Quintus, what the resolutions of the fathers, what Draco or what Solon ratified, and what laws Zaleucus gave to the Locrians, what Minos ruled under Jove, what Themis before Jove — these were better known to you than our Tullius and Maro, and whatever is stored in Latin history. Perhaps a long reading would have given you even those, had not Lachesis hastened the final journey. Tinged with the slight honour of our chair, having barely tasted the name of grammarian: thereafter you died in the distant shores of Cumae, to which you had crossed from the Sicilian shore. But now rejoice, commemorated in the company of the noble, if pious care reaches your shades.

23. TO DYNAMIUS OF BORDEAUX, WHO TAUGHT AND DIED IN SPAIN. But neither shall I defraud you, Dynamius, of a sad complaint — fellow-townsman of my homeland and advocate, whom rumour, wounding with a charge of adultery, drove off; whom little Ilerda cherished in its hiding-places; whom a Spanish wife enriched while you lay hidden; for there, with your name changed, you were a rhetor, a rhetor disguised under the surname of Flavinus, lest a fault could betray its fugitive. Though a late will had restored you to your homeland, soon the house of Ilerda drew you back, idle again. Whatever your flight and the report of your life may have been, you are joined to me by an ancient friendship; and receive my office, if the shades have any feeling, now late, death being met, Dynamius. Though you lie dead in distant shores, pious care commemorates you in sad elegies.

24. TO ACILIUS GLABRIO, GRAMMARIAN, THE YOUNGER, OF BORDEAUX. Fallen with an equal brevity of learning and of life, Glabrio, I shall commemorate you in sad elegies — a name drawn down from the pedigree of noble grandsires, Glabrio son of Acilinus, of Dardan progeny. You once my equal as a boy, soon my pupil, and thereafter, when I was made rhetor, a grammarian; in the forum a protection to the accused and a cultivator in the fields, worthy long to enjoy the goods you had won: obliging, glad, kindly, abstemious, as good ever in giving counsels as silent about those given; as much every glory of your own as soon their grief, snatched away before all by a bitter death, you forsake all things, Glabrio: leaving wife and children, father and mother — alas, by how many names undone! Long to be wept by us, never enough, take, Glabrio, the bitter farewell, commemorated forever.

25. CORONIS (Conclusion). Those whom you read, drawn from the first page of the book, know to have been the teachers of my homeland, in the study of the grammarian or of the rhetor, or of both, whom it is enough for me to have commemorated now that death has been met. Praise is an allurement to the living; it will suffice to summon by voice the names alone to their tombs. Therefore, you who read the sad leisure of my page, seek not eloquence, but the office by which pious care performs the rites for famous and learned men, while it recalls the glories of an excellent homeland.
26. THE POET. Farewell, shades of the renowned rhetors; farewell, upright teachers, whether history or the poetic pen or the forum made any of you noble, or the doctrine of the medical art or the Platonic gave to perennial glory; and if any care of the living pleases the dead, and the honour of the surviving gives joy: receive the sad observance of my song, woven with a tearful complaint. May the unmoved ash keep the seat of the tomb, may the memory of the names live, until that age returns, common to all by the gift of God the judge.

1. AUSONIUS TO HIS SON DREPANIUS. To whom do I give this charming new little book? So said the poet of Verona once, and straightway gave it, when found, to Nepos. But to whom shall we trust this unlovely, unpolished little book, these trifles, scraps, and follies, to be cherished in his bosom? I have found him — be still, you anxious trifles — one no less learned and more kindly than he whom Gaul furnished to Catullus. No one of my friends is dearer to me than he, whom the nine sisters esteem more than all the rest, Maro excepted. “You mean Pacatus, no doubt, poet?” He himself it is. Fly out fearlessly, my verses, and cherish your nest in his safe bosom. He will love you here, here he will wish to protect you; what is to be pardoned he will conceal, what is approved he will pass on. After him, fear no judgement. Farewell.

2. FROM THE GREEK: A PYTHAGOREAN SAYING ON THE UNCERTAINTY OF CHOOSING A WAY OF LIFE. What path of life shall I follow, if the courts are full of uproar, if the home is anxious with cares, if cares for his household pursue the man abroad, if ever-new losses await the merchant, if base poverty forbids one to rest; if toil harasses the farmer, if shipwreck's terror gives the sea ill repute, and there are heavy penalties in the celibate life, and a heavier and futile watchfulness for the cautious husband; if the work of Mars is bloody, if the gains of usury are base and swift interest cuts down the destitute? Every age has its care; to all, their own time of life displeases them. Sense is absent from little ones who boast, and the rudiments of boys are hard, and the youth of young men is rash. Fortune afflicts men through wars, through the sea, with wraths and snares and chained labours, ever to be exchanged for heavier ones. Old age itself, long awaited and longed for in our prayers — to ill purpose — exposes the body, easily torn, to countless diseases. We all alike despise the present; some, it is agreed, are unwilling to become gods. Juturna cries out: “To what end did he give me eternal life? Why was the condition of death taken from me?” So beneath the Caucasian crag Prometheus calls Saturn's son to witness, and ceases not by name to accuse Jove, because perennial life has been given him. Look too to the cultivation of the mind: thus, surely, an unhappy care for chastity destroyed chaste Hippolytus. On the other hand, whoever delights to spend a life stained by allurements, let him look upon the punishments and crimes of kings — of incestuous Tereus or soft Sardanapalus. The three Punic wars warn us to avoid treachery; but the destruction of Saguntum forbids us to keep faith. Live, and ever cultivate friendships. — For such a charge the learned school of Pythagorean sages perished. — Fearing this, then, cultivate none. — For such a charge Timon was once stoned in Pallas's Athens. The mind, ever beset, is divided amid uncertain wishes; nor is it enough for a man to have wished: he rejects what he longed for. To be held in honour pleases him; soon he repents; and that they may rule, men wish to serve. The same man, exalted by honour, is exposed to envy. Care keeps the eloquent wakeful all night; but the unpolished man lacks the adornment of life. Be a patron and defend the accused: but the gratitude of a client is rare. Be a client: the patron's person is grievous with its demands. The prayers of fathers urge this man on; soon harsh anxiety steals in with its cares. Childless old age is despised, and the heirless man is the prey of the legacy-hunter. Live thriftily: you shall be torn by report as a miser, and a heavier censure shall brand the lavish giver. All things are contrary to you in adverse chances. Therefore best is the saying of the Greeks: indeed they say that for man it is good not to be born, or, once born, to gain death quickly. This indeed is the Pythagorean apophasis, according to the distich here set below: “First, not to have been born among men is best; second, once born, to pass as quickly as possible through the gates of Hades.” But, against this, the follower of the other doctrine, disapproving what that teaches, learn what he says by reading below: “Therefore, since there is nothing in this life that we should love, yet it is not right that we believe ourselves born to no purpose, if we believe the author of life to be just: another life must be prepared for us by living for him, with whom, after this life, we may live; let them indeed hasten to descend to the Stygian shades, who, following the foolish doctrine of the Pythagoreans, prefer not to have been born rather than, being born, to live.”

3. ON THE GOOD MAN: A PYTHAGOREAN SAYING. The good and wise man — such a one as Apollo, when consulted, scarcely found a single one among all the thousands of men — is himself the judge of himself, and examines his whole self to the fingernail. What the nobles think, and what the fickle opinion of the empty crowd, he is unconcerned, like a sphere of the universe, smooth and round, that nothing of an external blemish may settle upon his polished surface. He reflects how long the day will be under the sign of Cancer, and how great the night stretches itself in the tropic of Capricorn; and he weighs himself in the just balance of the scale, lest anything sag, lest anything jut out, that the corner may meet in equal parts, that the level may nowhere swerve, that whatever lies beneath be solid, and that the blow, applied with knocking fingers, betray no hollows beneath. He does not bend his eyes to sweet sleep before he has reckoned over all the deeds of the long day: what things he has passed by, what was done in due season, what was not? Why did grace or reason fail this deed or that? What have I overlooked? Why did this opinion settle, which it had been better to change? Why, pitying some needy man, did I feel a grief with broken spirit? What did I will that it would be good not to have willed? Why, base, did I set the useful before the honourable? Was anyone wounded by a word or, in short, by a look? Why does nature draw me more than discipline? Thus, going through all his words and deeds, and reviewing all from evening's rise, offended at the crooked, he gives the palm and rewards to the upright.

4. YES AND NO: A PYTHAGOREAN PIECE. “Is” and “Not” — all men frequently use these well-known monosyllables. Take these away, and there is nothing for the speech of men to turn upon. All things are in these, and from these are all things, whether there is anything of business or of leisure, whether troubled or calm. By the one or the other alike — sometimes, often, by each apart — they oppose pursuits, as the contest finds men's characters and dispositions, easy or difficult. If agreement is reached, no delay intervenes: “Is, Is”; but if the matter is disputed, dissension will add “Not.” Hence the courts burst apart with shoutings, hence are the brawls of the furious circus, hence the broad sedition of the wedge-banked theatre, and the senate-house too stirs such quarrels. Wives and children with their fathers sow these words with peaceful zeal, speaking with affection unimpaired. Hence too the school, in harmony with its peaceful disciplines, stirs up its doctrinal quarrels in peaceful contest; hence every dialectical band of sages contends. Is it day? It is day, then! That does not follow; for whenever, by many torches or by lightnings, there is light for man by night, that light is not the light of day. So it is “Is” and “Not,” as often as it must be granted that there is light, but not that it is day. From this a thousand contests arise; hence many, brooding on such things in a hoarse murmur, gnaw at raging silences with their mouths shut. What a life of men, that two monosyllables keep in turmoil!

5. ON THE AGES OF LIVING THINGS: AFTER HESIOD. Thrice two and ten times nine and more the years run on, which the just life fills for men as they grow old. These the chattering crow surpasses nine times over in living, and the stag goes four times beyond the crow's generations; the raven thrice outdoes the wing-footed stag, and the Phoenix, the bird that renews itself, multiplies him nine times. Him we Hamadryad Nymphs surpass ten times over in our perpetual age — we whose life is longest. This limit confines the long-lived fates of living things. The rest, God, the arbiter of the hidden age, knows: what times Stilbon (Mercury) rolls round, what ages Phaenon (Saturn), what circuits Pyrois (Mars) holds, what Jupiter with his kindly fire, with what return kindly Venus hastens, who guides the Moon, what toils await Titan (the Sun), until, the year that is called Great being completed, the wandering stars come again into their ancient course, such as they stood from the origin of the ordered world.

6. ON THE PRINCIPLE OF THE BALANCE. Whoever you are who marvel that the vast bodies of the world endure, encompassed by the lofty orbit of the heaven, and that no decay befalls so great a mass — hear what you may marvel at more: the most minute first-beginnings of things so great, beginnings that admit not our sight. They consist of tiny atoms joined in a series; but in the tiny there is a solid segment, divisible by none. From this come vigour and strength and the eternal mobility of things, never to be overcome by any age. Human things may be set beside divine. So it is with the as, the solid unit: since it consists of twice six equal parts, yet in the smallest equal parts one same force remains. For if anything be lessened in number, the sum totters, and the wrenched parts fall, the body being shaken. As, if one tears the keystone from the arch, on which all things rest, the rest will at once follow downward and draw the whole into a common fall from the summit; not otherwise is it with the balance. If a single uncia is wanting, it will no longer be a whole as, and the name deunx, now void, will hold it. Nor does the dextans keep its name when the sextans is removed; the dodrans will lack the support of its founder, the quadrans being taken; and the divided triens forbids the bes to persist. Now you will have no quincunx, if you wrench away a gramma. And what semis is left to whom, the half, when the parts of the as perish? And whose seventh part of a pound is the septunx? It is a pound, then, only if it totters in no part. The balance of weight and number and conduct and works and waters: nor is there a measure that you may not mark by this name. The earth, which hangs in the midst of the air, is a balance; and its own balance confines the paths of sun and moon. The balance determines the equal hours of day and of sleep; the balance holds in the shoreless Caledonian tides. Do you too remain to me a sure balance of my conduct.

7. ON THE PRINCIPLE OF A TIMELY BIRTH. All things that we measure in the varied course of events, the dominion of the stars drives on; and to man belong only his earthly limbs: from the powers above come fortune and the breath of life, to be governed by the sevenfold choir; but over them presides the golden Sun, allotted the rule of the bright heaven. Nor in us alone does he govern the seasons of life, while we, anxious, draw out the brief span of our age: he is believed, by his seeing, to shape the hidden sowings and the times of the life that is to be borne in the mother's womb, and to ordain the laws of a life not yet brought forth. For when the conception has settled in the field of generation, it is not doubtful that the Sun stands upon some sign for each. When he has taken the station of the neighbouring star, he sheds no light into the adjacent risings. But when, the reins turned after the month's space, he climbs the third constellation already in his purple chariot, the slanting line sends down a slender light, breathing faint motions through the inert weights. In the fourth seat the indulgence of the first Sun is strong, and, poured in, persuades the tender embryo to grow together. With its brightness and its triangular aspect the vital ray flashes, gleaming clear and gentle, which from the angle of the fifth sign strikes the parent astonished, the infant being now quickened. For in the sixth place there is no force, because no rule of an equal side is marked out for Phoebus when he gazes. But when the seventh boundary has received, in flames, the standards of the sign-bearing cohort, its camp set in a right position in the mid-region: it sees the covenants of the swelling birth now under full light, and, bending the lightnings of no scant light, it warms with the whole fire of its crown. Hence comes this — that Lucina forestalls the lawful labours, and the woman in childbirth, hastening before the expected wish, feels the heavy pangs steal upon her; for unless, when he has poured his light from the seventh star, he has driven against the resisting bars of the slow birth, the later cannot, the earlier could — or is it because in the sixth the rival aspect of the eighth star, useless when seen, knows not how to form the matching figures of the sides? But the ninth, pressing upon its sign, lightens the lingering prayers of mothers, the following triangle lending its strength. And if difficult Ilithyia again draws it back, the square will release the bonds of doubtful delays.

8. ON THE NAMES OF THE SEVEN DAYS. The names that the year holds, suited to the seven coming days, the same number of wandering planets made, which the world, rolling them with unwearied turning, bids stray in the slanting station of the signs. The radiant Sun holds the first and the last day. Next succeeds the Moon to her brother's crown; third, Mavors (Mars) follows the Titanian light.
