Cymbals give sound at a clash, stages at beat of bounding feet, the taut skins of hollow drums give back a booming; Mareotie 3 sistra raise rattling din in Isis' honour nor does Dodona's brazen tinkling cease as oft as the lavers at the clappers' measured stroke obediently reply with rhythmic beat.1 2,; Thou, as though thou wert a mute citizen of Oebalian Amyclae,5 or Egyptian Sigalion 6 were sealing thy lips, stubbornly keepest silence, Paulinus. I recognise shame in thee, for continued negligence cherishes her own defeet, and in shame for long silenee thou dost resolve not to maintain interchange of courtesies; and lengthened idleness loves its own fault. Who forbids you to write hail and farewell with studied brevity, and to commit to paper these words of greeting? I do not demand that thy page should weave a long drawn out web of verse and burden thy letter with a multitude of words. Twas but one letter wherewith the Spartans made reply and, though refusing, pleased the angry king.1 For indeed terseness is courteous; so, report says, taught reborn Pythagoras.2 While babblers would be stringing indecisive words, in all cases he would answer only Yes or No. O stable rule of speech! For nothing is shorter and more adequate than these, which approve the valid or reject the invalid. None pleased by silence; many by brief reply. 45"But I, whither with foolish amplitude of speech have I been long careering? How distant from itself and yet how near is error! I with long speech, thou with utter silence, we both displease. Yet can not keep silence, for free affection never bears yoke, nor loves to screen truth with glozing words. Hast thou, dearest Paulinus, changed thy nature? Do Biscayan glades and sojourns in the snowy Pyrenees and doth forgetfulness of our clime work thus? What curse shall I not righteously call down on thee, O land of Spain? May Carthaginians ravage thee, may faithless Hannibal waste thee with fire, may banished Sertorius again seek in thee the seat of war! Shall then Birbilis or Calagorris clinging to its crags, or parched Ilcrda3 whose ruins, littered over rugged hills, look down on brawling Sicoris, possess him who is mine and his country's pride, the mainstay of the Senate? Here dost thou, Paulinus, establish thy robe consular and Roman curule chair, and wilt thou bury there thy native honours? But who is that unhallowed wretch who has urged you to so long silence? May he turn no sound to any advantage, may no joys enliven him, no sweet poets' lays, no melting harmonies of seductive elegy, may no cry of beast nor low of cattle nor song of bird cheer him, nor yet Echo, who hidden in shepherds' bosky groves consoles us while repeating our complaints. Sad, needy let him dwell in waste places and in silence roam the borders of Alpine hills, even as, 'tis said, in days of old Beller-ophon, distraught, avoided the company of men and wandered straying through untrodden places.1 This is my prayer, this cry, Boeotian Muses divine, receive ye and with Latin strains call back your bard!

THOU tellest me that my tongue keeps unbroken silence while thou art never dumb, and reproachest me with choosing idleness in secret retreats, and withal addest the charge of neglected friendship and tauntest me with terror of my spouse, launching a cruel line against my very heart.3 Cease, I prithee, to wound thy friend, and seek not to mingle bitterness—as wormwood with honey —with a father's words. My care has been and still, endures, to honour thee with every friendly token, to compass thee with faithful affection. No blemish, however slight, has ever marred my devotion towards thee; even by a look I have ever feared to hurt thee and to wrong thee with an. unguarded aspect; and when I have approached thee, out of respect I have the more heedfully ordered my looks and given my features a bright and cheerful cast, that no ungrounded suspicion might bring down a cloud upon thee, my revered father, even though arising from an unspoken thought. After like pattern my household has honoured and honours thee, and in love for thee we are as agreed together as our hearts are linked together in worship of Christ. What rancour, I beg of thee, against thy friends is crept over thy heart? With what idle tale has nimble Slander forced her way into thy ears, smitten thy fond heart, and aimed late blows against the tried affection of ancient faith, so as to harm a son by cozening a sire from his peace? But my heart is conscious of no feigned sincerity, my devotion, guiltless of neglect towards my father, hurls back with scorn every undeserved taunt, and brooks not to be scarred with a false charge because in truth innocent: as easy hurt as it is free from fault, it is the more sorely injured by an unjust blow. Thou dost complain that I have shaken off the yoke 1 wherewith I was joined with thee in the pursuit of letters. This I declare that I have never even borne. For only equals share one yoke: no one links the powerful with the weak, and no team works with one will, if the forced yoke-fellows are of unequal measure. If thou dost match calves with bulls or horses with wild-asses; if thou comparest moorhens with swans, and nightingales with owls, hazels with chestnuts, or rankest wayside shrubs with cypresses;—then place me beside thee: Tully and Maro scarce could uphold a like yoke with thee. If I be yoked in love, in that alone will

'Tis the fourth summer now returns for hardy reapers, and as oft has winter grown stark with hoary rime, since any syllable from thy lips reached me, since 1 saw any letter penned by thy hand— ere thy page, auspicious with its message of greeting, bestowed manifold the gift so long denied. For indeed 'twas a triple letter enriched with various flowers of composition, but the melodious sheets were a three-fold poem. Tilings sweet, though somewhat soured with manifold complaints, troubled affection had mingled with criticism. Put with me the father's gentleness rather than the critic's bitterness finds a resting place, and in my heart I draw from the kindly words what may weigh against the harsh. But these charges must be refuted in their proper place and canvassed in the sterner tones of the avenging heroic measure. Meanwhile, though briefly, lighter iambus shall hurry on ahead, in separate metre 1 paying back his debt of words. Now my elegiacs bid thee hail and having hailed thee, since they have made for others a beginning and a step, cease to speak. Paulinus to Ausonius Why dost thou bid the deposed Muses return to my affection, my father? Hearts consecrate to Christ give refusal to the Camenae, are closed to Apollo. Once was there this accord betwixt me and thee, equals in zeal but not in power—to call forth deaf Apollo from his Delphic cave, to invoke the Muses as divine, to seek from groves or hills the gift of utterance by the god's gift bestowed. Now 'tis another force governs my heart, a greater God, who demands another mode of life, claiming for himself from man the gift he gave, that we may live for the Father of life. To spend time on empty things, whether in pastime or pursuit, and on literature full of idle tales, he forbids; that we may obey his laws and behold his light which sophists' cunning skill, the art of rhetoric, and poets' feignings overcloud. For these steep our hearts in things false and vain, and train our tongues alone imparting naught which can reveal the truth. For what good thing or true can they hold who hold not the head of all, God, the enkindler and source of the good and true, whom no man seeth save in Christ. He is the light of truth, the path of life, the strength, mind, hand, and power of the Father, the sun of righteousness, the fount of blessings, the flower of God, born of God, creator of the world, life of our mortality and death of Death. He, the Lord of Virtues, to us God and for us Man, puts on our nature as we must put on his, linking God with man in perpetual intercourse, himself of each partaking. He, then, when he has launched his beams from heaven upon our hearts, wipes off the sorry filth of our dull bodies and renews the disposition of our hearts: he draws forth all which aforetime used to please, giving unsullied pleasure in return, and absolutely with a master's right claims both our hearts and lips and time. He seeks himself to engross our thoughts, our minds, belief and choice, himself to be feared and loved. Those aimless surges, which the toils of life stir up in the course of this present span of time, are brought to naught by faith in a life to come with God. This easts not a way the riches, which we are thought to seorn, as unhallowed or little worth, but, as more dear, bids them be laid up in Heaven in trust with Christ our God, who has promised more than he receives, to pay back with large usury those things now despised or rather laid up in his keeping. A faithful guardian, an unfailing debtor, he will repay with increase wealth entrusted to him, and of his bounty God with abundant interest will restore the money we have spurned. To Him given up, whether waiting or serving, in Him laying up my all, think me not, I beseech thee, slothful nor wayward, nor charge me with want of filial piety. How can piety be wanting in a Christian? For " piety " has the acquired meaning to be a Christian, and " the impious " one not subject to Christ. When I am learning to hold fast this, can I fail to show it toward thee, that is, towards my father, to whom God has willed that I should owe all sacred duties and names of affection? To thee I owe training, honours, learning, my pride of eloquence, of civil rank, of reputation, being by thee advanced, fostered, and instructed, my patron, tutor, father. But why do I live so long retired, thou askest reproachfully, and art stirred with a loving anger. It is expedient, or 'tis necessary, or 'tis my pleasure: whichever of these it be, it will be pardonable. Forgive me, as I love thee, if I do what is convenient; be thankful if I live as pleases me. PAULINUS TO AUSONIUS That I shall be absent from my native land full three years' space, and that I have traversed another world in aimless wanderings, forgetful of that fellowship in thy life, once cherished—thou dost reproach me with complaints hallowed by the love whence they spring. I welcome with reverence due the emotions of a father's heart and the anger which claims my gratitude leaving affection unimpaired. Yet for my return, my father, I would rather thou should'st ask it there where it can be granted. Shall I believe that thou canst call me back to thee while thou pourest forth barren prayers to beings not divine, suppliant to the Castalian Muses while God turns from thee? Not through such deities wilt thou bring me baek to thee and to my country. Thou call'st the deaf, implorest things of naught— a light breeze will bear away what is addressed to a nothing—the Muses, who are names but nonentities. The stormy winds whirl away ineffectual such prayers as these, which, not addressed to God, cateh in the empty clouds nor make their way into the starry court of the King of Heaven.

If thou carest for my return, look towards him and pray to him who with his thunder shakes the fiery heights of highest Heaven, who shoots forth his triple flash of flame, nor mingles it with idle sounds, who on the. crops graciously bestows sunshine and rains from heaven, who being above all that is, or wholly in all things everywhere, reigns over all through Christ who permeates all things: through whom he occupies and sways our minds, through whom he orders our times and places. Put if he ordains things opposed to our hopes, by prayer he may be turned aside to that which we desire Why blamest thou me? If thou mislikest the course which I pursue under God's influence, there is an earlier step: let the Author be accused, who is pleased either to shape or change my feelings. For if thou thinkest my nature is as of old and as 'twas known to thee, I will avow of myself that now I am not the man I was about that time when I was not thought wayward though wayward I was, seeing with the darkness of error, wise in what with God is foolishness,1 and living on the food of death. Wherefore thou art the more bound to pardon me, because by this the more readily 'tis permitted thee to recognize that this change is from the most high Father—that 'tis not in accordance with my nature: by this I shall not, methinks, be held to have admitted a lamentable distraction of a mind changed for the worse, since I have openly avowed that not my own mind has caused me to change my former life. I have a new mind, I confess—a mind not my own: not mine aforetime, though mine now through God's influence—and if in my deeds or thoughts he sees anything worthy for his gifts, to thee chief gratitude, to thee the glory falls due, since thy instruction has produced what Christ could love. Wherefore thou shouldst give thanks rather than complain because I—that son of thine, offspring of thy learning and thy character, Paulinus, whose parentage thou dost not deny, even now when thou believest me wayward—have so changed my principles that I have gained grace to become the child of Christ while I am the child of Ausonius. He will confer his rewards upon thy merit and from this tree of thine proffer the first fruit to thee. And so, I pray thee, think nobler thoughts and lose not the highest rewards by execrating good things which have their source from thee. For indeed my mind does not wander, nor even does my life flee from intercourse with men — even as thou writest that Pegasus' rider lived in Lycian caves 1—albeit many dwell in pathless places through God's leading, just as before them men famous among the sages did for the sake of their learning and their inspiration. Even so in these days also, they who with pure hearts have adopted Christ are wont to live—not as beside themselves, nor out of savagery choosing to dwell in desert places; but because—turning their faces to the stars on high, contemplating God, and intent to scan the deep wells of truth—they love repose void of empty cares, and shun the din of public life, the bustle of affairs, and all concerns hostile to the gifts of Heaven both by Christ's command and in desire for salvation. By hope and faith these follow God for the pledged reward which he, whose promise cannot fail, will bestow on such as persevere, if only this present life with its vain interests does not prevail, and the fiery perceptions, penetrating to Heaven's secret places, scorn what they see to gain what they see not. For things perishable are open to our sight, the eternal are denied; and now in hope we pursue what with the mind we see, scorning the various shapes, the images of things, and the attractions which provoke our natural sight. And yet such resolve has been found to lodge in those to whom already is revealed the light of the good and true, the eternity of the world to come and the emptiness of that which is. But I, who have not the same cause for boasting, why do I bear the same reproach? My surety of hope is no less; but since I dwell in pleasant places, and even now abide upon the agreeable shores of a prosperous coast,whence this so premature carping at my abode? I would that jealousy with good grounds may begin to pluck at me: bearing the name of Christ I shall welcome taunts. A mind strengthened by power divine feels no weak shame, and the praise I here despise is restored to me when Christ is judge. Do not, then, chide me, my honoured father, as though I had turned to these pursuits perversely, and do not twit me with my wife or with defect of mind: mine is not the perturbed mind of Bellerophon, nor is my wife a Tanaquil but a Lucretia. Nor am I now forgetful, as thou thinkest, of the heavens 'neath which my fathers dwelt, seeing that I look up to the all-highest Father, and that whoso worships Him alone he is truly mindful of Heaven.1 Believe then, father, that I am not unmindful of the heavens and do not live distraught in mind, but dwell in a civilized place: pursuits themselves bear witness to the character of righteous men; for an unrighteous race will not be able to know the most high God: granted that much of the country, much of the folk is unimproved and ignorant of laws, yet what tract is without its rustic worship? Or what offence in them is wiekeduess common to other parts? 1 And yet thou dost taunt me with the woodlands of Vasconin and snowy lodgings in the Pyrenees, as though I live tied down at the very frontier of the whole realm of Spain and have no place of my own anywhere in country or in town, where wealthy Spain outstretched along the world's boundary watches the suns dip down into the sea. Put suppose it had been my lot to dwell amid the hills of brigands, have I become a block in a savage's hut, changed into the very serfs amid whom I lived, partaking of their wildness? A pure heart admits no evil, even as filth spattered upon smooth bristles does not stick: if one without stain of wickedness spends his life in a Vasconian glade, his character, unblemished as before, draws no infection from his host's barbarity. Put why am I charged on that account when I dwell, as I have dwelt, in a far different country bordering on splendid cities and thickly covered with man's prosperous tillage? And if my life had been led on the borders of Vasconia, why should not the savage folk rather have been moulded after my mode of life, laying aside their barbarous customs to come over to our own? For whereas thou dost fix my Spanish dwelling-place in ruined cities, traversing in thy verse desolate towns, and eastest in my teeth mountain Calahorra, Bambola hanging from its jagged crags, and Lerida prostrate on its hill-side—as though, an exile from home and city, I were dwelling in these far from the dwellings and highways of men; dost thou believe these are the resources of the Iberian land, ignorant of the Spanish world where laden Atlas took his stand beneath the load of Heaven, he whose mountain, now the furthest fragment and boundary of the earth, shuts out with its lofty peak Calpe that lies betwixt two seas? Are only Bambola, Calahorra, Lerida, placed to the credit of this land which has its Saragossa, pleasant Barcelona, and Tarragona looking from majestic heights down to the sea? What need for me to tell over the cities, distinguished for their territories and walls which prosperous Spain thrusts forth between two seas; where Betis 1 swells the Atlantic, Hiberus 2 the Tuscan sea—Spain whose compass occupies the wide intervening tract which parts main from main, setting its bounds at the extreme verge of the world? If thou, O famous master, wert minded to describe the region where thou dwellest, wouldst thou be content to leave unnamed cheerful Bordeaux preferring to write of the pitchy Boii 3? And when thou bestowest thy leisure on the hot springs of Maroiahnn4 and permittest thyself to live amid shady groves, dwelling amid cheerful scenery and habitations marvellously built, dost thou inhabit murky hovels and cabins of twisted straw amid a wilderness fit for the skin-clad natives of Bigorre? Dost thou, a consul, scorn the proud walls of thine own Rome while not disdaining Bazas amid its sand hills? Or because the fertile country and green fields of Poiteau are about thee, shall I lament that the Ausonian consulate—alas! — has sunk to the level of Raraunum,5 and that the official robe grows shabby in some mouldering shrine; whereas in fact it hangs in the renowned city of Roman Quirinus along with the imperial palm-broidered robes, trophies of like distinction, there gleaming, long venerable, with unfrayed gold, keeping fresh the glorious bloom of thy deathless achievement? Or when thou art lodged under the roof of Lucanus,1 thy country house, inhabiting a pile vying with the halls of Rome, shall we take the pretext afforded by the place which gives its name to the vicinity, saying thou dwellest in the hamlet of Condate 2? Let much admit of jests, let sportive fiction also be allowed; but with a smooth tongue to strike against an aching tooth, to sport with stinging-compliments, and to season jests ill-relished with the vinegar of tart satire, oft befits a poet, never a father. For loyalty and natural affection demand that what slander-spinning Rumour instils into guileless ears, that the good-hoping mind of a father should not suffer to take hold and gain firm lodgment in the heart. Even the common herd, malignant in its brutal sneers towards habits formerly observed, does not always hold it crime to alter one's life: for to alter wisely is accounted praise. When thou hearest 1 am changed, ask what is ray pursuit and my business. If 'tis a change from right to wrong, from godliness to wickedness, from temperance to luxury, from honour to baseness, if I live slothful, sluggish, ignoble, take pity on a comrade strayed into evil; a gentle father well may be stirred with anger to restore a fallen friend to right living and by stern reproof to bring him back to better things.

Almighty Father of all things, to whom supreme power belongs, hear, if I pray aright. Let no day be passed by me in sadness, no night disturb my calm repose. Let others' goods not attract me, but rather let my own avail such as implore my aid: may none have a wish to hurt me or the means to hurt me. Let me have no occasion to will ill and let the unruffled power to do well be with me. Let my mind, content with its own and not given to base gains, overcome bodily enticements keeping the conscience of chaste conduct. Let that offending member, the ever-guilty tongue, well-pleasing to malicious ears for the poison it sheds, hate lewd jesting and unseemly words. Let me not be overcome by any man's decease, nor prosper through the death of any; let me never envy any man nor ever tell a lie. Be mine a cheerful home, and at my unpurchased 1 repasts may a well-fed slave bred in my house, my trusty comrade and prosperous henchman, serve blithely; and mine an obedient wife with children born of my clear wife. Upon pure conduct God bestows such gifts: such conduct assures itself of life unending against the world to come.

Paulinus to the justly respected lord Gestidius. IT is an insult to present a man of standing who has plenty of sea dainties with anything derived from the land and country-side. But, that I might have excuse for some converse with you, my bosom friend, and to make a show of accompanying these words of mine with some token of respect, I am sending a poor few of the very few fig-peckers which my lads bring home of an evening. And since I blush for their small number, I added on more words to my verses, as though indeed I could increase their number by my chatter. But since both alike are open to criticism, you will do a kind and friendly action by pardoning both, so as to make the fewness of the birds not appear mean, and my wordiness not tiresome. Take, then, these fowl fed in the thickets of the country-side, which the cunning fowler, lurking beneath a screen of bracken, while he beguiles and decoys birds with a call like their own, has taken hanging on his limed twigs—a silly tribe. Then, bringing home his light prey of no slight price, he sets out the catch upon his stall: and the array makes goodly show of prime birds in front gradually thinning out towards the back of the counter. That the more skinny may not displease, the fat birds with their attractive plumpness hold the foremost place, forestalling and delighting the gaze.

1. The Riddle of the Number Three. Drink thrice, or as many times three: such is the mystic law, whether for one who drinks three, or for one who multiplies three by three, to weave the cube from nine uneven threes. The right of three is the same as that of thrice three: all things are in these — the form of a begun human being and the completion of a full birth; and that end of fate which holds the last of nine times nine. Three brothers, begotten of Ops; three sisters, born in order, of the female sex — Vesta, Ceres, and Juno. Hence Jove's thunderbolts are three-forked, hence Cerberus, hence the trident, and the threefold egg of Helen with her brothers. Thrice the new purple filled the spindles of Nestor, and the crow, three times more long-lived than that age; whom, gathering the generations in nine triple courses, the bronze-footed stags surpass three times Nestor's span, three of whose ages the bird of Phoebus (the raven) outlives, whom nine times older the bird of the Ganges goes before — the bird whose temples are radiant in their cinnamon nest (the Phoenix). Threefold is Hecate, three the faces of the maiden Diana; three the Graces, three the Fates, threefold the voice, threefold the elements, three the Sirens in Trinacria; all things by threes: three winged ones, three half-goddesses, three half-girls, bidden, three times three, to contend with the Muses for the palm, singing with mouth, hand, breath, with the boxwood pipe, with the lyre-string, with the voice. Three the parts of philosophy, three the Punic wars, three-month the turns of the years and of the sky, and through the shadow of night the threefold watches; thrice the late sentinel, when Mars is caught, sings the bright signs of the coming dawn. And he who, conceived in the evening of a tripled night (Hercules), fixed four times three rich spoils to his trophies. And the lyric bards are of the number of the Memnosynes (Muses), three of whom alone the right hand of Phoebus once held; but Cithaeron three times consecrated three of them in bronze, by the religion of the fathers, who feared to have scorned the six. The triple three-night festivals were celebrated in the Tarentine games, such as the triennial rites at Thebes for twice-born Bacchus. The first three battles of the Thracian gladiators, in three wars in order, the sons of Junius sent as offerings to their father's tomb. She too (the Sphinx), seeking marriages through three riddles — what was two-footed and four-footed and three-footed, all alone — terrified Aonia: a bird, a lion, a three-formed maiden — the Sphinx, with the wings of a bird, the feet of a beast, the face of a girl. Three partnerships gleam in the Tarpeian temple. Three kinds of arts make human dwellings: he who lays the stones for the walls, he who lays the beams on the roof, and he who adorns the plastering with the final touch. Hence the cask of Bromius (wine-measure) and hence the Sicilian medimnus: the practice of measuring unfolds the one by three, the other by twice three. In physics, three first things: God, the world, the form given; a triple of all kinds — begetter, begettress, begotten. Through three kinds of triangles the rule runs: equilateral, or with equal legs, or unequal in all. The perfect number coalesces into three parts, so that the same, by the assembled triple, is dissolved through thrice three. Three, the first, has an even, an odd, and a middle; but it alone, as it divides three, so also divides five and seven; and, set in the whole number under the point of the centre, it marks off the solid thirds as the cube proceeds, sundering the equal parts from the odd by its triple; and a triple middle is in even numbers, when of four and six and twice four the same navel (omphalos) is distinguished. Threefold law, which the four times three Tables (the Twelve Tables) ratified: the sacred, the private, and that which is the common property of the people anywhere. A triple kind of interdicts: "from which I shall have been driven by force," or "in which of two places it shall have been," or "of whose goods." Threefold liberty, and threefold the diminution of civil status. Threefold the kind of speaking: the sublime, the moderate, and that of a slender thread. Threefold too the manner of healing, whose names are by reason, or by method, or by experience; and medicine is threefold: to preserve, to prevent, to cure. Three the cultivations of the orators: that which Rhodes, ruled by its Colossus, and you, Attic Athens, loved; and that which prose of Asia drew from the stages to the stern benches, imitating in lawsuits the numbers of the choruses. Hence the tripods of Orpheus, because they are three — earth, water, flame. A triple consideration for the stars: position, distance, form. And music, both the measure and the mother of melodies, is threefold: mingled in books, secret in the stars, made common in the theatres. Martial Rome is threefold: in cavalry, plebs, and senate; by this number the tribes, and the tribunes of the sacred mount. Three squadrons of the knights, three names of the nobler sort. Three are the names for the lyre-strings, three the names for the month. The Geryons are threefold, threefold the framing of the Chimaera; Scylla is threefold, made of three — dog, maiden, fish. The Gorgons and the Harpalycae and the Furies are in a band of three; and the three prophetic Sibyls, of a common name, whose fatal songs are three books, which the cultivation of thrice five men preserves. Drink thrice. Three is the number above all things; three is the one God. Here too, lest the game run by with an inert number, let it have ten times three threes and ten times nine.

22.po. To his Grandson Ausonius. The Muses too have their sports: leisure is mingled with the songs, my honey-sweet grandson; nor does the imperious voice of the harsh master ever exercise the boys without ceasing, but rest and the turns of study keep their fixed times. And it is enough for a retentive boy to have read gladly, and it is allowed to pause. School is named by a Greek name (scholē, leisure): let just leisures be granted to the toil-bearing Muses. Wherefore learn the more gladly that alternating play surely follows: we give the intervals that shall soothe the long labour. A boy's zeal grows weary, unless glad things be varied with austere, holidays with workdays. Learn gladly, and do not detest, grandson, the reins of a stern teacher: never is the look of a master a thing of horror. Though he, sad with age and not serene of voice, threaten the harsh quarrels of a knit brow, he will never be monstrous, who has once steeped his face in a placid habit. He will love the wrinkles of his nurse who flees his mother; grandfathers and trembling grandmothers the late-born prefer to their fathers — grandsons, a new care. So neither did Chiron, mingled with the Thessalian horse, terrify Achilles son of Peleus, nor the pine-bearing Atlas the boy son of Amphitryon (Hercules), but each, gentle, soothed his tender charges with mild addresses. Do you too not fear, although the school resound with many a stroke and the old master wear a truculent face: fear convicts degenerate spirits; but do you stand firm, undismayed, and let no shout and sounding blows, no dread under the morning hours, agitate you. That the sceptre of the rod is brandished, that there is much furniture of switches, that the deceitful soft leather covers the scourge, that your benches seethe with anxious tumult — these are the pomp of the place, and the scene is painted with a vain terror. These things once your father and your mother followed, and soothed my untroubled old age into peace for me. Do you, who bear your grandfather's name, in your first promise, my first grandson, hold out to me, whether in reality or in hope, an old age — whatever, as the years glide on, the fates shall give — to be enjoyed. Now I shall behold you a boy, soon in your youthful years, and now a man, if chance so bid; or if there be envy in it, I shall hope nonetheless, nor shall my prayers grow weary, that, mindful both of your father and of me, you may ever, eloquent, desire the lofty rewards of the Muses, and one day walk this road, on which we went before, and which your father the proconsul, your great-uncle the prefect, press upon. Read through whatever is memorable; I shall give the first counsels. The author of the Iliad and the lovely beginnings of Menander must be unrolled by you: do you, with the bending and keenness of your voice, bring out the numberless numbers (rhythms) with learned accents, and, as you read, put on the feelings: division increases the sense, and the intervals give vigour to the dull. And when shall those gifts fall to my old age? When will you renew for me, declaiming, so many poems forgotten, and so many strung through the ages of history — the comic shoes and the curtains of kings, the melic and lyric measures — and make the senses, overlaid in an old man, grow young again? With you leading the way, grandson, it is right to learn over again the measured poems of Flaccus (Horace) and high-sounding Maro. And you, dear Terence, who run over the stages in chosen speech, courteous, in the tight-laced sock of Latium, compel my scarce-remembering old age to your new dialogues. Now your crime, Catiline, and the tumult of Lepidus; now, beginning from Lepidus and Catulus, the affairs and times of Rome I connect in a series through twice six years. Now I read of the war mingled with civil strife, which Sertorius the exile stirred up with his Iberian ally. Nor do I, an unskilled grandfather, give these counsels; but, having trained a thousand talents, I myself, in my boastful years, reared many; and, cherishing them in my bosom and loosing their murmurs, I snatched their tender age from the coaxing nurses; soon, by soft admonition and gentle fear, I enticed the boys, that, mild, they might seek their advancement through hard things, about to pluck the sweet fruit of a bitter root. The same boys, taking on the toga in the stir of grown age, I led forward to good morals and arts and the vigour of speech, although they refused to bear the rein upon their neck, and would not offer their mouths to the inserted bits. Hard is the temperance, hard the experience, rare the outcome, proved by a long use of affairs, that a mild censorship should rule unteachable youth — which was endured by me, until at last the toil grew pleasant, and good habit, by use, lightened the labour; until I was summoned to the pious duties of the Augustan instruction, and, increased, was girded with various honour, when I was bidden to obey at the golden palace. Let Nemesis stand aloof, and let Fortune bear with me as I jest: I presided over the empire, while the prince, still wearing the boy's gown in the purple, set before himself, with his sceptre and his throne, the rights of his master, and Augustus thought our honours the greater. These, soon ripe, he brought forth with lofty increase: that I should be made quaestor to the Augusti, father and son; that I should put on a double prefecture and the curule chair, the consular robe and the embroidered toga — my rewards, a consul — and be held foremost in my own annals. By these I sought for my grandson how great a merit, a consul and grandfather, and I shine forth as the light of your life. Although you have long been famous by your father's name, and could be held adorned, or could be held burdened; yet from us a renowned honour has accrued. Now do you bring it to pass that it be no burden, that through yourself, striving upward to the heights, you may climb, and may hope for your own fasces with you as consul.

1. AUSONIUS THE CONSUL TO DREPANIUS THE PROCONSUL, greeting. Whether you think these things should be pardoned or examined, read them through, Drepanius, with attentive judgement. I shall be content with you as judge, whether you think the verses I have given should be read or covered up; for the first thing is to have earned your favour, Pacatus: the next will be the care of a vindicated modesty. I can bear the censure of a severe reader, and I can please myself with a modest praise. The horse knows how to love the sound of his patted neck; he knows too, undismayed, how to endure the slow blows of the whip. What discipline did the censor Aristarchus and the standard of Zenodotus seek for Maeonian Homer! Set down your obeli, then, the marks against the first poets: I shall think them palms, not faults of mine; and I shall call them corrected rather than condemned, the touches which the file of a learned man will apply to me. Meanwhile, about to undergo the weight of so great a judgement, I shall wish that I may please; if not, that I may lie hidden.

2. Prologue. The Seven Sages, to whom an earlier age gave that name, and a following age did not take it away, come forth today onto the stage in their Greek cloaks. Why do you blush, you toga-clad Roman, that men so famous will enter the stage? For us this is something to be ashamed of, but not for the Athenians too, for whom the theatre serves in place of the senate-house. To our affairs their own places have been allotted: the field of Mars for the assemblies, as the senate-house for the enrolled senators; the forum and the rostra the law of the citizens keeps apart. At Athens, and in all Greece, there is one seat of a public place for taking counsel, which in our city luxury established late. Of old the aedile gave a planked stage, raised on a sudden with no mass of stone. So did Murena and Gallius — I tell what is known. Afterward the powerful, not fearing expense, believed they would gain an everlasting name, if once a mass, built on a foundation of stone, should establish a place for the games for all time: this wedge-banked vastness of the theatre grew up. Pompey gave it, and Balbus, and Caesar Octavian, vying in expenses. But why do I tell these things? I came forth hither not for this cause, to set forth who built the theatres, who the forum, who the several parts of the walls: but that I might go before, and open up, men to be revered and praised by the gods, and what they wish for themselves. They are wont to pronounce their own sayings, which each of the wise men has already brought forth. You surely know what they are; but if memory halts at old matters, the player will come, the expounder of those which I hold less well.

3. THE PLAYER. The story is that Solon the Athenian wrote at Delphi γνῶθι σεαυτόν, which in Latin is: "Know yourself." Many think this belongs to Chilon the Laconian. Spartan Chilon, whether it be yours or not, they dispute, that which is reported next, ὅρα τέλος μακροῦ βίου, you who bid us look to the end of a long life. Many judge that Solon said this to Croesus. And fame says that Pittacus the Lesbian said γίγνωσκε καιρόν: he bids you know the time. But that καιρός is the timely time. Bias of Priene said οἱ πλεῖστοι κακοί, which in Latin is: "the greater part of men are bad"; but know that he called bad the unskilled. μελέτη τὸ πᾶν, that is Periander's of Corinth, who thinks that practice can do everything. Cleobulus of Lindus says ἄριστον μέτρον is best: that is, "measure is best for all things." But Thales brought forth ἐγγύα, πάρα δ' ἄτα, who forbids us to stand surety, because the bondsman is harm. This warning of ours does not please those who lend at interest. I have spoken; I shall withdraw. Solon the lawgiver comes.

4. SOLON. By Greek custom I, Solon, come forth onto the stage, to whom fame gave the palm of the Seven Sages. But fame has not the severity of judgement; for I think myself not the first, but one of them, since equality knows not how to endure rank. Rightly once the Delphic god counselled the foolish man who asked which of the sages should be first, that he set the garland of names in a smooth circle, lest any be first, or any be last. From the middle of their ring I, Solon, come forth, that what I am thought to have said to King Croesus, every sect of men may think said for itself. In Greek it has been compressed: ὅρα τέλος μακροῦ βίου, which becomes longer if you say it in Latin: I bid all men look to the end of life. Therefore avoid calling men wretched or blessed, because they are ever in a doubtful state. So it is, indeed. If I can, I will tell it in few words. Croesus, king or tyrant of Lydia, was among these blessed ones, rich beyond madness, who gave the gods temples with golden walls. He summoned me. I come, obedient to his word, that the Lydians might use a better king. He asks that I declare a blessed man, if I know any. I name Tellus, a citizen not ignoble: he, fighting for his homeland, had given up his life. He scorned this, seeks another. I found Aglaus: he had never gone beyond the bounds of his own little field. But he, laughing: "In what place do you then put me, who alone am called blessed in the whole world?" I say the end of life must first be looked to; then it must be judged, if the happiness remains. Croesus took the saying ill: I leave the king; he prepares war against the Persians. Setting out, conquered, bound, given over to the king, he stands, awaiting now the likeness of his own funeral, where the flame gave itself through the whole compass, rolling on high its swelling globes in the heat. And almost too late Croesus, with a mighty sound, "O truly a prophet," he says, "O Solon, Solon" — and with a great cry thrice he calls Solon by name. Moved by this voice, Cyrus bids the burning pyre be extinguished throughout its whole ring and destroyed: and just in time a shower poured from the clouds checked the fire. Croesus is straightway led to the king through a chosen band of soldiers: he is asked what Solon he meant, and what cause he had for crying out the name. He sets forth all to the king, through the whole sequence. The king pities him, and, seeing the force of fortune, praises Solon; thereafter holds Croesus among his friends, and bids him pass the whole of what was left of his life with him, bound with golden fetters. I, by the testimony of two kings, was praised and approved by both. And what was said to one, let each think said for himself. I have now finished the cause for which I came forth hither. Lo, Chilon comes. Farewell, you all, and applaud.

5. CHILON. My loins ache from sitting, my eyes from watching, while I wait for Solon, until he should take himself off. Ah, how few words, you gods, the Attic men speak! He has at last finished one saying in three hundred verses, and, looking back at me, departs. I am the Spartan Chilon, who now come forth. With the well-known brevity which we Laconians use, I commend our γνῶθι σεαυτόν, "Know yourself," which is now held on the Delphic column. That troublesome labour is of the best fruit: to discern what you can bear and what you cannot; by night and by day, what you do and what you have done, to examine right to the likeness of the finest point. All duties — modesty, honour, steadfastness — are in this; and any glory has been scorned by us. I have spoken. Farewell, and remember; I do not wait for applause.

6. CLEOBULUS. I am Cleobulus, citizen of a small island, but the author of a great saying, by which I am renowned: ἄριστον μέτρον, which they think I said. Interpret it, you who sit nearest the orchestra, on the neighbouring steps, among the fourteen rows: whether ἄριστον μέτρον is "measure is best," tell! You have nodded? I am grateful; I will follow it through in order. He has already said from that place — your African poet (Terence) — ut ne quid nimis ("that nothing be in excess"); and a certain one of ours, μηδὲν ἄγαν ("nothing too much"). Both senses bear on this, whether Italian or Dorian. Of speaking, of being silent, of sleep, of waking, this is the measure; of benefits, of thanks, of injury, of zeal, of labours: whatever there is in all of life requires that measure of the best moderation. I have spoken; I shall withdraw — let there be a measure. Thales comes.

7. THALES. I am Thales of Miletus, who said that water is the first principle for the creating of things, as the prophet Pindar did; and to whom once, by Apollo's command, the fishermen gave a golden tripod, drawn up from the sea; for they, at the bidding of the Delian god, had chosen me, because he had sent this gift to the wise. I, refusing, did not accept it, but gave it back to be borne to others, whom I believed my betters. Then, sent and sent back through all the seven sages, again they bring it to me. I, having received it, consecrated it to Apollo; for if Phoebus bids a wise man be chosen, it is fitting that no man be believed wise, but a god. That, then, is who I am. But there was a cause for my coming onto the stage, the same as for the two before me, that I might become the defender of my saying. It will displease — not, however, the prudent, whom use has taught and made skilled. Lo, ἐγγύα, πάρα δ' ἄτα, we say in Greek: in Latin it is, "Stand surety, but harm is at hand for you." Through a thousand examples I could run, to prove that bondsmen and sureties are defendants of repentance. But I will name no one by name: let each of you say it to himself and think within himself to how great a loss and ill standing surety has been to him. Yet let this office remain welcome to both parties. Applaud, then, you one part; you the other, offended, hiss.

8. BIAS. Because I, Bias of Priene, said οἱ πλεῖστοι κακοί, I suspect it is rendered in Latin as: "the greater part are bad." I would not have said it; truth begets hatred. But I called bad the unskilled and the barbarous, who neglect law and equity and sacred ways. For this people, by which the theatre is girt, is wholly of the good. The land of our enemies holds those whom you believe I called the greater part bad. But let no one be so bad a judge as not now to couple himself to the parties of the good, whether he is truly good or eager to be called so. Now that hated name of "bad" has fled. I go. Farewell, and applaud, you greater part who are good.
9. PITTACUS. Sprung of Mytilene, I am Pittacus the Lesbian, who taught the saying γίνωσκε καιρόν. But that καιρός warns you to know the time, and that there is a καιρός which they call the timely. So too there is a Roman saying: "Come in good time." Your comic poet Terence too declares that of all things the time is first, when the slave Dromo had come to Antiphila, finding her hindered by nothing, watching the turn of the time. Reflect, all of you, how often offence occurs to one for whom the opportunity has not been watched for. The time warns me not to be tiresome. Applaud.

10. PERIANDER. Born of Ephyra (Corinth), I, Periander, come forth hither, who said μελέτη τὸ πᾶν, and I now approve the saying — that it belongs to practice, what you do rightly. For he alone is effective in managing an affair who first reflects on the whole business. The comic poet Terence declares that the adverse or the favourable in affairs must be reflected on by all. Whoever wishes to place his abode, to wage war or to lay it down, to manage great or moderate things, even small ones too, it ever befits him to reflect; for all are too sluggish in new undertakings if reflection on the affair to be managed has been wanting. There is nothing that demands a fuller care than to consider what is to be done. Thereafter chance, not counsel, rules the unreflecting. But I now betake myself to my exit. Applaud, and, by reflecting, may you care for your commonwealth.

pr. I had crossed the swift Nava with its misty stream, marvelling at the new walls added to ancient Vincum, where Gaul once matched the Latin disaster of Cannae and the helpless, unwept hordes lie scattered over the fields. Setting out from there through trackless wooded wilds, alone, and seeing no trace of human cultivation, I passed by parched Dumnissus amid lands thirsty on every side, and Tabernae, watered by an ever-flowing spring, and the fields of the Sarmatians, lately measured out to settlers. And at last on the first borders of the Belgae I catch sight of Noiomagus, the famed camp of the divine Constantine. Here the air over the plains is purer, and Phoebus, now clear of cloud, unbars purple Olympus with serene light. No longer, where the branches are interlaced in mutual bonds, is the sky sought for, shut out by green gloom; but the open daylight's free breeze does not grudge the beholder its clear radiance and ruddy brightness. Indeed, into a likeness of my homeland and the trim grace of shining Bordeaux all things struck me with their winning aspect: the rooftops of villas set high on the overhanging banks, the hills green with the vine, and the pleasant waters of the Moselle gliding below with a hushed murmur.

Hail, river, praised by the fields, praised by the husbandmen, to whom the Belgae owe the walls honoured with imperial rank! River, your vine-clad ridges planted with fragrant Bacchus, your grassy banks planted too, O greenest of rivers! Ship-bearing like the sea, you slope downward into your descending waters; like a river you flow, yet with your glassy depth you rival the lakes, and you can match the brooks with your quick course, and surpass the cold springs in the clearness of your draught. You alone possess all that a spring has, all that a brook and a river have, and a lake, and the tidal sea that ebbs back with twofold flow. You glide past with placid waters, and you suffer no murmur of the wind, no struggle of any hidden rock. You are not forced to hurry your rapid currents over a foaming shoal; nor, broken by jutting lands in mid-channel, do you let an island sever your excluded stream, lest it rob you of the honour of your rightful name. You have been allotted a double path: both when you glide down with the favouring current, so that the swift oars strike the troubled shallows, and when the sailors, the towrope nowhere slackening along the banks, strain the cables of the masts against their necks. How often do you yourself marvel at your own eddies in the stream, and think your lawful course flows almost too sluggishly? You do not fringe your bank with marsh-bred sedges, nor sluggishly drench your shores with foul mire: the footprints go down to the water's very edge and stay dry. Go now, and inlay your smooth floors with Phrygian marbles, stretching a marble plain through panelled halls! But I, scorning what wealth and riches have given, will marvel at the work of Nature, not at that ruinous extravagance in which a spendthrift poverty, glad to squander, runs riot. Here solid sands carpet the moist shores, and the pressed footprints keep no remembering shapes.

Gazing through the smooth surface into the glassy deep, the river keeps nothing hidden; and just as the kindly air spreads itself open to the unobstructed gaze, and no calm winds bar the eyes as they range through the void, so we discern things sunk far below, our sight enduring to the inmost depth, and the secret recess of the hidden deep lies open, when the shallows move gently and the flow of the clear waters reveals the shapes scattered in the blue light: how the furrowed sand ripples in a light eddy, how the bending grasses tremble on the green bottom. Down beneath the native springs the swaying water-weeds endure the quivering waters; the pebble now gleams, now hides, and the gravel sets off the green moss. Such is the whole shore that lies open to the Caledonian Britons, when the tide lays bare green seaweeds and red corals and the whitening pearls, the spawn of shells, men's delights; and beneath the wealthy waves the imitating necklaces counterfeit our own adornments. Not otherwise does the discoloured weed reveal, beneath the glad shallows of the placid Moselle, the variegated pebbles mingled there.

Yet the fish, gliding playfully to and fro, slippery shoals, weary the eyes that strain unceasingly in error. But it is neither permitted, nor does he allow it to whom the care of the second realm and the guardianship of the sea-trident has fallen, to set forth so many kinds, and their slanting swimming-courses, and the ranks that advance up against the stream, and the names and all the nurslings of the teeming stock. Do you for me, O Naiad, dweller on the river's banks, set forth the dances of the scaly throng, and tell over the bands that float in their blue stream beneath the clear channel.
The scaly chub gleams among the grassy sands, its very tender flesh stuffed thick with bones, and not fit for the table after twice three hours have passed. And the salar, star-spangled on its back with crimson spots, that will harm no one with the sharp point of its spine, the smooth trout that escapes the eye by its swift swimming. And you, harried through the gorge of the winding Saravus, where its six mouths roar among the rocky piers: when you have flowed down into a river of greater fame, more freely, O barbel, you ply your loose swimming. You are the better for being of the worse age; to you it has fallen, out of the whole number of living things, to enjoy an old age not without praise.

Nor would I pass you by, O salmon, ruddy with crimson flesh, whose broad tail's wandering lashes are carried up from mid-channel to the surface of the waters, when the hidden stroke is betrayed upon the calm surface. You are scaly upon your mailed breast, smooth in the forehead, and you shall make the dishes of an uncertain feast; you bear unspoiled through long delays the seasons, marked above all by the spots of your head, you whose lavish paunch hangs heavy and whose belly flows with fattened abdomen. And you, weasel-fish, who are caught throughout Illyricum and through the pools of the two-named Hister by the tell-tale foam of your swimming, brought up into our waters, lest the glad streams of the Moselle should be cheated of so celebrated a nursling. With what a natural colouring Nature has painted you! Black dots mark your back above, where a tawny ring runs round; a dark blue dye draws over your slippery back; to the middle of your body you grow plump and full, but from there onward, right to the very end of your tail, the dry skin is rough and scaly.

Nor will I keep silent about you, perch, delight of the table, worthy to be ranked among the sea-fish though river-born, the only one that can readily contend with the crimson red mullets; for neither is your savour dull, and in your solid body the portions join in sections, yet are kept apart by the bones. Here too is the pike, a laughing-stock even by its Latin name, the haunter of the pools, a foe most deadly to the querulous frogs, who besieges the dark lagoons amid sedge and mire, fit for no use upon the choice tables, and seething with its rank reek in the smoky cookshops.
Who would not know also the green tench, the common folk's comfort, and the bleak, the prey of boys' hooks, and the shad that hiss upon the hearths, the fare of the poor? And you, of two kinds and yet neither and both, who are not yet salmon nor any longer salar, and ambiguous in the midway of the two, O sario, caught while still of doubtful age! You too must be named among the river bands, O gudgeon, no bigger than two hands without the thumb, very plump, rounded, the more swollen for your egg-laden belly, and imitating, O gudgeon, the trailing beards of the barbel.

Now, O cattle of the waters, you shall be honoured, mighty sheatfish; you whose back is, as it were, anointed with Attic oil, and whom I take to be a river-dwelling dolphin: so you glide great through the channels, and scarcely uncoil the ranks of your long body, caught now in the shallow waters, now in the river's weeds. But when you set about your tranquil courses in the stream, the green banks marvel at you, the blue throng of swimmers marvel at you, the clear waters marvel at you: the swell spreads through the channel, and the outermost waves run forward over the margin. Such was once the whale in the Atlantic deep, when by wind or its own motion it is driven to the shores of the land: the sea, shut out, overflows, and great waters rise, and the neighbouring mountains fear to be diminished. Yet here, here our gentle whale of the Moselle is far from working ruin, and is an honour added to the great river.

Now that I have gazed enough upon the clear ways and the slippery ranks of fish, and have counted enough the manifold shoals, let the spectacles of the vine bring on another show, and let the gifts of Bacchus solicit the roving eyes, where the lofty summit, over a long ridge, and the cliffs and the sunny slopes of the height, its bends and hollows, rise up with vines as in a natural theatre. So does the kindly vintage clothe the ridge of Gaurus, and Rhodope and Pangaeus shine with their own Lyaeus; so the Ismarian hill grows green above the Thracian seas; so do my vineyards paint the golden Garonne. For along the highest ridges of the slope that stretches to the farthest part, the riverside margin is planted with the green Lyaeus. The folk glad in their toil and the hastening husbandmen now hurry on the topmost peak, now on the downward slope, vying with their stupid shoutings; thence the wayfarer, treading the ground beneath the banks, and here the boatman gliding by, sing their gibes at the laggard cultivators: the cliffs and the trembling wood and the hollow river ring back to them.

Nor does the scenery of the place delight men alone: here I could believe that even the rustic Satyrs and the grey-eyed Naiads gather on the farthest banks, when wanton mischief drives the goat-footed Pans, and they leap upon the shallows and terrify the trembling sisters beneath the stream, beating the water with their unschooled blows; and often Panope of the river, having stolen the grapes from the midst of the hills, flees amid her Oread friends from the wanton Fauns, the rustic powers. It is said, too, that when the fiery sun has stood in mid-orbit, at the common stream the Satyrs and the glassy sisters celebrate their shared dances together, when the more burning heat has granted hours secret from the gathering of men. Then the Nymphs sport, leaping over their own waters, and plunge the Satyrs in the shallows, and slip out, who know not how to swim, through their very hands, while they grasp at the slippery limbs of the deceiver and the watery waves yield to them in place of a body. But let it not be lawful for me to tell of these things, seen by none nor known to sight, except in part; let that hidden reverence be veiled, and lie concealed, entrusted to its own streams.

That sight may be enjoyed openly, when the grey-green river answers to the shaded hill, and the river-waters seem to put forth foliage, and the stream is planted with vine-shoots. What is that colour upon the shallows, when Hesperus has driven on the late shadows and bathes the Moselle from the green hillside! The whole ridge floats with rippling movements, and the absent vine-tendril quivers, and the vintage swells in the glassy waves. The boatman, deceived, counts up the green vines, the boatman floating over the waters in his hollow skiff, midway where the image of the hill mingles itself with the river, and the river joins the borders of the shadows.
How sweet, too, the shows these spectacles celebrate, when the oar-footed skiffs contend in mid-stream and run through their various windings, and along the green shores graze the budding shoots of the close-cropped meadows! To watch the nimble helmsmen exult at the sterns and the prows, and the youthful crew roaming over the river's surface, while the day passes by in watching: they set their serious business below their play; a new delight shuts out the old cares. Such are the games that Liber looks down upon in the Cumaean waters, when he goes over the planted ridges of sulphurous Gaurus and through the vineyards of the vapour-bearing Vesuvius; when Venus, glad at the Actian triumphs of Augustus, bade the wanton Loves play their fierce battles; such battles as the Nile's fleets and the Latin triremes waged beneath the citadels of Apollo's Leucas; or the Euboean boats recall the Mylasan perils of the Pompeian war over echoing Avernus; harmless clashings of the vessels and jesting fights, such as the blue sea renews under its green image while Sicilian Pelorus looks on at the naval show. No other aspect does their boyhood add to the wanton youths, both the river's youthful prime and the painted beaks of the gaily-coloured skiff. When the sun has bathed these in its Hyperionian heat, it gives back the sailors' forms beneath the glassy flood, and renders the bent shadows of the inverted body. And as they ply their nimble strokes to right and left and shift the burden with the changing oars, the wave gives back other sailors, watery semblances. The youthful crew themselves rejoice in their own image, marvelling that the deceiving shapes return upon the river. So, when a little maiden is about to display her ordered locks (when the nurse has first brought to her dear charge the wide-shining honour of the searching mirror), she gladly enjoys the unfamiliar sport and thinks she sees the form of a sister-girl: she gives the gleaming metal kisses that cannot be returned, or feels first at the fixed pins, or at the edge of her brow tries with her fingers to draw out the curled locks: such is the youthful crew, enjoying the mockeries of shadows, the ambiguous shapes of true and false.

Now indeed, where the bank affords easy approach, the plundering crowd searches the whole depth for the fish, alas! ill-defended in their inmost river. Here one, far off in mid-stream, drawing the dripping nets, sweeps up the shoals deceived by his knotted toils; but here, where the river slips by with tranquil flow, another draws his floating nets marked by cork; while that one, leaning forward over the waves cast down from the rocks, inclines the curved tip of his pliant rod, throwing in the hooks baited with deadly lures. When the wandering throng of swimmers, unaware of the trick, have seized them in their jaws, and through the inmost part of their gaping throat have felt too late the wounds of the hidden iron, while they struggle, the sign comes up, and the nodding reed answers the rippling quiver of the vibrating line; and without delay the boy, deft, snatches the shaken prey crosswise with a whistling stroke; the air takes the blow, as when whips are once driven through the void, the breeze cracks, and the wind hisses through the stirred air. The wet spoils leap upon the dry rocks, and dread the deadly shafts of the light-bringing day. To each, beneath its own stream, its vigour remained; in our air, made sluggish, it spends its life in panted breaths. Now the feeble beating throbs in the powerless body, now the numb tail suffers its last tremors, nor do the jaws close, but the gill, breathing out, gives back in its gasps the deadly breaths it has drawn. So, when the blast plies the smith's fires, the woollen shield, sporting with the beechen cavities, takes in and shuts off the winds through its alternate vent. I myself have seen some, trembling at the verge of death, gather their spirits, then, springing aloft, throw their bodies headlong down into the river beneath, regaining once more the waters they had despaired of. The thoughtless boy, ill brooking his loss, attacks them from on high and tries to grasp them with his stupid swimming. So Glaucus of Anthedon, through the Boeotian straits, after he had made trial by tasting of Circe's deadly herbs, and had taken up the grasses cropped by the dying fish, went, a new dweller, beneath the Carpathian sea. He, mighty with hooks and net, the searcher of hidden Nereus, wont to sweep the sea's Tethys, floated, a plunderer, amid the captive throngs.

Such sights do the villas look down upon, hanging on the rocks with their towering height, in a long line through the blue waters, which the river divides as it strays midway in its winding bends, and the mansions adorn the banks alternately. Who now would marvel at the Sestian sea, the strait of Helle daughter of Nephele, who at the channels of the Abydene youth? Who at the sea spanned from the Chalcedonian shore, the work of the great king, where the Euripus amid the waves forbids the lands of Europe and Asia to meet? Here there is no dread fury of the strait, no savage battles of the raging north-winds; here it is permitted to join the commerce of speech and to weave converse with answering stroke; the kindly shores mingle saving voices — voices and almost hands — and the echo, meeting the waves, carries back the resounding words from either side.

Who is able, unfolding the countless ornaments and fashions, to set forth through each several estate the architectural forms? Not the winged man of Gortyn would scorn this work, the builder of the Euboean temple, whom, as he tried to fashion in gold the fall of Icarus, a father's grief drove back; not Philo the Athenian, nor he who, praised by the enemy, drew out the famous contests of the Syracusan war. Perhaps too the famous toils of men and works had their place here: the hebdomad of Marcus, celebrated in his tenth volume; here flourished the arts of renowned Menecrates, and the admired hand of Ephesian Ictinus — or upon the citadel of Minerva — for whom the owl, smeared with magic dye, lures every kind of bird and destroys them by its gaze. Here perhaps was the builder of the Ptolemaic hall, Dinochares, for whom the pyramid itself rises into four-square peaks with a cone and consumes its own shadows; who, once bidden, because of a covenant of unhallowed love, suspended Arsinoe in the air of the Pharian temple — for the agate breathes its power through the vaulted roof and draws to itself the girl, breathed upon, with her iron-laden hair. These men, then, or men like them, it is fitting to believe set up the scenes of the dwellings in the land of the Belgae, having built lofty villas, the adornments of the river.

This one stands by nature high upon a mound of rock; this one is founded on the edge of the jutting bank; this one shrinks back and, in its bay, claims the captured river for itself. That one, holding a hill which towers most over the river, takes up easy prospects over cultivated and over rugged ground, and like a wealthy watchtower enjoys its own lands. Nay more, that one, set on its low foundation in the watered meadows, makes up for itself the natural goods of a lofty mountain, and, threatening with its lofty roof, breaks into the upper air, displaying a high tower, like the Memphian Pharos. It is the special privilege of this one to catch the fish enclosed in the fenced pool among the sunny clearings of the rocks. That one, resting upon the highest ridges, watches the streams gliding far below with a gaze now growing dim. Why should I tell of the halls set beside the greening meadows? Of the roofs gleaming above on countless columns? Of the baths that smoke, built up on the river's edge, when Mulciber, drawn within, rolls the panted flames through the hollow facings of the heated chamber, gathering the enclosed vapour with its breathing heat? I myself have seen men, wearied with the much sweat of the bath, scorn the pools and the cold of the fishponds, that they might enjoy the living waters; and soon, refreshed in the river, drive on the cool stream with splashing swimming. But if a stranger from the Cumaean shores were to be present here, he would believe that the Euboean Baiae had given their slender semblances to these places: so great is the elegance and brightness that allures, and the pleasure breeds no excess.

But what end at last is there for me of telling of your grey-green waters, and of recording the Moselle as worthy of the sea, since countless rivers far and wide rush into you through your various mouths? — though they could put off their courses, yet they hasten to consume their name in you. For both the Sura, aided by the flow of the Promea and the Nemesa, hastens, no degenerate stream, to go beneath your waters — the Sura, gratified by the intercepting of its tributaries, more nobly mingled beneath your name than if, with its mouth unknown, it strove with father Pontus. The swift Celbis, the Erubris bright with marble, hasten to lap you as soon as may be with their attendant waters: the Celbis, renowned for its noble fish; the other, whirling the corn-grinding stones in its headlong spin and dragging the shrieking saws over the smooth marbles, hears from either bank the unceasing din. I pass over the slender Lesura and the thin Drahonus, nor do I lay claim to the unscorned waters of the Salmona; the ship-bearing Saravus has long with its sounding mass called me with its whole robe — the river that put off its course far, so that, wearied, it might roll its mouth beneath the Augustan walls. Nor less than this is that which, gliding silently through the rich soil, the happy Alisontia grazes the fruitful banks. A thousand others, as each one's own impulse the more urges it, desire to be yours: so great is the eagerness of the hastening waters, or the custom. But if to you, divine Moselle, Smyrna had given its own bard, or famous Mantua, the Simois, renowned upon the shores of Ilium, would yield, nor would the Tiber dare to set its honours before yours. Grant pardon, grant it, mighty Rome! Let envy, I pray, be driven off and depart, and the Nemesis unknown to the Latin tongue: this better glory has fallen to you, Tiber, that you guard the seat of empire and the household gods of Rome.

Hail, great parent of crops and of men, Moselle! You the famous nobles, you the youth trained in war, you the eloquence that rivals the Latin tongue adorns; nay more, Nature has granted to your nurslings character and a glad disposition with serene brow. Not Rome alone displays her ancient Catos, nor does Aristides alone, that great beholder of the just and the fair, prevail and shed lustre on ancient Athens. But why, having ranged too far with loosened reins, overcome by love of you, do I wear down your praises? Put away, O Muse, your lyre, the highest strings being struck in this last song. The time will come, when, as I soothe my cares by the studies of an obscure leisure and cherish the sunny days of old age, the honour of the theme may commend me; when I shall sing one by one the deeds of the Belgae and the famous glories of their fathers' ways. The Pierides will spin for me soft songs on a fine thread and run over the webs fitted with thin woof: a purple too shall be granted to our spindles. Who then shall not be named by me? I shall record the peaceful husbandmen, and those shrewd in the laws and powerful in speech, a lofty defence for the accused; whom the senate-house saw as the highest chiefs of the townsmen and its own senate; whom the celebrated eloquence of the youthful school, while still wearing the boy's gown, brought to be praised alongside the old Quintilian; and those who governed their own cities and made their pure tribunal and their harmless axes illustrious, free of blood; or who held the peoples of Italy and the north-born Britons under a prefecture's title in the second rank; and him who governed Rome, the head of the world, both people and senators, almost under the foremost name — though he was the equal of the foremost. Let Fortune hasten at last to undo her error, and, making good the prizes she has barely tasted, render now the heights of true honour, to be claimed again by his noble descendants. But for now let the work begun be woven out, and, deferring the praise of these men, let me tell, in a glad course through the green countryside, of the happy river, and consecrate it in the waves of the Rhine.

Now, O Rhine, spread your blue bays and your robe green with crystal, and measure out the space of this new stream, you who must be heaped up by your brother's waters; and not in your waves alone is the prize, but in this — that, coming to the walls of the august city, it beheld the joined triumphs of son and father, the foe driven out beyond the Neckar and Lupodunum, and the source of the Hister, unknown to the Latin annals. This laurel of the war just brought low has only now come; hence it shall bear others and yet others. Go on together, you two, and drive forward the purple sea with your twin course; nor fear, most beautiful Rhine, to seem the lesser: the guest holds nothing of envy, you shall possess an everlasting name; do you, free of care for your fame, adopt your brother. Rich in waters, rich in Nymphs, a giver to both, your channel shall stretch out its partings with its twin banks, and shall open common ways through its various mouths. Strength shall be added, such as Francia and such as the Chamavi and the Germans may dread: then you shall be held a true frontier. So great a twin name shall accrue to you from so great a river; and though you flow, one, from your source, you shall be called two-horned. This I, drawing my race from a Viviscan origin, known among the Belgae by their hospitality and not by any new compact — I, Ausonius, a Latin name, by homeland and by household placed among the farthest Gauls and lofty Pyrene, where glad Aquitania tempers free-born ways — I sing, bold with my scant assurance. May it be lawful for me to have touched the sacred river with the slender libation of my Muse. Nor do I aim at praise; I ask pardon. You have many, O kindly river, who are wont to stir the sacred waters of the Muses and to drink dry the whole of Aganippe. But I, with however great a vein of my own waters shall offer itself — when Augustus, the father, and his sons, my greatest care, shall send me, adorned with the Ausonian fasces and the curule honour, back to Bordeaux, my homeland and the nest of my old age, after the duties of a service well discharged — I shall pursue more widely the praises of the northern river; I shall add the cities by which you glide in your silent channel, and the walls that look out upon you with their ancient ramparts; I shall add the strongholds founded for protection in doubtful times, but now, with the Belgae secure, not camps but granaries; I shall add the happy settlers on either bank, and you, amid the labours of men and oxen, grazing the banks and cleaving the rich tillage. Not to you shall the Loire prefer itself, nor the headlong Aisne, nor the Marne set as the boundary between Gauls and Belgae, nor the Charente itself, flowing back with the Santonican tide; you shall yield, O Dordogne, river rolled down from the cold mountain; and Gaul shall set the gold-bearing Tarn after you, and the Tarbellic Adour, rushing madly far and wide over the rolling rocks into the purple sea — yet only after the divine power of its mistress Moselle has been adored.

O horned Moselle, to be celebrated through foreign shores, and to be celebrated not in your own places alone, where at your topmost source you put forth the gilded honour of your bull's brow, or where you draw your placid courses, winding through the fields, or where you open your mouths beneath the German harbours: if any honour shall wish to breathe upon my slender Camena, if anyone shall deign to lose his leisure upon these Muses, you shall go upon the lips of men and be cherished with glad song. The springs and the living lakes shall know you, the blue rivers shall know you, and the ancient groves, the glory of the hamlets; you shall the Drone honour, you the Durance, uncertain with its scattered banks, and the Alpine streams, and the Rhone that flows through a double city and gives its name to the Right Bank; you I shall commend to the Garonne, blue with its pools, great with its sounding rivers, the Garonne of the sea.

pr2. Likewise, a preface set down in verse. The names of my dear ones, now buried with due funeral, wept before with tears, I shall now commemorate in measures — bare, without ornament, and lacking the cultivation of fine speech: the funeral honour suffices for the dead. O dirge, dutiful enough with funereal complaints, do not pass over the yearly gifts with silence — those rites which Numa dedicates to kindred shades, as the degree of death or of birth demands. This is enough for the tombs, enough for those who lack earth: to summon the souls by voice has the worth of a funeral. The buried ashes rejoice to have their own names spoken; the monuments too command this with their inscribed fronts. He too, for whom the urn of a sad sepulchre was wanting, will be almost buried when his name is thrice spoken. But you, whoever you are, reader, who deign to commemorate the fates of my own in sad elegies, may you run through the unshaken times of your life, and weep no deaths beyond what is just.

1. JULIUS AUSONIUS, MY FATHER. First among these is my father Ausonius, whom, though a son might hesitate, order bids me set first. A care of God, who, having enjoyed the honour of a peaceful old age, lived eleven times two Olympiads (eighty-eight years). All that he wished, he saw prosperous; whatever he desired fell to him as he wished — not because of any excessive indulgence of the fates, but because that man's wishes were so moderate. His own age compared him with the seven sages, whose doctrine he cultivated by his conduct, so as to live it rather than speak it, by the art of the wise — though he was not unpractised in eloquent genius — and, gifted, both to prolong the lives of men by the method of healing and to enlarge for the fates their delays. Hence too this reverence remains for his completed life, that our age gave him this title: as Ausonius had no one whom he might follow, so he has no one now who might imitate him.

2. AEMILIA AEONIA, MY MOTHER. Next, you, my mother Aeonia, of blood mingled from a Tarbellic mother and an Aeduan father. To you fell all the virtue of a compliant wife: the fame of chastity and of the wool-working hand, and fidelity in marriage, and the care of guiding your children, and a courteous gravity and a glad seriousness. Having forever embraced the peaceful shade of your husband — once alive, cherish his bed; now dead, cherish his tomb.
3. AEMILIUS MAGNUS ARBORIUS, MY UNCLE. My piety has been cultivated, my father first being named and my mother; but a third, Arborius, shrinks from being named, whom it would be wrong for me to commemorate first, my father being second, yet again almost wrong not to place first. A balance must be applied, and he must be called next before the others, though he will be second to my father. You, my mother's brother and of one mind with my father, and who were to me what father and mother were, who adorned me — suckling, boy, young man, and man — with the arts which it is a joy to have learned; you whom the learned gown of Palladian Toulouse preferred before itself, whom Narbonese Gaul set foremost, whose tribunal you adorned with Latin speech, and the forums of the Iberians and of the Nine Peoples; whence, your fame growing, you, sought as far as Europe, made Constantinople flourish as its rhetor. You, learned in a thousand modes, in a thousand oracles of speech, eloquent, swift, and retentive; you, after, entrusted to you in my first years, I pleased you, said that I was son enough for you. Me you professed to be a glory to yourself, to my forefathers a bright honour, and you dictated words for my fates to mark. Therefore farewell, my uncle, who have gained an Elysian seat: these songs I pour to you as a libation from your own Muses.

4. CAECILIUS ARGICIUS ARBORIUS, MY GRANDFATHER. Do not forsake your pious task, O dutiful page: after these let us commemorate my mother's father, Arborius, a name drawn from an Aeduan pedigree, embracing many houses in nobility, where the province of Lyons is, and where the powerful Aedui, and where Vienne lies on its Alpine ridge. But too envious an affliction lay upon his race and his proud wealth; for his grandfather and father were proscribed, when Victorinus held the leadership of the realm, and the empire fell to the Tetrici. Then, a fugitive in the lands through which the Adour bursts forth and the fury of the Tarbellic ocean roars, long dreading the shafts of marauding fortune, the condition of a poor Aemilia entangled him. Soon a slender sum, sought with much effort, gave you a solace for your weariness, but not wealth.
