You were skilled in the numbers of the heaven and the stars privy to fate, pursuing your study in concealment; not unknown to you was the formula of my life too, which you had stored in sealed tablets, never betrayed; but my mother's care unfolded it, the assiduous care which a timid grandfather kept hidden. When you had drawn out your life nine times ten years, having experienced the shafts to be guarded against of the goddess Fortune, you wept your son lost through three decades, wounded; by that death you were bereft of your light. But you said that long solace cherished you, that a special honour awaited my fates; and now, mingled in the councils of the souls of old, you surely know the fates of your grandson. You feel that, as quaestor, as prefect, and the same as consul, I commemorate you with this honorific gift.

5. AEMILIA CORINTHIA MAURA, MY GRANDMOTHER. Now tell of my grandmother Aemilia, the pious care of a grandson — she who was wife to the aforesaid Arborius. A jesting name was given her, because once, dark of skin, she was called Maura (the Moor) among her companions. But she was not black in soul, which was brighter than a swan and whiter than untrodden snow; and not ready to pardon shameful indulgences, she kept herself and her own to the plumb-line. She, when I was snatched from the cradle and from my mother's breast, schooled me, kind beneath her stern rule. Grant a tranquil ash to my grandmother, O shades eternally at rest, if I speak pious words.
6. AEMILIA HILARIA, MY AUNT, A VOWED VIRGIN. And you, by degree of kinship my aunt, but to be commemorated in a mother's stead with a son's pious affection, Aemilia, who got in the cradle the surname Hilarius, because, glad and courteous, you resembled the image of a boy: you gave back truly, not in disguise, the likeness of a youth, in the manner of men practising the arts of medicine. Hatred of the female sex was ever yours, and thence grew the love of vowed virginity, which you cultivated through nine times seven years; and the end of your life was the very end of your chastity. These last rites I, your son, render, because, like a mother, you cherished me with counsels and love.

7. CLEMENS CONTEMTUS AND JULIUS CALLIPPIO, MY UNCLES. And recall my uncles too, O elegy, in your song: Contemtus, whom the Rutupine land (Britain) covers; for whom a great sum, sought by various chance, perishes, unprotected by the name of any heir; for, snatched in glad and still-flourishing years, he died across the sea, his brothers unaware. Julius prolonged his fate into a long old age, afflicted with countless losses; who, courteous and charming and obliging at his rich table, had us as heirs in name only. Both dutiful, alike in face, mingling jest and earnest, they had not an equal fortune of life; though you lie apart in tombs and in honour, take this gift common to you both. Farewell.
8. ATTUSIUS LUCANUS TALISIUS, MY FATHER-IN-LAW. Whoever shall wish to celebrate the chiefs and the old senate and the bright pedigrees of Bordeaux from its rise, let him record you and your race, Lucanus Talisius, who adorned your old forefathers by your character: fair in the honour of your face, courteous with a tranquil breast, though greater for your eloquent genius; passing your whole age in the hunt and the cultivation of the land and the elegance of your living, despising public affairs; wishing to be known among the first, refusing to be first, living apart by your own judgement. You wished me for a son-in-law in my flourishing youth: to wish this only, not also to have it, was granted. The gods above approve our prayers, and the fates, favouring holy minds, fulfil what good men have wished. And now you feel, beneath the honour of a perpetual tomb, how reverent I remain toward your daughter and toward you. For, a widowed son-in-law, I now pay these pious gifts; for I shall never cease to be both widowed and a son-in-law.

9. ATTUSIA LUCANA SABINA, MY WIFE. Thus far our dirge, performing its rites in pious measures, has sung of those dear, and likewise wept with due funeral. Now my grief and torments and the wound not to be touched — the death of my wife, snatched away, must be commemorated by me. Noble from your forefathers and of the bright origin of the senate, but more bright, Sabina, for your good character: you I, a young man, mourned, cheated in my first years, and for nine Olympiads, widowed, I weep you. Nor is it permitted to lull the grief, overlaid with age, to sleep; for it ever grows raw for me, almost fresh. Others admit the solaces of a grieving time: long days make these wounds heavier. I torment my grey hairs, cheated by a celibate life; and the more alone I am, the more sorrowful I pass my days. The wound is fed by the silent, mute house and the cold bed, because I share my ills with none, my goods with none. I grieve if another's wife is good; I grieve, on the other hand, if she is bad: as a pattern you are ever before me. From either side you come to me as a torment: whether she is bad, because you would have been unlike her; or good, because like. I do not lament empty wealth and idle joys, but that you, young, were snatched from me, your young husband. Glad, chaste, dignified, renowned in race and renowned in beauty, both the grief and the glory of Ausonius your husband: you, about now to complete four times seven Decembers, left behind two children, our pledges. They, by the favour of God, as your prayers were, flourish, heaped with the goods you desired; and I pray that they thrive, and that at last, both surviving, my embers may announce this to your ash.

10. AUSONIUS, MY LITTLE SON. I will not defraud you, unwept, of a mindful complaint, you, my firstborn son, called a boy by my name: whom, while you were practising to loose your murmurs in your first words, of full promise, we mourned with funeral rites. You, set in your great-grandfather's bosom, a shared funeral, that you might not suffer the reproach of a tomb of your own.
11. PASTOR, MY GRANDSON BY MY SON. You too, untimely boy, broke off the ripe griefs, a bitter mourning for your grandsire, dear grandson Pastor, whose sure hope you would have been, the third offspring of your father Hesperius. The name, which chance had given (because a shepherd's pipe first piped a pastoral melody at your birth), was late understood as a token of a brief life: because the breath flees from the reeds blown upon, you die, struck by the weight of a hurled tile, which a workman's hand cast down from the roof. This was no workman's hand: that was the sure hand of bloody fate, that would put up a guilty one. Alas, what vows of mine, what joys you break, Pastor! That tile, hurled, sought my own head; O worthier you, who would have bemoaned the fates of my old age and complained, mourning, at my funeral!

12. JULIA DRYADIA, MY SISTER. If there was any virtue which a prudent woman would wish to be her own, my sister Dryadia by no means lacked it; nay, she had many which the stronger sex and the nobility of men would wish to have: learned enough to guard her life by the distaff and her good name, learned in good morals, herself teaching her own; to whom truth was dearer than life, and her one care to know God and to love her brother before all others. While still young she lost her husband, but, shunning frivolity, she equalled the austere old in character, and prolonged a cheerful life through six decades, and died in the home and under the roof where her father had died.
13. AVITIANUS, MY BROTHER. Avitianus, my own brother, O Muse, present with a funeral complaint. He, younger than I in birth, but my elder in genius, took up our father's arts. But hostile Atropos forbade him to enjoy the glad flower of youth and to pass beyond the bounds of grown age. Alas, what grief for his companions! Alas, how great the glories of life, what cultivation of hope, O brother, you, a young man, forsake — my brother by the law of the flesh and by the rise of blood, but almost a son in love!

14. VALERIUS LATINUS EUROMIUS, MY SON-IN-LAW. O glory of an illustrious race, O bitter death to me, Euromius, son-in-law chosen from the company of young men, you die, snatched from me in the flower of your earliest youth, scarcely well known as the father of a glad child. You, sprung from the stock of chiefs, and surpassing even those from whom the race of bright nobility came; comely of face, good in genius, eloquent and vigorous in every dexterity, and outstanding in fidelity. This the prefecture's seat, this the Illyrian shore experienced with you as governor, and the treasury itself as your client. Yet nothing of your praise was taken by the brevity of your life: ripe in disposition, you die, bitter in your funeral.
15. POMPONIUS MAXIMUS, MY KINSMAN. And you, my brother not by blood but in a brother's stead, Maximus, now dead, our dirge shall sing; for you, allied to me as the husband of my sister, leave her a widow, robbed of the fruit of your years. Not your house alone felt this: the wounded senate-house of Bordeaux, alas, felt the bitter calamity, thriving while you were foremost, sinking when you failed, and, at your death, falling into the rank of a Valentinus. Alas, why, Maximus, snatched from us, do you not enjoy your son, in the fruit and flower of grandchildren? But you do enjoy them, if a divine portion dwells among the shades, and it is granted to know what joys shall one day be: here too a longer fruition of glad things is held — to have anticipated long what now you share.

16. VERIA LICERIA, WIFE OF ARBORIUS, MY SISTER'S SON. You too, whether mine by the name of daughter-in-law or in a daughter's stead, Veria, have the song of the last honour. If your uprightness, if your beauty and fame and fidelity, the wool-working hands of a compliant wife, were now to be praised, the voice of your great-grandfather Eusebius would have to be summoned from afar, from the depths of the shades. Since he, long since buried, his life now done, has transferred his part into my words, receive, my niece, wept over, the funereal complaints, wife of my Arborius, to be commemorated; to whom, leaving small solaces of a great grief, you forsake your children, whereby the more you torment me. But, that the care of your beloved husband may not be wanting to you, you cultivate the monuments now joined to your marriage-chamber. Here, where was your first wedding, there is the sad seat of your tomb: you may be called a bride more than one entombed.

17. POMPONIUS MAXIMUS HERCULANUS, MY SISTER'S SON. Nor let the dirge, with its sad modulation, leave you, my sister's son, silent and without honour — you, upon whose grown promise there was a great abundance of high praise. But it will befit rather to commemorate than to praise the dead. This glory, my mother's and mine, in the time of grown age the envious force of fate struck down. Alas, what a fruit, Maximus, eloquent and musical and keen, good in mind, vast in genius, swift of foot, fair of body, shrewd in tongue, melodious in voice! Take the sad gifts of your forefathers, the beginnings of a tearful complaint, which, in funereal modulation, your sorrowing uncle offers you.
18. FLAVIUS SANCTUS, HUSBAND OF PUDENTILLA, WHO WAS SISTER OF MY SABINA. You who cultivate jest and gladness, who condemn sad things and fear no one and do nothing to be feared, who catch no one with snares nor provoke with lawsuit, but lead a just and clement and wise life: revere with pious lips and good words the tranquil shade and the gentle end of Sanctus, who passed his military service assiduously without any storm, governor under whom the Rutupine land (Britain) rejoiced, whose tranquil old age of eighty years no worse day altered. Therefore pray, favouring, that such repose as were the seasons of his life, Sanctus may pass among the shades.

19. NAMIA PUDENTILLA, MY KINSWOMAN. And you address Pudentilla with the last words, you who have care for fame and for uprightness. Noble, thrifty, upright, glad, chaste, comely — she held continuously the marriage of Sanctus. Keeping inviolate the praises of a chaste life, she ruled her own wealth while her husband lived at leisure; not for that reason reproaching, nor with brow clouded against her husband, that a woman alone managed the whole house. Alas, too young, but glad with her son and husband surviving, she met, patient, her last fates: of one mind with our Sabina, and once her sister, and called by me sister with an unblemished name. Now too pious care recalls her peaceful shade and honours Pudentilla with the honour of speech.
20. LUCANUS TALISIUS, THEIR SON. Nor now shall you, sole hope of your mother, the youth Talisius, my cousin, be unremembered, snatched in the first years of flowering age — yet already a husband, already too soon a father. You might think that fate had hastened, lest your father, so quickly made a grandfather, should call this a bitter funeral.

21. ATTUSIA LUCANA TALISIA AND MINUCIUS REGULUS, MY KIN. Our acquaintance with you was slight, Attusia, and with your husband, Regulus, plainly none. But you are the own sister of our Sabina, and you too, Regulus, have the name of kinsman. Having drawn names so dear to us, let us, mournful, bind them in the homage of our song, although the funeral honour reaches them as they lie afar, their shades in the Santonican land.
22. SEVERUS CENSOR JULIANUS, FATHER OF MY SON'S WIFE. Cease, you ancients, you Calpurnian names, to hold this title of Frugi (the Thrifty) as the peculiar glory of your race; nor let Cato alone ever please himself as censor with these titles, nor Aristides alone as the just for himself; for whoever was wise and cultivated truth and faith, let him bear himself as your companion, Censor. You, grave and courteous, relaxed with justice, learned to join a balance to austere things; you wished to ally our houses, though I was not adopted by you nor joined by blood. Surely some likenesses of your character in me, an image of my genius, provided the cause; or already the turning of Fortune was so wheeling, that such good vows gave weight to the fates. If you feel anything among the shades, this cherishes your mind — that what you had wished to come to pass, God willed it.

23. PAULINUS AND DRYADIA, CHILDREN OF PAULINUS AND OF MEGENTIRA, MY SISTER'S DAUGHTER. You who bore the name and face of your father, Paulinus, who were the image of your lost sire; because of whom the grief of your wretched mother had begun to abate, when your form set forth your father, and gave back his ways, and to those ways would have added that eloquence which Paulinus your father lacked: you are snatched in glad and budding years, and you trouble your mother's heart, still raw. For we weep also a sister snatched from the marriage-bed, alas, by no ripe death — Dryadia. We weep, I in the first place, who am her mother's uncle, and you I love as the offspring of children. She died amid her mother's hands and her father's kisses; you, far off in the Spanish region — you, tender, are plucked, a new flower in your earliest age, a youth not yet with purple-cinctured cheeks! Four children had this mother, now dead, brought forth, but she has already given doubled funerals to the tombs. Let this be enough, father Paulinus; the division is made: the rest of the offspring is owed to the mother.

24. PAULINUS, MY SISTER'S SON-IN-LAW. Whoever loves a glad genius, whoever loves fair character, and whoever cultivates faith with holy piety, let him revere with me the shade of Paulinus, sprinkling friendly tears and bearing the yearly libations. My contemporary, Paulinus, and having gained my sister's daughter in marriage: thus almost my son-in-law. Your mother was of Aquitanian stock; for to your father Cossio Vasates was the home, a municipal race. Having deserved the office of the prefect's archives, then set over the Libyan accounts, you take rich rewards. For Iberian Tarraco offered you the tribunal of a corrector, eager to be your client. You, cherishing your mother-in-law in a mother's stead, could not be reckoned a kinsman, since you enjoyed the place of a son. Among concordant friends you lived, faithful, having completed eighteen Olympiads.

25. AEMILIA DRYADIA, MY AUNT. You too, my aunt Dryadia, I revere with tearful measures and pious lips — I, the son of your sister, almost your son — you whom envious death snatched from the marriage-chamber and the nuptial torches; and the funeral honour changed your bed in the bier's stead. You were learning in me, my aunt, how to become a mother; whence now I, a son, render you this sad office.
26. JULIA CATAPHRONIA, MY FATHER'S SISTER. Nay, impart to my aunt Cataphronia too, O Muse, your funereal complaints. Unwed, she cultivated the love of vowed virginity, and, a sparing old woman; and to me, what she could, though out of a poor sum, she gave, as a mother. Therefore, commemorated, hail; and, summoned in a mother's stead, sad farewell.
27. JULIA VENERIA, MY FATHER'S SISTER. And my aunt Veneria died early: to her I sing again brief, measured melodies, that her gentle little ash may thrive after its labour, and, swift-footed, may approach the silent places of Erebus.

28. JULIA IDALIA, MY COUSIN. Little Idalia too there was, who, endowed with the name of the Paphian (Venus), deserved also the beauty of Venus; who was born to me almost as a sister, for she was the daughter of my aunt, whom the dirge celebrates in pious honour with a funereal song.
29. AEMILIA MELANIA, MY SISTER. And you, Aemilia, a sister scarcely known to me, receive the laments which sad elegies owe to your ash. An equal-aged infancy joined our cradles, although you were older by one consulship. But too envious Lachesis, hastening, completed your times, and gave bitter funerals to the shades. Sent on before, then, farewell, and revere the shades of our parents, of him who came in greater age and of her in less.
30. POMPONIA URBICA, MOTHER OF MY SON'S WIFE, WIFE OF JULIANUS THE CENSOR. As a woman of illustrious race, so of the morals of the ancients, Urbica, ennobled by the marriage-bed of the Censor; strong in inborn virtues, and increased by those which your husband taught, which your father and mother taught — such as Tanaquil had, such as Pythagorean Theano, and such as she who, without precedent, met death at her husband's slaying. And had fate granted you so to exchange your lot, the Censor would still be living in this our time; but neither did you, long tormented under a widowed age, follow your husband at once to the desired end. Now I, Ausonius, with your son-in-law and your children, father of your son's wife, bring you the yearly rites with sad complaints.

3. Verses both begun and ended with monosyllables, so that they run back from the end of the verse to the beginning. The frail affairs of men Chance feeds and rules and destroys — Chance, doubtful and forever wavering, which kindly Hope cherishes — Hope, bounded by no age, whose limit is Death — Death, greedy, which Night drowns in infernal gloom — Night, that shall pass away in its turn, when the golden Light shall have returned — Light, granted as a gift of the gods, whose forerunner is the Sun — the Sun, from whom mighty-in-arms Mars does not hide in the theft of Venus — Mars, sprung of no father, whom the Thracian race worships — that unbridled race of men, for whom into every crime rushes the law (Fas) — to slaughter a man in their rites: that is the savage custom of the place — the savage custom of a bold people, whom no law holds — the law which Justice founded by a natural command — Justice begotten of the piety of men, Justice, the sure mind of God — the Mind, which with heavenly sense waters the deserving Heart — the Heart, vigorous, holding the likeness of the world, the strength and force of the soul: yet here there is no force; it is only a jest and a thing of naught.

5. Rival of the gods, imitator of Nature, all-bearing Art, that my game may be eager to please Pacatus, be the leader of my work. Though the law be strict, unlovely, and not suited to songs, yet under so great a judge it shall receive the right of utterance; for to the ridiculous too glory is given, unless chance forbid.
6. ON THE LIMBS. In boys a new tooth marks the first seventh year; a stronger voice anticipates the years of puberty. Unconquered both by winds and by suns is the forehead of men; with their flesh the sinews unite the hard bone. Restless, vigorous, rounded, keen, and warm, the heart palpitates, whence the senses are strong, which the ruling mind quickens; and the talkative mouth renders them into words by a measured law. How strong is the dark gall — how small a portion of a man! How slender, and how great a bodily mass it bears — the leg! Under how great a weight does the foot guide our way!

7. ON DISCONNECTED THINGS. Often in marriages the dowry becomes harmful, if it is too great. Either sex is powerful, but the male prevails in command. He who acts rightly, not he who lords it, shall be king. Strife harasses friendships and dissolves treaties. Begin whatever you do: the first part of a work is as good as the whole. Praise insinuates the deserving into heaven and sets them among the gods. A city is crowded both with disciplines and with vices. In safe cities, more fortified than the cities is the citadel. Great is the honour of gold, yet the price of gold is bronze. The long day is laborious for a man, but a temperance is night, of which the wakeful, restless race of the Ethiopians is deprived, where the clear light ever abides in eternal revolution.
8. ON THE GODS. The heaven-dwellers too have their monosyllables. First of the gods is Fas, which is Themis to the Greeks; after her Rhea, who to the Latins is Ops; then the brother of Jove and Consus, Tartarean Dis; and the sister and wife of her brother, the queen of the gods, Vis (Force, that is, Juno-Vesta); and the father who is found with a four-yoked chariot, the Sun; and he who stirs the fierce motions of war, mighty-in-arms Mars, whom never does piety, never does good Peace solicit. Nor shall you be passed in silence, dweller of the groves, Maenalian Pan; nor the genius of houses, the Lar begotten of Larunda; and prevailing over the rivers of Italy, the sulphurous Nar; and she who avenges the perjuries against the gods, night-coloured Styx; and the leveller of the sail-flying sea, the white south-west wind, Libs; and Hope, that never forsakes a man in doubtful straits.

9. ON FOODS. Nor shall I keep silent of our foods, which ancient custom holds, to which is added, for a relish, the salt of the sea. Once a common food for the herd and for man was the acorn, before indeed the spiky grain was at hand in the fields. Soon spelt, and the porridge-making meal from the flour of spelt, with which the people of Romulus once furnished their tables — hence food, hence drink, when the porridge was diluted with water. Among the grains is the cumin, equalling pepper in its bite; and from the Pelusian seed the flat, rounded lentil; and, defended by a double shell, the five-kinded nut; and what is pleasing for food and drink, the keen labour of the bees, honey: that liquor of a strange nature, on whose top the lees float.
10. ON HISTORIES (Myths). A new solace it gave you, Phoebus, the Oebalian flower (Hyacinth). By another flower the spring made sacred is guilty of the death of Narcissus. The evil glory of the slaying of Adonis is the lightning-swift boar. The perjured Lapith (Ixion) the Junonian cloud mocks; and the Parnassian lot of the Delphi-dweller (Apollo) mocks the grandson of Aeacus too. The Thracian, the Libyan, and the Cimmerian strait the cow (Io) cuts through. Not without the fate of a Hamadryad falls the tree-trunk of the forest. By that with which Venus was begotten, the Saturnian sickle, it was cut off. Dry amid the Scythian rocks stood the cross for the birds (where Prometheus hung), whence from Prometheus' body a bloody dew sprinkles the crags, and the whetstone-rock breeds dire aconite. When Ibycus perished, the high-flying crane was the informer. At the tomb of the grandson of Aeacus (Achilles) was slaughtered the sister-in-law of Andromache (Polyxena). In the Argive prison slow death came upon Philopoemen. The third spoils of honour the despoiled Armorican lord gave. A late death, by a poisoned draught, took off Hannibal. What great undeserved affairs of Asia did treachery give over to death! The avenging torch blazed from the Euboean rocks. He stands at the cup of Jove whom Dardanian Tros begot (Ganymede). On swift wings borne above the air, the man of Crete (Daedalus). The savage Thracian (Tereus) brought unchaste violence upon you, Philomela. Barbarous is the Lydian, deceitful the Getan, womanish the Phrygian; treacherous the Ligurians; held at no value the Carian. The robe-trailing Seres comb the woolly fleeces of the forest. Known among three-bodied portents is the Theban Sphinx. Known to the Caledonian brides is the womanish creature, the Strix (screech-owl).

11. ON EARLY SPRING. When the year, from its rise, unbars the flower-bearing spring, all things thrive: every grove grows green, the golden-haired country shines, and the root that is to spread shadows is driven up from its base. No longer, gathered in a dense fall to the earth, flows the snow. The fragrance of these breathes, like the glory of Mount Lebanon, the frankincense. Now over the sea flits the robe-trailing Seres-merchant.
12. BY QUESTION AND ANSWER. Who goes in for the penalty in a capital trial? The surety (vas). What if the suit be one of money — who shall be given? The bondsman (praes). Who is matched against the murmillo? The equal-handed Thracian (Thraex). Among the virtues, what is the name for Mercury? The thief (fur). Censers and bowls — what is the third vessel of the gods? The platter (lanx). What land, girt by the sea, bred Hippocrates? Cos. Does the flock or the kingdom trouble the daughter of Minos more? The flock (grex). What, besides a cloud, was set upon the Phaeacians? A mountain (mons). Tell, in the absence of food and sleep, what is fatter? The dormouse (glis). Tell, what makes hides suit shields? Glue (glus). Of "sponte" (the ablative case), what will be the nominative? Spons. What four-foot creature is joined to the auspices by birds of song? The mouse (mus). What floats on the sea, that does not swim in a river? Pitch (pix). What contains twelve equal parts? The as. If a third part be wanting, what remains? The bes.

13. ON GREEK AND LATIN MONOSYLLABIC LETTERS. The leader of the elements thrives in Latin studies — A; and last among the Argive characters is written Ω (omega). What Eta is among the Aeolians, and what Epsilon avails, this is the Latin E. The Latin E, always short, the Doric voice supplies as Ε. With this rounded and shrill sound the Attic race denies — Ο (omicron). What Ω and O are, the Roman voice balances as Greek with O. I am a letter, a full voice like Iota, commanding — I. Unknown to the Cecropian (Greek) characters, sounding funereal — V. Pythagoras' fork, I lie open with ambiguous branches — Y. In Greek words I am never seen last — M. A reclining Zeta, if it should rise, will be the character that is read as N. Imitating the Maeander and its wandering bends, I wander — Ξ (xi). The divided monosyllable of Beta is the Italic B. Not the form, but the voice of Delta I bear — the Roman D. What the form of a hostile yoke is, that Π (pi) will make. If you write the Latin P (Pe), I shall be the Cecropian P (rho). And the Rho which is Greek will be changed into the Latin P. As a mast bears the sailyard on its top, so am I — T. The breath here, with its blowing quickening the slightest things — H. This, added in Latin to three names only — K, after C prevailed, having before performed the office of Gamma; and, doubled, it gave another title in its own stead — G. Girt with two handles, when it is Iota, you shall read — Ϡ (sampi). In Latium the number ten, but among the Argives — Χ (chi). This image of a crane, the Palamedean, is stretched out — Φ (phi). Coppa I was once in Boeotia, now the Latin Q. With my three-horned-forked shape, I am nearly the last — Ψ (psi).

14. THE GRAMMARIAN-SCOURGE. And word-craft? Hiss now, you who, too fierce, condemn frivolous things: even a worthless ware has its price! As Ennius records, may a gladdening "gau" (joy) fill you. May the livid mind of men cook up the congealed pus of gall. Tell, what does the Catalepton of Maro signify? In these he set the "al" of the Celts; there follows, no clearer, "tau." Is "sil" the word of a foreign name or of Latium? And what, ill-mingled with its german, is the death-bearing "min"? Why does one thing (res) mark command, lawsuit, and love? In twin skiffs decked over the sea, is it "pons" (a bridge)? In the Bucolics Maro said "saepes" (hedge); why does Cicero say "saeps"? The familiar word, best known to all — if you recall — "lac" (milk): why is it condemned, so that reason rather makes it "lact"? Or is "seps," the deadly bane of Libya, a Roman word? If the innocent is good, and his opposite, the accused — is there "sons" (the guilty)? Rich in wealth — why does it have the name "dis" from Stygian Jove? Whence does the man of Rudiae (Ennius) say of the high-sounding house of the gods "cael"? And by whose custom is it that he added "endo" "suam do" (into his own house)? Or, speaking of foliage, why does he say the poplar "fros" (frond)? But whither do I advance? What is the end, what the measure and the goal? Indulge me, Pacatus, a good man, learned, easy of temper; this whole work is scattered, like the hair of Antiphila: peace.

The [wife] of godlike [Antenor], priestess of Athena of battle-rousing Pallas golden of the Argives, to Odysseus [son of Laertes] and Menelaus, the royal son of Atreus, [deep]-waisted Theano spoke well-built with the gods heart [at midnight]
led and their father, the wise hero, made the whole speech of the Achaeans known to king Priam and his sons.
Then heralds rushed through the broad town and brought together the ranks of the Trojans into the assembly-place of the army. Loud rumor ran everywhere;
and raising their hands to the immortal gods, they prayed for an end to their griefs. Muse, who was the first to begin the words of justice? Menelaus son of Pleisthenes spoke with enchanting words and voice, having conferred with the Graces with beautiful robes:
Battle-loving Trojans: Zeus, the ruler on high who sees all, is not to blame for the great woes of mortals; all men have a chance to reach unswerving Justice, the attendant of holy

Eunomia and prudent Themis. Prosperous are they whose children take Justice to live with them.
But shameless Hybris, flourishing with shifty greed and lawless empty-headedness, who will swiftly bestow on a man someone else's wealth and power, and then send him into deep ruin—Hybris destroyed the arrogant sons of the Earth, the Giants.
A dark-prowed ship, carrying Theseus, steadfast in the din of battle, and twice seven splendid Ionian youths, was cleaving the Cretan sea;
for northern breezes fell on the far-shining sail, by the will of glorious Athena, shaker of the aegis. And the holy gifts of Cypris with her lovely headband scratched the heart of Minos.
He no longer kept his hand away from the maiden; he touched her white cheeks. And Eriboea cried out to the descendant of Pandion with his bronze breastplate. Theseus saw, and he rolled his dark eyes under his brows; cruel pain tore his heart, and he spoke: Son of greatest Zeus, the spirit you guide in your heart is no longer pious. Hero, restrain your overbearing force.

Whatever the all-powerful fate of the gods has granted for us, and however the scale of Justice inclines, we shall fulfill our appointed destiny when it comes. As for you, hold back from your oppressive scheme. It may be that the dear lovely-named daughter of Phoenix went to the bed of Zeus beneath the brow of Ida and bore you, greatest of mortals, but I too was borne by the daughter of rich Pittheus, who coupled with the sea-god Poseidon, and the violet-haired Nereids gave her a golden veil. And so, war-lord of Knossos,
I bid you to restrain your grievous violence; for I would not want to see the lovely immortal light of Dawn if you were to subdue one of these young people against her will.
Before that we will show the force of our arms, and what comes after that a god will decide.

So spoke the hero, excellent with the spear; and the sailors were astonished at the man's extraordinary boldness. The son-in-law of Helios was angered in his heart, and he wove a new scheme, and spoke: Father Zeus, great in strength, hear me! If indeed the white-armed Phoenician girl bore me to you, now send forth from the sky a fire-haired lightning bolt, a conspicuous sign. And you, if Troezenian Aethra bore you to Poseidon the earth-shaker, bring this splendid gold ornament on my hand back from the depths of the sea, casting your body boldly down to your father's home. And you shall see whether my prayers are heard by the son of Cronus, lord of the thunder and ruler of all.
And Zeus, great in strength, heard his blameless prayer, and brought about a majestic honor for Minos, wanting it to be seen by all for the sake of his dear son; he sent the lightning. And the hero, steadfast in battle, seeing the marvel which pleased his spirit, stretched his hands to the glorious sky and said, Theseus, you see Zeus' clear gifts to me. It is your turn to leap into the loud-roaring sea. And your father lord Poseidon, son of Cronus, will grant you supreme glory throughout the well-wooded earth. So he spoke. And Theseus' spirit did not recoil; he stood on the well-built deck, and leapt, and the precinct of the sea received him willingly. And the son of Zeus was astonished in his heart, and gave an order to hold the ornate ship before the wind; but fate was preparing another path.

The swift-moving ship hurtled forwards; and the north wind, blowing astern, drove it along. But the race of Athenian youths was afraid, when the hero jumped into the sea, and they shed tears from their lily eyes, awaiting grievous compulsion. But sea-dwelling dolphins swiftly carried great Theseus to the home of his father, lord of horses;
and he came to the hall of the gods. There he saw the glorious daughters of prosperous Nereus, and was afraid; for brightness shone like fire from their splendid limbs, and ribbons woven with gold whirled around their hair. They were delighting their hearts in a dance, with flowing feet. And he saw in that lovely dwelling the dear wife of his father, holy, ox-eyed Amphitrite. She threw a purple cloak around him and placed on his curly hair a perfect wreath, dark with roses, which once deceptive Aphrodite had given her at her marriage. Nothing that the gods will is unbelievable to sensible men. Theseus appeared beside the ship with its slender stern. Oh, from what thoughts did he stop the war-lord of Knossos, when he emerged unwetted from the sea, a marvel to all, and the gifts of the gods shone on his body.

The splendid-throned maidens cried out with new-founded joy, and the sea resounded. Nearby the young people sang a paean with lovely voices.
God of Delos, may the choruses of the Ceans warm your heart, and may you grant god-sent noble fortune.
:
King of sacred Athens, lord of the luxuriously-living Ionians, why has the bronze-belled trumpet just now sounded a war song?
Does some enemy of our land beset our borders, leading an army? Or are evil-plotting robbers, against the will of the shepherds, rustling our flocks of sheep by force? What is it that tears your heart? Speak; for I think that you of all mortals have the aid of valiant young men at your disposal, son of Pandion and Creusa.
:
Just now a herald arrived, having come by foot on the long road from the Isthmus. He tells of the indescribable deeds of a mighty man. That man killed overweening

Sinis, who was the greatest of mortals in strength; he is the son of Lytaeus the Earthshaker, son of Cronus. And he has slain the man-killing boar in the valleys of Cremmyon, and reckless
Sciron. He has closed the wrestling school of Cercyon; Procoptes has met a better man and dropped the powerful hammer of Polypemon.
I fear how this will end.
:
Who is the man said to be, and from where? How is he equipped? Is he leading a great army with weapons of war?
Or does he come alone with only his attendants, like a traveller wandering among foreign people, this man who is so strong, valiant, and bold, who has overcome the powerful strength of such great men? Indeed a god impels him, so that he can bring justice down on the unjust; for it is not easy to accomplish deed after deed and not meet with evil.

In the long course of time all things come to an end.
:
The herald says that only two men accompany him, and that he has a sword slung over his bright shoulders and two polished javelins in his hands, and a well-made Laconian hat on his head with its fire-red hair. A purple tunic covers his chest, and a woolen Thessalian cloak.
Bright red Lemnian fire flashes from his eyes. He is a boy in the prime of youth, intent on the playthings of Ares: war and battles of clashing bronze.
He is on his way to splendor-loving Athens.
There are countless paths of divine song for one who has received gifts from the Pierian Muses, and upon whose songs the violet-eyed maidens, the garland-bearing Graces, cast honor. Now, much-praised Cean ingenuity, weave something new, in lovely, prosperous Athens. It is fitting for you to travel the greatest road, since you have received an outstanding honor from Calliope.

when the golden heifer, the rose-fingered daughter of Inachus, left Argos, land of horses, by the counsels of widely powerful, greatest Zeus?
When Argus, who could see all around with untiring eyes, was bidden by golden-robed Hera, the greatest queen, to guard the lovely-horned heifer, unresting and unsleeping;
and the son of Maia could not evade him, neither by shining day nor by sacred night. Did it then happen that the swift-footed messenger [of Zeus] then killed [the son of Earth] with mighty offspring Argus? Or was it that unutterable cares?
Or did the Pierian Muses bring about rest from troubles?
For me, the most secure [path?] is the one which when she arrived at the flowery banks of the Nile, [gadfly-driven] Io, bearing the child Epaphus. There [she bore him?] ruler over linen-robed teeming with majestic and greatest mortal from this race Cadmus, son of Agenor, begat Semele in seven-gated Thebes, and she bore the rouser of Bacchants,

Daughters of Zeus ruling on high, famed for the lyre, Pierian Muses weave
Isthmian land son-in-law of wise Nereus of the island god-built gates of Pelops' shining island yoked horses to chariots, and they flew thick maidens of sleep, like honey to the mind our ancient city [homes] on the shores of the sea
the rays of the sun and Makelo, loving the distaff, by the fair-flowing stream speaks fawning with the voice
I am bereaved with double-edged grief deprivation totally on the third day warlike Minos came with a host of Cretans in fifty ships with flashing sterns.
And by the will of Zeus Eukleios he subdued the deep-waisted maiden Dexithea, and left with her half of his people, battle-loving men, to whom he gave the craggy land as their share; and then he sailed off to the lovely city of Knossos, the king, the son of Europa. And in the tenth month the bride with beautiful hair bore

Euxantius, to be ruler over the glorious island daughters city cut deep by the sun's rays.
From his (Euxantius'?) family descended Argeius, who has a strong hand and the spirit of a lion, whenever the need for battle befalls him; and he is light on his feet, and does not the fine qualities of his father, those which Apollo, famed for the bow, bestowed on Pantheides: the art of healing, and friendly honor towards guests. With a good share of the Graces, and admired by many men, when he ended his life he left behind five greatly-praised sons, one of whom the son of Cronus seated on high has made a victor at the Isthmus, in return for good deeds, and has given a share of other shining garlands. I say it now and I always will: excellence has the greatest glory.
Wealth keeps company with worthless men as well, and it tends to swell a man's thoughts; but he who does well to the gods cheers his heart with a more glorious hope.

If a mortal has been granted health and can live off his own goods, he rivals the most fortunate. There is joy in all human life as long as it lacks disease and helpless deprivation. The rich man desires great things the same way the poor man desires less.
But it is not sweet for mortals to get everything easily; they always seek to catch what flees from them.
A man whose spirit is whirled about by the lightest ambitions has honor only as long as he lives. Excellence is a difficult struggle, but when the struggle is completed rightly it leaves a man, even when he dies, the enviable ornament of renown.
Clio, giver of sweet gifts, sing the praises of the mistress of most fertile Sicily, Demeter, and of her violet-garlanded daughter, and of Hieron's swift horses, racers at Olympia;

for they sped with majestic Victory and with Aglaia by the wide-whirling Alpheus, where they made the son of Deinomenes a prosperous man, a victor winning garlands.
And the people shouted,
Ah! thrice-blessed man! Zeus has granted him the honor of ruling most widely over the Greeks, and he knows not to hide his towered wealth under black-cloaked darkness.
The temples teem with cattle-sacrificing festivities; the streets teem with hospitality. Gold flashes and glitters, the gold of tall ornate tripods standing before the temple, where the Delphians administer the great precinct of Phoebus beside the Castalian stream. A man should honor the god, for that is the greatest prosperity.
For indeed, once the ruler of horse-taming Lydia,
Croesus—when Zeus was bringing about the decreed fate, and Sardis was being sacked by the Persian army—Croesus was protected by the god of the golden lyre,

Fortunate in your fate, commander of the Syracusans, riders of whirling horses: you, if any man on earth today, will rightly understand this honor, sweet gift of the violet-garlanded Muses. Now, calm your righteous mind; rest it from cares, and consider: a hymn, woven with the help of the deep-waisted Graces, is sent from the holy island to your glorious city by your guest-friend, the brilliant servant of Ourania with her golden headband. He wants to pour forth his voice from his heart to praise Hieron. High above, slicing the deep air with his swift golden wings, the eagle, messenger of loud-thundering, wide-ruling
Zeus, trusts boldly in his powerful strength, and thin-voiced birds crouch in fear. The peaks of the great earth do not restrain him, nor the rough, choppy waves of the untiring sea. In the everlasting void he shifts his delicate wings, riding the gusts of the west wind, a conspicuous sight for men.

So now for me there are countless paths of song leading in every direction, thanks to dark-haired Nike and Ares with his bronze breastplate, to sing of your excellence, noble sons of Deinomenes. May the god not tire of doing good. Beside the wide-whirling Alpheus, golden-armed Dawn saw the victory of the chestnut horse Pherenicus, a runner swift as a wind-storm, and she saw him win in very holy Pytho. Laying my hand on the earth, I make this declaration: never in any contest has he been fouled by the dust of faster horses as he strained toward the finish-line. In force he is like Boreas; obeying his rider, he speeds a new victory and new applause to hospitable Hieron.
Prosperous is he to whom a god has given a share of fine things, and a rich life to live out with enviable luck. For no man on earth was born to be fortunate in everything.

So it was, they say, that the gate-destroying unconquerable son of Zeus of the flashing thunderbolt went down to the halls of slender-ankled Persephone to bring up into the light from Hades the razor-toothed dog, son of the fearsome Echidna. There he saw the souls of miserable mortals by the streams of Cocytus, like leaves swirled by the wind along the sheep-pasturing headlands of shining Ida. Among them, the shade of Porthaon's bold, spear-wielding descendant stood out.
When the marvellous hero, son of Alcmene, saw him shining in his armor, he stretched the clear-sounding bowstring onto his bow, and opened the lid of his quiver and drew out a bronze-tipped arrow. But the soul of Meleager appeared in front of him and spoke to him, knowing him well: Son of great Zeus, stand where you are, and calm your spirit—

Do not shoot a harsh arrow from your hands in vain against the souls of those who have perished. You have no need to fear. So he spoke. And the son of Amphitryon was astonished, and said, What god or mortal raised such a fine young plant as you? In what land? Who killed you? No doubt Hera with her beautiful belt will soon send that killer after me. But that must be the concern of golden-haired Pallas. And Meleager answered him, in tears, It is hard for men on earth to sway the minds of the gods;
for otherwise my father, horse-driving Oineus, would have appeased the anger of holy, white-armed Artemis with her garland of buds, when he entreated her with sacrifices of many goats and red-backed cattle. But the maiden goddess' anger was unconquerable; she sent an immensely violent boar, a ruthless fighter, to Calydon, the place of lovely choruses; there, his strength raging like a flood, he cut down vine-rows with his tusk, and slaughtered flocks, and whatever mortals came across his path.

We, the best of the Hellenes, fought hard to sustain the hateful battle against him, for six days continuously. But when some god gave the upper hand to the Aetolians, we buried those whom the loud-roaring boar had killed in his violent attacks: Ancaeus, and Agelaus, the best of my dear brothers, whom
Althaea bore in the far-famed halls of Oineus.
Ruinous fate destroyed For not yet did the hostile goddess, the savage daughter of Leto, [stop] her anger. We fought hard for the beast's fiery hide with the Couretes, steadfast in battle. Then I killed, among many others, Iphiclus and noble Aphares, my mother's swift brothers; for strong-spirited Ares does not discern a friend in battle—shafts fly blindly from the hands against the souls of the enemy, and bring death to whomever the god wishes.

My mother, the hostile daughter of Thestius, did not take this into account; she brought about my evil fate, the fearless woman, and planned my destruction.
She took the log of my swift doom out of the ornate chest, and burned it. Fate had marked off that this should be the boundary of my life. I happened to be slaying
Clymenus, Daïpylus' valiant son, whose body was flawless; I had overtaken him in front of the towers. The others were fleeing to the well-built ancient city of Pleuron. And my sweet soul diminished; I knew that my strength was gone, aiai! I breathed my last breath in tears, as I left behind splendid youth.
They say that was the only time that the son of Amphitryon, fearless in battle, ever wetted his eyes with tears, pitying the fate of the man who endured grief. And he answered him in this way:

A Boeotian man, Hesiod, attendant of the sweet Muses, said this: He whom the gods honor has a good name among men as well.
I am easily persuaded to send to Hieron my illustrious voice, not from the path. For in this way the roots of fine fortune flourish; may the great father
Zeus guard them, undisturbed, in peace.
Graces with golden distaffs, give fame, which moves the minds of men; for the divinely inspired prophet of the violet-eyed Muses is ready to sing the praises of Phlius and the flourishing plain of Nemean Zeus, where white-armed Hera reared the sheep-slaughtering, deep-voiced lion, the first of Heracles' far-famed labors.
There the heroes with red shields, the best of the Argives, held games for the first time in honor of Archemorus, whom a fiery-eyed monstrous dragon killed in his sleep: a sign of the slaughter to come.

Powerful fate! The son of Oicles could not persuade them to go back to the streets thronged with good men. Hope robs men [of their sense]:
it was she who then sent Adrastus son of Talaus to Thebes to Polyneices The mortal men who crown their golden hair with the triennial garland from those glorious games in Nemea are illustrious;
and now a god has given it to the victorious Automedes, for he stood out among the pentathletes as the shining moon in the mid-month night sky outshines the light of the stars.
In such a way, amid the vast circling crowd of the Greeks, did he display his marvellous body, hurling the wheel-shaped discus, and raise a shout from the people as he flung the shaft of the dark-leaved elder-tree from his hand into the steep sky.
He executed the flashing movement of wrestling, and brought strong-limbed bodies down to the earth with such high-spirited strength, then returned to the dark-whirling waters of the Asopus, whose fame has reached every land, even the farthest reaches of the Nile. And the women skilled with the spear who live by the fair-flowing stream of Thermodon, daughters of horse-driving Ares, have met with your descendants, much-envied lord of rivers, and so has Troy, the city of high gates. Countless reports of your offspring tread wide paths everywhere, of your daughters with shining belts, whom the gods established, with good fortune, as founders of cities that were never to be sacked.

Who does not know the well-built city of dark-haired Thebes, or renowned Aegina, who went to the bed of great Zeus and bore the hero who the land of the Achaeans trials with beautiful robe and Peirene with her twisted garland, and as many other honorable daughters of the ancient resounding river who were overcome in the glorifying beds of gods. city victory the cries of flutes to speak well of golden, violet-haired Cypris, the glorious mother of unbending passions for mortals hymn even for one who is dead everlasting time, would always declare to later generations your victory at Nemea. A fine deed which attains genuine songs of praise is stored up on high with the gods.
With the true remembrance of men, the finest adornment of the [deep-waisted] Muses is left behind even [after death].

There are many of men; but the mind of the gods distinguishes what is hidden in the darkness of night and the better few men what will be.
gave grace and Dionysus city honored by the gods to dwell golden-sceptered whoever takes a fine thing praise for the son of Timoxenos sing praises, with processions [of young men], for his victory in the pentathlon.
Fame, you visit the races [of men?], and eyes peaceful respite now for him his sister's husband has moved the clear-voiced island bee so that the immortal ornament of the Muses will be at hand as a common joy for men, revealing your excellence to men on earth, by the will of Victory you have crowned your golden head with blossoms and brought glory to broad Athens and fame to the Oeneidae, when, in Poseidon's far-famed games, you displayed to the Greeks the swift surge of your feet.

For when he reached the finish-line of the racecourse, breathing out a storm of hot breath, and again moistened the cloaks of the spectators with olive oil, rushing into the close-packed crowd when he rounded the fourth turn of the course, the spokesmen of the wise judges proclaimed him twice an Isthmian victor, and twice in Nemea, beside the sacred altar of Zeus son of Cronus.
Glorious Thebes also welcomed him fittingly, and spacious Argos, and Sicyon, and those who dwell in Pellene, and in Euboea rich in grain, and on the holy island Aegina. Each man seeks a different path on which to walk to attain conspicuous glory; and the forms of knowledge among men are countless.
Indeed, a man is skillful if he has a share of honor from the Graces and blooms with golden hope, or if he has some knowledge of the prophetic art; another man aims his artful bow at boys; others swell their spirits with fields and herds of cattle.

The future begets unpredictable results: which way will fortune's scale incline? The finest thing is to be envied by many people as a noble man.
I know also the great power of wealth, which makes even a useless man valuable. Why have I steered my song in its straight course so far off the road? Delight is appointed for mortals after victory of flutes mix must
Victory, giver of sweet gifts—to you alone the father seated on high in golden Olympus, standing beside Zeus, you judge the achievement of excellence for immortals and mortals alike. Be gracious, daughter of Styx with her long hair, the upright judge. For your sake even now Metapontion, the city honored by the gods, is filled with delight and with victory processions of young men with fine limbs. They sing the praises of the Pythian victor, the marvellous son of Phaiscus.

To her once the son of Abas and his daughters with beautiful robes set up an altar where many prayers are offered. All-powerful Hera drove these daughters in fear from the lovely halls of Proetus; she yoked their minds to a violent maddening compulsion. For, while still virgins, they entered the sanctuary of the purple-belted goddess, and said that their father far surpassed in wealth the golden-haired consort of holy, widely powerful Zeus. In anger at them, she put a twisted thought into their minds, and they fled to the wooded mountain with terrible screams, leaving behind the city of Tiryns and its god-built streets. For it was now the tenth year since the heroes with their bronze shields, fearless in battle, had left Argos, the city loved by the gods, and lived in Tiryns with their much envied king, because an insurmountable quarrel had arisen, from a slight beginning, between the brothers Proetus and Acrisius. They were destroying their people with lawless feuding and grievous battles, and the people entreated the sons of Abas that, since they had as their share a land rich in barley, the younger one should be the founder of Tiryns, before they fell under ruinous compulsion. And Zeus son of Cronus, honoring the race of Danaus and of horse-driving Lynceus, was willing to put an end to their hateful woes. And the mighty Cyclopes came, and toiled to build a most beautiful wall for the glorious city, where the godlike far-famed heroes lived when they had left behind horse-pasturing Argos. It was from Tiryns that the dark-haired unsubdued daughters of Proetus rushed in their flight.

And woe overcame Proetus' heart, and an alien thought smote him. He decided to plant a double-edged sword in his chest; but his spearmen restrained him with calming words and with the force of their hands. For thirteen whole months his daughters roamed wildly through the shadowy forests and fled through sheep-nurturing Arcadia.
But when their father came to the beautiful stream of Lusus, he washed his skin with its water and called on Leto's daughter with her crimson headdress, the ox-eyed goddess, stretching his hands to the rays of the steed-swift sun, and asked her to deliver his children from their deranged miserable madness. I will sacrifice to you twenty unyoked red oxen. And the huntress, whose father is the highest god, heard him praying. She persuaded Hera, and stopped the godless mania of the bud-garlanded girls.

They built her a sanctuary and an altar right away, and stained it with the blood of sheep, and set up choruses of women. From there you accompanied battle-loving Achaean men to their horse-nurturing city;
and with good fortune you dwell in Metapontion, golden mistress of the people. And a lovely precinct beside the fine waters of the Casas
~ their ancestors established? ~ when at last, by the counsels of the blessed gods, they sacked the well-built city of Priam together with the Atreidae with their bronze breastplates. Whoever has a just mind will find, throughout all time, countless deeds of valor done by the Achaeans.
Clio
He shall stop them from arrogant violence, bringing about judgments of law for mortals:
look how the descendant of Perseus brings his hand down heavily on the neck of the bloodthirsty lion with every type of skill!

For the gleaming, man-subduing bronze refuses to pierce the lion's fearsome body; the sword was bent back. Someday, I prophesy,
there will be a strenuous toil for the Greeks, competing for garlands in the pancratium.
beside the altar of Zeus, the greatest ruler, the blossoms of glory-bringing Victory nurture for men golden, conspicuous fame throughout their lives—for a select few—and when the dark cloud of death covers them, the undying glory of their fine deed is left behind, secure in its destiny.
You too have attained this at Nemea, son of Lampon;
your hair crowned with garlands of flourishing blossoms, [you walk] the lofty streets of the city [of Aeacus, so that] your ancestral island [teems] with gentle-voiced victory processions, in which mortals delight, revealing your overweening strength in the pancratium. Kindly Aegina, daughter of the whirling river,

gave you great honor, shining [your new victory?] like a torch among all Greeks. And a proud maiden [sings the praises of your strength?]
often lightly springing with her feet like a carefree fawn on the flowery [hills]
with her far-famed [companions] who live nearby.
The maidens wear garlands of crimson blossoms and rushes, the native decoration, and sing of your [child], mistress of the all-hospitable [land], and of rosy-armed Endaïs, who bore [godlike Peleus] and the helmeted warrior Telamon, having gone to bed with Aeacus.
Of their battle-rousing sons I shall sing, and of swift Achilles, and the high-spirited son of beautiful Eriboea, Aias, the shield-bearing hero, who stood on the stern of his ship and stopped bold-hearted, bronze [helmeted] Hector in his rush to burn the ships with dread fire, at the time when the son of Peleus stirred fierce wrath [in his breast]

and released the [Dardanians from ruin]. Before they had not left the [many-towered]
marvellous town of Ilium, but had cowered, dazed by fear, before the fierce battle, when Achilles raged destructively across the plain, shaking his murderous spear. But when the fearless son of the violet-garlanded Nereid withdrew from battle,
—as when the North wind, on the dark-blossoming sea, afflicts the spirits of men beneath the waves, when it comes upon them as night begins, but it withdraws with the break of Dawn, who shines on mortals, and a gentle breeze smooths the sea;
they billow their sail with the breath of the South wind, and eagerly reach unhoped-for dry land— in such a way, when the Trojans heard that the spearman Achilles was remaining in his tent because of the golden-haired woman Briseis with lovely limbs, they raised their arms to the gods, seeing a bright gleam from out of the storm. With all speed they left the walls of Laomedon and rushed onto the plain, bringing violent battle, and roused terror in the Danaans. Ares, god of the spear, urged them on, and Loxias Apollo, lord of the Lycians. And they came to the shore of the sea, and fought beside the ships with their fine sterns, and the dark earth ran red with the blood of men slain by the hand of Hector, heroes through the onslaught of godlike with great hopes, and arrogant shouts, the Trojan horsemen the dark-eyed ships the god-built city would have and feasts, in But before that could be they were doomed after all to redden with blood the whirling Scamander, dying at the hands of the tower-destroying [Aeacidae.] Of these, if or on a [pyre] piled high with wood for all-shining Excellence is not hidden and effaced in the lightless [veil?] of night, but always abounding in unfailing glory she roams the earth and the shifting seas. And truly she honors the fame-bringing [island] of Aeacus; she guides the state with garland-loving Eucleia and sound-minded Eunomia, to whom festivities belong, and who guards the cities of pious men in peace.

I cry "alas" for Adonis: fair Adonis is dead.
"Fair Adonis is dead," the Loves cry in answer.
No longer, Cypris, sleep in your purple robes;
wake, wretched one, and clad in dark, beat
your breast and tell all: "Fair Adonis is dead."
I cry "alas" for Adonis: the Loves cry in answer.
Fair Adonis lies in the mountains, his thigh by the tusk,
his white thigh struck by the white tusk, and he grieves Cypris
as he breathes out faintly; the black blood drips
down his snowy flesh, and beneath his brows his eyes grow dim,
and the rose flees from his lip; and about him
dies too the kiss that Cypris will never carry away again.
To Cypris the kiss is dear even of one no longer living,
but Adonis does not know that she kissed him as he died.
I cry "alas" for Adonis: the Loves cry in answer.

A cruel, cruel wound has Adonis in his thigh;
but a greater wound does Cytherea bear against her heart.
About that boy his dear hounds howled,
and the mountain Nymphs weep; and Aphrodite,
loosing her tresses, wanders through the thickets
mourning, unbraided, unsandaled; and the brambles
tear her as she goes and gather her sacred blood;
and shrilly wailing she is borne through the long glens,
crying out for her Assyrian lord and calling her boy.
And about him the black blood welled up around his navel,
and his breast grew crimson from his thighs, and the nipples below
that before were snowy turned purple for Adonis.
"Alas for Cytherea," the Loves cry in answer.
She lost her fair lord, and with him she lost her sacred beauty.
Fair was the form of Cypris while Adonis lived;

but her beauty died with Adonis. "Alas for Cypris,"
all the mountains say, and the oaks say "Adonis."
And the rivers weep for the griefs of Aphrodite,
and the springs in the mountains shed tears for Adonis,
and the flowers redden for sorrow; and Cythera,
through all the slopes, through every glen, sings piteously,
"Alas for Cytherea, fair Adonis is dead."
And Echo cried back, "Fair Adonis is dead."
Who would not have wept "alas" for the dread love of Cypris?
When she saw, when she marked the unstaunchable wound of Adonis,
when she saw the crimson blood about his withering thigh,
spreading wide her arms she wailed: "Stay, Adonis,
ill-fated, stay, Adonis, that for the last time I may reach you,
that I may embrace you and mingle lips with lips.
Wake a little, Adonis, and kiss me one last time,

kiss me as long as the kiss may live,
until you breathe out into my mouth and into my heart
your spirit flows, and I may drain your sweet love-draught,
and drink down your love, and keep this kiss
as Adonis himself, since you, ill-fated, flee me,
flee far, Adonis, and go to Acheron,
to the hateful and savage king, while I, wretched,
live on and am a goddess and cannot follow you.
Take, Persephone, my husband; for you yourself are
far stronger than I, and all beauty flows down to you;
but I am all-luckless, and I bear insatiable grief,
and I weep for Adonis, who is dead to me, and I dread you.
You die, thrice-longed-for, and my longing flits away like a dream,
and Cytherea is widowed, and idle through the house are the Loves.
With you too the girdle has perished. Why, rash one, do you hunt?

Fair as you were, why did you so madly wrestle with a beast?"
So Cypris lamented; the Loves cry in answer,
"Alas for Cytherea, fair Adonis is dead."
The Paphian sheds as many tears as Adonis
sheds blood; and all upon the ground become flowers.
The blood begets the rose, and the tears the anemone.
I cry "alas" for Adonis: fair Adonis is dead.
No longer in the thickets mourn your husband, Cypris.
No fit couch is a lonely bed of leaves for Adonis;
let Adonis, dead though he is, have your own bed, Cytherea.
Even a corpse he is fair, a fair corpse, as one asleep.
Lay him in the soft robes in which he used to slumber,
in which by night beside you he wrought his sacred sleep
upon the all-golden couch; it too longs for grim Adonis.
And cast upon him garlands and flowers; let all things with him,

since he is dead, let all the flowers also wither.
And sprinkle him with Syrian unguents, sprinkle him with myrrh;
let all perfumes perish: your perfume, Adonis, has perished.
Delicate Adonis lies in purple raiment;
and about him, weeping, the Loves groan aloud,
having shorn their locks for Adonis; and one cast down arrows,
another a bow, another a feather, another a quiver;
and one loosed the sandal of Adonis, and others in a basin
of gold carry water, and one washes his thighs,
and another from behind with his wings cools Adonis.
"Alas for Cytherea," the Loves cry in answer.
Hymenaeus quenched every torch upon the doorposts,
and scattered the wedding garland; no longer "Hymen,"
no longer "Hymen" sings he his song, but he chants
"alas" and Adonis still more than "Hymenaeus."

The Graces weep for the son of Cinyras,
saying to one another, "Fair Adonis is dead,"
and shrilly they cry "alas" far more than the paean.
And the Fates call Adonis back, "Adonis,"
and chant their spell over him; but he does not hearken to them;
not that he is unwilling, but the Maiden will not release him.
Cease your moaning, Cytherea, for today; refrain from beating your breast;
you must weep again, again in another year shed your tears.

MYRSON
Will you now sing me, Lycidas, some sweet Sicilian strain,
lovely, honey-hearted, amorous, such as the Cyclops
Polyphemus sang to Galatea by the shore?
LYCIDAS
I too, Myrson, am glad to pipe; but what shall I sing?
MYRSON
The Scyrian love, Lycidas, the sweet love men envied,
the secret kisses of the son of Peleus, the secret bed,
how the boy put on a robe, and how he belied his form,
and how among the daughters of Lycomedes, heedless,
Deidameia came to know Achilles within the bridal chamber.
LYCIDAS
Once the herdsman carried off Helen, and led her to Ida,
a bitter grief to Oenone. And Lacedaemon was wroth,
and gathered all the Achaean host, and no Greek,

neither of the Mycenaeans nor of Elis nor of the Laconians,
stayed at home in his hall, fleeing wretched war.
But hidden among the daughters of Lycomedes was Achilles alone,
and instead of arms he was learning to handle wool, and in his white hand
he held a maiden's task, and seemed like a girl;
for he made himself womanly as they were, and so great a bloom
flushed his snowy cheeks, and with the gait
of a maiden he walked, and covered his hair with a veil.
But the heart of a man he had, and the love of a man he had;
and from dawn to night he would sit beside Deidameia,
and at times he kissed her hand, and often
he lifted up her fair warp-thread, and praised her intricate webs;
and he ate with no other companion, and did all things
hastening toward their shared sleep. He spoke this word too to her:

"The other sisters slumber with one another,
but I sleep alone, and you, maiden, sleep alone.
We two girls, companions of one age, we two fair ones,
yet alone in our beds we sleep; but the wicked,
the crafty Nysaea cruelly divides me from you.
For I do not ... of you ..."

CLEODAMUS
Of spring, Myrson, or of winter, or of autumn,
or of summer—what is sweet to you? Which do you most pray to come?
Is it summer, when all that we labor for is brought to its end?
Or sweet autumn, when hunger is light for men?
Or even idle winter? Since in winter too many,
warming themselves, are charmed by idleness and ease.
Or has fair spring rather pleased you more? Say, what does your heart
choose? For our leisure has given us leave to talk.
MYRSON
It is not fitting for mortals to judge the works of the gods;
for all these things are holy and sweet. But for your sake,
Cleodamus, I will declare what is sweeter to me than the rest.
I do not wish it to be summer, for then the sun scorches me.
I do not wish it to be autumn, for that season breeds disease.
And ruinous winter I cannot bear: I dread the snow and frost.

May spring, thrice-longed-for, be with me through the whole year round,
when neither cold nor sun weighs heavy upon us.
In spring all things conceive, in spring all sweet things bloom,
and night for men is equal and alike to day . . .
A fowler-boy, still in the leafy grove,
hunting birds, saw the wayward Love
seated upon the branch of a box-tree; and when he saw him,
rejoicing because the bird seemed a great one to him,
joining together all his rods one upon another,
this way and that he lay in wait for Love as he hopped about.
And the boy, vexed, when no end of it came,
threw down his rods and went to an old plowman
who had taught him this craft, and told him,
and showed him Love sitting there. But the old man,
smiling, shook his head and answered the boy:
"Spare yourself the hunt, and do not go after that bird.

Flee far away. An evil thing is that creature. You will be blessed
so long as you do not catch him; but if you come to a man's full measure,
this very one who now flees and hops away, of his own accord
coming suddenly, will settle upon your head."
Great Cypris stood beside me as I yet slept,
leading the infant Love by his fair hand,
with eyes cast down to the ground, and spoke to me this word:
"Take Love, dear herdsman, and teach him to sing."
So she spoke; and she departed, and I, fool that I was,
taught Love whatever herdsmen's lore I knew, as one willing to learn:
how Pan invented the cross-flute, how Athena the pipe,
how Hermes the lyre, how sweet Apollo the cithara.
These things I kept teaching him; but he heeded not my words,
and instead himself sang me songs of love, and taught me

the longings of mortals and immortals, and the deeds of his mother.
And I forgot all that I had been teaching Love,
but all the love-songs that Love taught me I learned.
The Muses do not fear savage Love,
but love him from their hearts and follow at his very heel.
And if anyone whose soul is loveless should sing,
him they shun and refuse to teach;
but if anyone, his mind shaken by Love, makes sweet music,
toward him they all stream, eager and hurrying.
I am witness that this saying has proved true for all.
For if I sing of some other mortal or of one of the immortals,
my tongue stammers and no longer sings as before;
but if again I make any music to Love and to Lycidas,
then with joy the song flows through my mouth.
. . . I know not, nor is it fitting to labor at what we have not learned.

If my little songs are fair, then these alone
shall bring me glory, which Fate of old bestowed on me;
but if these are not pleasing, why should I toil at more?
For if either the son of Cronus or many-turning Fate
had given us a double span of life, so that one part might be spent
in gladness and delights, and the other in toil,
then perhaps, having toiled, one might afterward receive good things.
But if the gods have decreed that men come to one
span of life, and that one brief and less than all,
how long, wretched as we are, shall we labor at toils and works,
and how long shall we cast our soul after gain and after crafts,
ever longing for far greater wealth?
Have we then all forgotten that we were born mortal,
and that we have obtained but a brief time from Fate? . . .

Blessed are they who love, when they are loved in equal return.
Blessed was Theseus while Pirithous was at his side,
even though he went down to pitiless Hades.
Blessed was Orestes among the harsh Inhospitable peoples,
because Pylades chose to share his roads with him.
Blessed was Achilles, the grandson of Aeacus, while his comrade lived;
and blessed was he in dying, because he warded off a dread fate from him.
Hesperus, golden light of lovely Aphrodite,
Hesperus, dear holy ornament of the dark-blue night,
as much fainter than the moon as you are foremost among the stars,
hail, friend, and as I lead a revel to the shepherd,
give me your light in place of the moon, since she
today, but newly risen, too quickly set. I do not go
to steal, nor to trouble those who travel by night;

but I am in love, and it is fair to aid one in love.
Gentle Cyprus-born, child of Zeus or of the sea,
why are you so grievous to mortals and immortals?
A little thing, I would say; why now were you so hateful even to yourself,
as to bear for all an evil so great as this Love,
savage, heartless, in form no way like his mind?
And why did you grant that he be winged and far-shooting,
so that, bitter as he is, we cannot escape him?
. . . Speechlessness seized Phoebus as he looked upon your wound.
He sought all remedies, and tried his skillful art,
and anointed with ambrosia and with nectar, anointed all
the wound; but against the Fates all remedies are without cure . . .
. . . But I shall go my way down to the slope
yonder, toward the sand and the shore, murmuring my song,

beseeching cruel Galatea; and the sweet
hopes I shall not abandon, even unto my last old age . . .
. . . It is not well, my friend, to bring every matter to the craftsman,
nor to hold yourself in need of another for all things; but yourself too
fashion a pipe; the task is easy for you . . .
May Love call the Muses, may the Muses bring Love.
May the Muses ever grant me, in my longing, the song,
the sweet song, than which no remedy is sweeter.
. . . By the frequent dripping, as the saying goes, when it falls ever,
even the stone is hollowed into a cleft . . .
. . . And do not leave me unrewarded, since even Phoebus when he sings
receives his wage. And honor makes things better . . .
. . . Beauty is the fair thing for women, but for a man, strength . . .
All things, when a god wills it, are achievable; all things for mortals

I THAT with youthful heat did verses write, Must now my woes in doleful tunes indite. My work is framed by Muses torn and rude, And my sad cheeks are with true tears bedewed: For these alone no terror could affray from being partners of my weary way. The art that was my young life's joy and glory Becomes my solace now i m old and sorry; Sorrow has filched my youth from me, the thief! My days are numbered not by time but Grief. a Untimely hoary hairs cover my head, And my loose skin quakes on my flesh half dead. o happy death, that spareth sweetest years, And comes in sorrow often called with tears. Alas, how deaf is he to wretch's cries; And loath he is to close up weeping eyes;
While trustless chance me with vain favours crowned, that saddest hour my life had almost drowned Now she hath clouded her deceitful face, My spiteful days prolong their weary race. My friends, why did you count me fortunate? He that is fallen, ne'er stood in settled state.

Alas, how thy dull mind is headlong cast In depths of woe, where, all her light once lost, She doth to walk in utter darkness haste, While cares grow great with earthly tempests tost. He that through the opened heavens did freely run, And used to travel the celestial ways. Marking the rosy splendour of the sun, And noting Cynthia's cold and watery rays; He that did bravely comprehend in verse The different spheres and wandering course of stars, He that was wont the causes to rehearse Why sounding winds do with the seas make wars, What spirit moves the world s well-settled frame, And why the sun, whom forth the east doth bring, In western waves doth hide his falling flame, Searching what power tempers the pleasing Spring Which makes the earth her rosy flowers to bear, Whose gift it is that Autumn s fruitful season Should with full grapes flow in a plenteous year, Telling of secret Nature every reason, Now having lost the beauty of his mind Lies with his neck compassed in ponderous chains; His countenance with heavy weight declined, Him to behold the sullen earth constrains.

Then fled the night and darkness did me leave, Mine eyes their wonted strength receive, As when swift Corus spreads the stars with clouds And the clear sky a veil of tempest shrouds The sun doth lurk, the earth receiveth night, Lacking the boon of starry light, But if fierce Boreas, sent from I brace, make way For the restoring of the day, Phoebus with fresh and sudden beams doth rise, Striking with light our wondering eyes.
Who mildly can his age dispose, And at his feet proud destiny throws: Who stoutly doth each chance behold, Keeping his countenance uncontrolled; Not him the ocean s rage and threat, Stirring the waves with angry heat, Nor hot Vesuvius when he casts From broken hills enflamèd blasts, Nor fiery thunder can dismay, Which takes the tops of towers away.

The hearts of kings can steer, To whom so many crouch with trembling fear. O Thou that joinest with love All worldly things, look from Thy seat above On the earth s wretched state; We men, not the least work thou didst create, With fortune s blasts do shake; Thou careful ruler, these fierce tempests slake, And for the earth provide Those laws by which Thou heaven in peace dost guide.
When hot with Phoebus' beams The Crab casts fiery gleams, He that doth then with seed Th' unwilling furrows feed, Deceivéd of his bread Must be with acorns fed. Seek not the flowery woods For violets sweet buds. When fields are overcast With the fierce northern blast. Nor hope thou home to bring Vine-clusters in the Spring If thou in grapes delight; In autumn Bacchus' might With them doth deck our clime. God every several time With proper grace hath crowned Nor will those laws confound Which He once settled hath. He that with headlong path This certain order leaves, An hapless end receives.

When stars are shrouded With dusky night, They yield no light Being so clouded. When the wind moveth And churneth the sea, The flood, clear as day, Foul and dark proveth. And rivers creeping Down a high hill Stand often still, Rocks them back keeping, If thou wouldst brightly See Truth's clear rays, Or walk those ways Which lead most rightly. All joy forsaking Fear must thou fly,
And hopes defy, No sorrow taking For where these terrors Reign in the mind, They it do bind In cloudy errors.
He that a fruitful field will sow. Doth first the ground from bushes free. All fern and briars likewise mow, That he his harvest great may see. Honey seems sweeter to our taste, If cloyed with noisome food it be. Stars clearer shine when Notus' blast Hath ceased the rainy storms to breed. When Lucifer hath night defaced, The day's bright horses then succeed. So thou, 'whom seeming goods do feed. First shake off yokes which so thee press That Truth may then thy mind possess.

How the first reins of all things guided are By powerful Nature as the chiefest cause, And how she keeps, with a foreseeing care, The spacious world in order by her laws, And to sure knots which nothing can untie, By her strong hand all earthly motions draws— To show all this we purpose now to try Our pliant string, our musick's thrilling sound. Although the Libyan lions often lie Gentle and tame in splendid fetters bound, a And fearing their incensed master's wrath, With patient looks endure each blow and wound, Yet if their jaws they once in blood do bathe, They, gaming courage, b with fierce noise awake The force which Nature in them seated hath, And from their necks the broken chains do shake; Then he that tamed them first doth feel their rage, And torn in pieces doth their fury slake. The bird shut up in an unpleasing cage, Which on the lofty trees did lately sing,

Though men, her want of freedom to assuage, Should unto her with careful labour brine The sweetest meats which they can best devise, Yet when within her prison fluttering The pleasing shadows of the groves she spies, Her hated food she scatters with her feet, In yearning spirit to the woods she flies, The woods delights do tune her accents sweet. When some strong hand doth tender plant constrain With his debased top the ground to meet, If it let go, the crooked twig again Up toward Heaven itself it straight doth raise. Phoebus doth fall into the western main, Yet doth he back return by secret ways, And to the earth doth guide his chariot's race.
