Each thing a certain course and laws obeys, Striving to turn back to Ins proper place; Nor any settled order can be found, But that which doth within itself embrace The births and ends of all things in a round.

Although the rich man from his mines of gold Dig treasure which his mind can never fill, And lofty neck with precious pearls enfold, And his hit fields with many oxen till. Yet biting cares will never leave his head. Nor will his wealth attend him being dead.
Though fierce and lustful Nero did adorn Himself with purple robes, which pearls did grace, He did but gain a general hate and scorn. Yet wickedly he officers most base Over the reverend Senators did place. Who would esteem of fading honours then Which may be given thus by the wickedest men?
Who would be powerful, must His own affections cheek, Nor let foul reins of lust Subdue his conquered neck. For though the Indian land Should tremble at thy beck, And though thy dread command Far Thule's isle obey. Unless thou canst withstand And boldly drive away Black care and wretched moan, Thy might is small or none.

The general race of men from a like birth is born. All things one Father have, Who doth them all adorn, Who gave the sun his rays, and the pale moon her horn,
The lofty heaven for stars, low earth tor mortals chose; He souls fetched down from high in bodies did enclose; And thus from noble seed all men did first compose. Why brag you of your stock? Since none is counted base, If you consider God the author of your race, But he that with foul vice doth his own birth deface.
All pleasure hath.this property, She woundeth those who have her most. And, like unto the angry bee Who hath her pleasant honey lost, She flies away with nimble wing And in our hearts doth leave her sting.
Alas, bow ignorance makes wretches stray Out of the way! You from green trees expect no golden mines Nor pearls from vines, Nor use you on mountains to lay your net Fishes to get, Nor, if the pleasant sport of hunting please, Run you to seas. Men will be skilful in the hidden eaves Of the ocean waves, And in what coasts the orient pearls are bred, Or purple red,

Also, what different sorts of fishes store Each several shore, But when they come their chiefest good to find, Then are they blind, And search for that under the earth, which lies Above the skies. How should I curse these fools? Let thirst them hold Of fame and gold, That, having got false goods with pain, they learn True to discern.
O Thou, that dost the world in lasting order guide, Father of heaven and earth, Who makest time swiftly slide, And, standing still Thyself, yet tram st all moving laws, Who to Thy work wert moved by no external cause:
But by a sweet desire, where envy hath no place, Thy goodness moving Thee to give each thing his grace, Thou dost all creatures' forms from highest patterns take. From Thy fair mind the world fair like Thyself doth make. Thus Thou perfect the whole perfect each part dost frame. Thou temp'rest elements, making cold mixed with flame And dry things join with moist, lest fire away should fly, Or earth, opprest with weight, buried too low should lie. Thou in consenting parts fitly disposed hast Th' all-moving soul in midst of threefold nature placed, Which, cut in several parts that run a different race Into itself returns, and circling doth embrace The highest mind, and heaven with like proportion drives. Thou with like cause dost make the souls and lesser lives, Fix them in chariots swift, and widely scatterest O'er heaven and earth; then at Thy fatherly behest They stream, like fire returning, back to Thee, their God. Dear Father, let my mind Thy hallowed seat ascend, Let me behold the spring of grace and find Thy light, That I on Thee may fix my soul's well cleared sight.

Cast off the earthly weight wherewith I am opprest, Shine as Thou art most bright, Thou only calm and rest To pious men whose end is to behold Thy ray, Who their beginning art, their guide, their bound, and way. a
Come hither, all you that are bound, Whose base and earthly minds are drowned
By lust which doth them tie in cruel chains: Here is a seat for men opprest, Here is a port of pleasant rest; Here may a wretch have refuge from his pains. No gold, which Tagus' sands bestow, Nor which on Hermus' banks doth flow, Nor precious stones which scorchéd Indians get, a Can clear the sharpness of the mind, But rather make it far more blind, And in the farther depth of darkness set, For this that sets our souls on work. Buried in caves of earth doth lurk. But heaven is guided by another light, Which causeth us to shun the dark, b And who this light doth truly mark, Must needs deny that Phoebus beams are bright.

He that would seek the truth with thoughts profound And would not stray in ways that are not right, He to himself must turn his inward sight, And guide his motions in a circled round, Teaching his mind that ever she design Herself in her own treasures to possess: So that which late lay hidden in cloudiness More bright and clear than Phoebus' beams shall shine. Flesh hath not quenched all the spirit's light, Though this oblivion's lump holds her opprest. Some seed of truth remaineth in our breast. Which skilful learning eas'ly doth excite.
For being askt how can we answer true Unless that grace within our hearts did dwell? If Plato's heavenly muse the truth us tell, We learning things remember them anew. a
Happy is be that can behold The well-spring whence all good doth rise, Happy is he that can unfold The bands with which the earth him ties. The Thracian poet whose sweet song Performed his wife s sad obsequies, And forced the woods to run along When he his mournful tunes did play, Whose powerful music was so strong That it could make the rivers stay; The fearful binds not daunted were, But with the lions took their way, Nor did the hare behold with fear The dog whom these sweet notes appease. When force of grief drew yet more near, And on his heart did burning seize, Nor tunes which all in quiet bound Could any jot their master ease, The gods above too hard he found, And Pluto's palace visiting. He mixed sweet verses with the sound Of bis loud harp's delightful string, All that he drank with thirsty draught From his high mother s chiefest spring, All that his restless grief him taught, And love which gives grief double aid, With this even hell itself was caught, Whither he went, and pardon prayed for his dear spouse (unheard request). The three-head porter was dismayed, Ravished with his unwonted guest, The Furies, which in tortures keep

The guilty souls with pains opprest, Moved with his song began to weep. Ixion's wheel now standing still Turns not his head with motions steep. Though Tantalus might drink at will, To quench his thirst lie would forbear, The vulture full with music shrill Doth not poor Tityus' liver tear. 'We by his verses conquered are,' Saith the great King whom spirits fear. 'Let us not then from him debar His wife whom he with songs doth gain, Yet lest our gift should stretch too far, We will it with this law restrain, That when from hell he takes his flight, He shall from looking back refrain.' Who can for lovers laws indite? Love hath no law but her own will. Orpheus, seeing on the verge of night Eurydice, doth lose and kill Her and himself with foolish love. But you this feigned tale fulfil, Who think unto the day above To bring with speed your darksome mind. For if, your eye conquered, you move Backward to Pluto left behind, All the rich prey which thence you took, You lose while back to hell you look.

For I have swift and nimble wings which will ascend the lofty skies, With which when thy quick mind is clad, it will the loathéd earth despise, And go beyond the airy globe, and watery clouds behind thee leave, Passing the tire which scorching heat doth from the heavens swift course receive, Until it reach the starry house, and get to tread bright Phoebus' ways, Following the chilly sire's path, a companion of his flashing, lays, And trace the circle of the stars which in the night to us appeal, And having staged there long enough go on beyond the farthest sphere, Sitting upon the highest orb partaker of the glorious light, Where the great King his sceptre holds, and the world's reins doth guide aright, And, firm in his swift chariot, doth everything in order set. Unto this seat when thou art brought, thy country, which thou didst forget, Thou then wilt challenge to thyself, saying: 'This is the glorious land Where I was born, and in this soil my feet for evermore shall stand. Whence if thou pleasest to behold the earthly night which thou hast left, Those tyrants which the people fear will seem of their true home bereft.'

The kings whom we behold In highest glory placed And with rich purple graced, Compassed with soldiers bold; Whose countenance shows fierce threats, Who with rash fury chide, If any strip the pride From their vainglorious feats; He'll see them close oppressed Within by galling chains. For filthy lust there reigns And poisoneth their breast, Wrath often them perplexeth Raising their minds like waves, Sorrow their power enslaves And sliding hope them vexeth. So many tyrants still Dwelling in one pool heart, Except they first depart She cannot have her will.
The sails which wise Ulysses bore, And ships which in the seas long lime did stray The eastern wind drave to that shore Where the fair Goddess Lady Circe lay, Daughter by birth to Phoebus bright, Who with enchanted cups and charms did stay Her guests, deceived with their delight And into sundry figures them did change, Being most skilful in the might And secret force of herbs and simples strange; Some like to savage boars, and some Like lions fierce, which daily use to range Through Libya, a in tooth and claw become. Others are changed to the shape and guise Of ravenous wolves, and waxing dumb Use howling in the stead of manly cries. Others like to the tiger rove b Which in the scorched Indian desert lies. And though the winged son of Jove c From these bewitched cups' delightful taste To keep the famous captain strove, Yet them the greedy mariners embraced With much desire, till turned to swine

Instead of bread they fed on oaken mast. Ruined in voice and form, no sign Remains to them of any human grace; Only their minds unchanged repine To see their bodices in such ugly case. O feeble hand and idle art Which, though it could the outward limbs deface, Yet had no force to change the heart. For all the force of men given by God's arm Lies hidden in their inmost part. The poisons therefore which within them swarm More deeply pierce, and with more might, For to the body though they do no harm, Yet on the soul they work their spite.
Why should we strive to die so many ways, And slay ourselves with our own hands? If we seek death, she ready stands, She willing comes, her chariot never stays. Those against whom the wild beasts arméd be, Against themselves with weapons rage. a Do they such wars unjustly wage, Because their lives and manners disagree, And so themselves with mutual weapons kill? Alas, but this revenge is small. wouldst thou give due desert to all? Love then the good, and pity thou the ill.

Who knows not bow the stars near to the poles do slide, And how Boötes his slow wain doth guide, And why he sets so late, and doth so early rise, May wonder at the courses of the skies. If when the moon is full her horns seem pale to sight, Infested with the darkness of the night, And stars from which all grace she with her brightness took, Now show themselves, while she doth dimly look, A public error straight through vulgar minds doth pass, And they with many strokes beat upon brass. a None wonders why the winds upon the waters blow. Nor why hot Phoebus beams dissolve the snow.
These easy are to know, the other hidden lie, And therefore more our hearts they terrify. All strange events which time to light more seldom brings, And the vain people count as sudden things, If we our clouded minds from ignorance could free, No longer would by us admired be.

If thou would st see God's laws with purest mind, Thy sight on heaven must fixed be, Whose settled course the stars in peace doth bind. The sun's bright fire Stops not his sisters team, Nor doth the northern bear desire Within the ocean s wave to hide her beam. Though she behold The other stars there couching, Yet she uncessantly is rolled About high heaven, the ocean never touching. The evening light With certain course doth show The coming of the shady night, And Lucifer before the day doth go.
This mutual love Courses eternal makes, And from the starry spheres above All cause of war and dangerous discord takes. This sweet consent In equal bands doth tie The nature of each element, So that the moist things yield unto the dry, The piercing cold With flames doth friendship keep, The trembling fire the highest place doth hold, And the gross earth sinks down into the deep. The flowery year Breathes odours in the spring The scorching summer corn doth bear, The autumn fruit from laden trees doth bring. The falling rain Doth winter s moisture give. These rules thus nourish and maintain All creatures which we see on earth to live. And when they die, These bring them to their end, While their Creator sits on high, Whose hand the reins of the whole world doth bend. He as their King Rules them with lordly might. From Him they rise, flourish, and spring, He as their law and judge decides their right. Those things whose course Most swiftly glides away His might doth often backward force, And suddenly their wandering motion stay. Unless His strength Their violence should bound, And them which else would run at length,

Should bring within the compass of a round, That firm decree Which now doth all adorn Would soon destroyed and broken be, Things being far from their beginning borne. This powerful love Is common unto all, Which for desire of good do move Back to the springs from whence they first did fall. No worldly thing Can a continuance have Unless love back again it bring Unto the cause which first the essence gave.
Revengeful Atreus son did ten whole years employ In wars, till he his brother's loss repaid with ransacked Troy. He setting forth the fleet of Greece upon the seas, And knowing well that only blood the angry winds would please, Forgot a father's part, and with his cruel knife Unto the gods did sacrifice his dearest daughter's life. Ulysses wailed the loss of his most faithful men, Whom Polyphemus did devour enclosed in his den But when his hands by sleight had made the Cyclops blind, Most pleasant joy instead of former tears possessed his mind. Hercules famous is for his laborious toil, Who tamed the Centaurs and did take the dreadful lion's spoil. He the Stymphalian birds with piercing arrows strook, And from the watchful dragon's care the golden apples took. a He in a threefold chain the hellish porter led,

And with their cruel masters flesh the savage horses fed. He did th' increasing bends of poisonous Hydra burn, And breaking Achelous' horns, did make him back return. a He on the Libyan sands did proud Antaeus kill, And with the mighty Cacus' blood Euander's wrath That world-uplifting back the boar's white foam did fleck. To hold on high the sphere of heaven with never bending neck Of all his many toils the last was, and most hard, And for this last and greatest toil the heaven was his reward. You gallant men pursue this way of high renown, Why yield you? Overcome the earth, and you the stars shall crown.
In the Achaemenian rocks, where Parthians with their darts In their dissembled flight do wound their enemies, Tigris from the same head doth with Euphrates rise, And forthwith they themselves divide in several parts, But if they join again, and them one channel bound, Bringing together all that both their waves do bear; The ships and trees, whose roots they from the bank do tear, Will meet, and they their floods will mingle and confound, Yet run tins wandering course in places which are low,

And in these sliding streams a settled law remains. a So fortune, though it seems to run with careless reins, Yet hath it certain rule, and doth in order flow.
Sweet Homer a sings the praise Of Phoebus clear and bright. And yet his strongest rays Cannot with feeble, light Cast through the secret ways Of earth and seas his sight, Though 'all lies open to his eyes.' b But He who did this world devise- The earth's vast depths unseen From his sight are not free, No clouds can stand between, He at one time doth see What are, and what have been, And what shall after be. Whom, since he only vieweth all, You rightly the true Sim may call.
What cause of discord breaks the bands of love? What God between two truths such wars doth move? That things which severally well settled be Yet joined in one will never friendly prove? Or in true things can we no discord see, Because all certainties do still agree? But our dull soul, covered with members blind, Knows not the secret laws which things do bind, By the drowned light of her oppressed fire. Why then, the hidden notes of things to find, Doth she with such a love of truth desire? If she knows that which she doth so require, Why wisheth she known things to know again?

If she knows not, why strives she with blind pain? Who after things unknown will strive to go? Or will such ignorant pursuit maintain? How shall she find them out? Or having so, How shall she then their forms and natures know? Because this soul the highest mind did view, Must we needs say that it all nature knew? Now she, though clouds of flesh do her debar, Forgets not all that was her ancient due, But in her mind some general motions are, Though not the skill of things particular. He that seeks truth in neither course doth fall; Not knowing all, nor ignorant of all, He marketh general things which he retains, And matters seen on high doth back recall, And things forgotten to his mind regains, And joins them to that part which there remains.
Cloudy old prophets of the Porch a once taught. That sense and shape presented to the thought From outward objects their impression take, As when upon a paper smooth and plain On which as yet no marks of ink have lain We with a nimble pen do letters make. But if our minds to nothing can apply Their proper motions, but do patient lie Subject to forms which do from bodies flow,

As a glass renders empty a shapes of things, Who then can show from whence that motion springs By force of which the mind all things doth know? Or by what skill are several things espied? And being known what power doth them divide. And thus divided doth again unite, And with a various journey oft aspires To highest things, and oft again retires To basest, nothing being out of sight, And when she buck unto herself doth move, Doth all the falsehoods by the truth reprove? This vigour needs must be an active cause, And with more powerful forces must be deekt, Than that which from those forms, that do reflect From outward matter, all her virtue draws. And yet in living bodies passion s might Doth go before, whose office is to incite, And the first motions in the mind to make. As when the light unto our eves appears, Or some loud voice is sounded in our ears, Then doth the strength of the dull mind awake Those phantasies which she retains within, She stirreth up such notions to begin, Whose objects with their natures best agree, And thus applying them to outward things, She joins the external shapes winch thence she brings With forms which in herself included be.

1. A stranger from Atarneus once put this question to Pittacus
of Mytilene, the son of Hyrrhadius:
"Old father, two marriages are courting me. The one bride
matches my own rank in both wealth and birth;
the other is above me. Which is the better? Come, advise me,
which of the two shall I lead to the wedding?"
So he spoke; and the old man, lifting his staff, an elder's weapon,
said, "Look there—those children will tell you the whole tale."
Now those children, whipping their swift tops along,
were spinning them in the broad crossroads.
"Follow in their tracks," he said. And the man drew near
to where they stood; and they were saying, "Drive the one that matches you."
Hearing this, the stranger held back from grasping
at the greater house, taking to heart the children's omen,

and led the lesser bride home to his dwelling.
So you too, go your way and drive the one that matches you.
2. Someone told me of your death, Heraclitus, and it brought
a tear to my eye; and I remembered how often
the two of us sank the sun in talk together. But you, I suppose,
my Halicarnassian friend, are long since ash;
yet your nightingales live on, and on them Hades,
who carries off all things, shall never lay his hand.
3. [Sharp on every side about the tomb are thorns
and brambles; you will hurt your feet if you draw near.]
I, Timon the man-hater, dwell here. But pass on,
saying many curses if you will—only pass on.
4. Do not bid me rejoice, evil heart, but pass on.
For me it is the same joy that you do not laugh.
5. Timon—for you are no longer—which is hateful to you,

the dark or the light?
"The dark; for more of you are in Hades."
6. A shell am I, Lady of Zephyrium, of older days; but now you,
Cypris, hold me, the first offering of Selenaea,
a nautilus that sailed upon the seas: if there were winds,
spreading my sail from my own forestays;
but if Calm, that gleaming goddess, then rowing hard with my feet—
so my name accords with my work—
until I fell beside the shores of Iulis, that I might become
your far-seen plaything, Arsinoe;
nor any longer in my chambers, as before—for I am breathless—
let the egg of the dewy halcyon be hatched within me.
But grant your grace to the daughter of Cleinias; for she knows
how to do noble things, and she is from Aeolian Smyrna.
7. I am the labour of the Samian, who once received in his house
the divine singer; I sing of Eurytus, all that he suffered,

and of golden-haired Iole; and I am called a Homeric
writing. For Creophylus, dear Zeus, this is a great thing.
8. A boy was crowning the gravestone of his stepmother, a small stone,
thinking her life and her ways had changed with death;
but the stone fell and killed the boy as he bent over the tomb.
Flee, you stepsons, even the grave of a stepmother.
9. Theaetetus walked a pure road. And if that path of his
does not lead to your ivy, Bacchus,
heralds shall sound the names of others for a brief season,
but of him Hellas shall proclaim the wisdom forever.
10. Small, Dionysus, is the speech allotted
to the poet whose work goes well; he says only, in his longest, "I win,"
but the one on whom you do not breathe with favour—if anyone asks
"How did you fare?"—says, "Things go hard."

May this be the word for him who broods on unjust things;
but for me, my Lord, the brief and few-syllabled.
11. Here Saon, son of Dicon, of Acanthus, sleeps
a sacred sleep. Do not say that the good are dead.
12. If you seek Timarchus in Hades, to learn
something about the soul, or how you yourself will be again,
seek the son, of the tribe of Ptolemais, whose father
was Pausanias; you will find him among the pious.
13. The stranger was brief; therefore this verse too, which will say no long thing:
"Theris, son of Aristaeus, a Cretan"—and to me even that is long.
14. If you come to Cyzicus, it is little trouble to find Hippacus
and Didyme; for their family is in no way obscure.
And you will tell them a grievous word, yet say
this all the same: that here I hold Critias, their son.

15. "Is it under you that Charidas rests?" "If you mean the son
of Arimmas of Cyrene, he is under me."
"O Charidas, what is below?" "Deep darkness." "And the ways up?"
"A lie." "And Pluto?" "A tale." "We are undone."
"This is my true word to you; but if you want
the pleasant kind: a great ox in Hades costs a Pellaean penny."
16. Who knows well the daemon of tomorrow? When even you,
Charmis—you who were before our eyes but yesterday—
we buried, weeping, on the next day. Nothing more grievous
than this did your father Diophon ever see.
17. "Timonoe." "Who are you? By the gods, I should not have known you,
had not the name of your father Timotheus stood
upon the stone, and Methymna, your city." "Truly, I declare,
your widowed husband Euthymenes grieves greatly."
18. Crethis, full of tales, who knew how to play sweetly,

the daughters of Samos often seek—
their sweetest fellow-worker, ever full of chatter; but she sleeps
here the sleep that is owed to all.
19. Would that swift ships had never been! For then we
should not be mourning Sopolis, son of Diocleides.
But now his corpse drifts somewhere on the sea, and in his place
we pass by a name and an empty tomb.
20. Lycus the Naxian died not on land but on the sea,
and saw his ship and his life perish together,
when he was sailing, a merchant, from Aegina. He, a corpse,
is in the waters; and I, a tomb that holds only his name,
proclaim this wholly true word: "Avoid, O sailor,
putting to sea with the Kids when they are setting."
21. Twelve years old, his father Philippus laid the boy
here—his great hope—Nicoteles.
22. At dawn we were burying Melanippus; and as the sun

was setting, the maiden Basilo died
by her own hand; for to live, having set her brother on the pyre,
she could not bear. And the house looked upon a twofold evil,
the house of their father Aristippus; and all Cyrene
bowed its head, seeing the home of fair children left desolate.
23. Whoever you are that carry your foot past my tomb, know
that I am the son and the father of Callimachus of Cyrene.
You would know them both: the one once led
his country's arms; the other sang songs stronger than envy.
No cause for resentment: those children whom the Muses have looked upon
with no sidelong eye, they do not, when grey, cast off as friends.
24. Astacides the Cretan, the goatherd, a Nymph carried off
from the mountain, and now Astacides is holy.
No more beneath the Dictaean oaks, no more of Daphnis

shall we shepherds sing, but ever of Astacides.
25. Saying "Farewell, O Sun," Cleombrotus of Ambracia
leapt from a high wall down into Hades,
having seen no evil worthy of death, but having read
one writing of Plato's, the one on the soul.
26. A hero, the warder of Eëtion of Amphipolis,
I am set up, small upon a small porch,
holding a coiled serpent and a single sword; angered
at a man of Epeus, he settled me here on foot as well.
27. Callignotus swore to Ionis that never would he
hold any friend, man or woman, dearer than her.
He swore; but they say truly that the oaths of lovers
do not enter the ears of the immortals.
And now he burns with love for a man; and of the poor
girl, as of the Megarians, there is no word nor reckoning.
28. I had from little means a scanty living, doing

nothing terrible, wronging no one. Dear Earth,
if I, Micylus, ever praised anything base, may you not lie
light upon me, nor you other powers that hold me.
29. Hesiod's is the song and the manner; not the last of singers,
no—but I fear the man of Soli has milked off
the sweetest of his verses. Hail, you slender
discourses, the strained vigil of Aratus.
30. I hate the cyclic poem, nor do I take pleasure
in the road that carries many this way and that;
I loathe too the much-courted darling, nor do I drink
from the public fountain; I am sick of all common things.
Lysanias, you are indeed fair, fair—but before Echo
can say it clearly, someone else says, "He belongs to another."
31. Pour, and again say "To Diocles!" Not even Achelous
perceives those sacred ladlefuls.
The boy is fair, Achelous, exceedingly fair; and if anyone

says he is not—may I alone know what is fair.
32. Thessalian Cleonicus, wretched, wretched, no, by the keen
sun, I did not know you. Poor man, what has become of you?
Bones you are, and only hair still left. Has my own
daemon seized you? Have you met a harsh dispensation of the god?
I know it: Euxitheos has carried you off, and you too, coming,
gazed upon the fair one, poor wretch, with both your eyes.
33. The hunter, Epicydes, on the mountains tracks every hare
and the prints of every doe,
trudging through frost and snow; but if someone says,
"Here, this beast is struck down," he will not take it.
Such too is my love: it knows how to chase what flees,
but flies past what lies ready in its path.
34. I know that my hands are empty, empty of wealth; but, Menippus,
do not, by the Graces, tell me my own dream.

I grieve, hearing this bitter word continually;
yes, dear friend, of all that comes from you, this is the least loving.
35. Artemis, to you Phileratis set up this image here;
do you accept it, lady, and keep her safe.
36. Me, lion-strangling, boar-slaying lord, a branch of oak—
who set me here? "Archinus." Which one? "The Cretan."
"I accept it."
37. Past the tomb of the son of Battus you carry your feet—of one who knew
both song well, and well how to laugh in season over wine.
38. Lyctian Menitas,
having spoken these words,
dedicated this bow:
"Here, I give you my horn
and quiver, Sarapis;
but the arrows the Hesperitae have."
39. Her gifts to Aphrodite,

Simon, who wanders the streets, set up—an image of herself,
and the girdle
that kissed her breasts, and the torch,
and the very thyrsus that the poor woman used to carry.
40. To Pylaean Demeter,
to whom that man of the Pelasgians,
Acrisius, built this temple—these gifts the man of Naucratis,
and to her daughter below,
Timodemus dedicated,
a tithe of his gains; for so indeed he had vowed.
41. Priestess of Demeter once was I, and again of the Cabiri,
sir, and thereafter of the Dindymene Mother;
I, the old woman, now dust, who in the [pains of Eleutho]
was the patroness of many young wives.
And two sons were born to me, and I closed my eyes in their
arms in a fair old age. Go your way rejoicing.

42. Half of my soul still breathes; the other half I know not
whether Love or Hades has seized—only it is vanished.
Has it gone off again to one of the boys? And yet I forbade them
often: "Young men, do not receive the runaway."
Go, someone, and search there; for there, I know, that stone-worthy
and ill-loving thing of mine is somewhere turning about.
43. If of my own will, Archinus, I came reveling, blame me ten thousand times;
but if I come unwilling, let the rashness be.
Strong wine and Love compelled me; of these the one
dragged me, the other would not let me leave off my rashness.
And coming, I did not shout out who I was or whose, but kissed
the doorpost. If that is a wrong, I do wrong.
44. The stranger had a wound, and it went unnoticed. How painfully—
did you see?—his breath came through his chest. He drew it up

the third time as he drank, and the roses, shedding their leaves
from the man's garlands, all fell to the ground.
He is well roasted by something great; by the gods, it is no random
guess I make—a thief, I have learned the tracks of a thief.
45. There is something, yes by Pan, that is hidden; there is, yes
by Dionysus, here a fire beneath the ash.
I am not confident; do not embrace me. Often a quiet river,
unnoticed, gnaws away a wall;
so now too I fear, Menexenus, lest this silent creeper
slip in upon me and cast me into love.
46. "You will be caught; flee round about, Menecrates," I said
on the twentieth of Panemos; and "On what day of Loios?"—"the tenth"—
the ox came under the yoke of its own will. Well done, my Hermes,
well done, mine! I make no complaint over the twenty days.

47. What a good charm Polyphemus discovered
for the lovesick! Yes, by Earth, the Cyclops was no fool.
The Muses, Philippus, make love grow lean.
Truly, wisdom is an all-healing medicine for everything.
This, I think, is the one good that hunger too holds, even among hardships:
it cuts away the disease of love for boys.
And to me it is granted to say without stint to Love:
"Here, boy, your wings are clipped, little child,
and not a crumb do we fear you; for the charms,
both of them, are at home for the cruel wound."
48. The salt-cellar, on which, eating frugal salt,
Eudemus escaped great storms of debts,
he dedicated to the Samothracian gods, saying that this, according to his vow,
O people, having been saved from the sea, he set up thus.
49. Asking for good learning when he gave me, Simon, the son of Miccus,

to the Muses; and they, like Glaucus,
gave a great gift in return for a small one. And I lie here
gaping wide, the double Samian, the tragic
Dionysus, listening to the boys; and they say,
"The lock is sacred"—that is my dream to me.
50. Say, stranger, that I, Pamphilus, am dedicated here as the witness
of the truly comic victory of Agoranax the Rhodian;
not wholly bitten by love, but half resembling
a roasted fig and the lamps of Isis.
51. The Phrygian Aeschra, good milk, in every good thing
Miccus, while she lived, tended in her old age;
and when she died he dedicated her to be seen by those to come—
how the old woman keeps the grace owed for her breasts.
52. Four are the Graces; for besides those three, one more
was lately fashioned, and still is moist with perfumes.

Blessed and conspicuous among all is Berenice,
without whom not even the Graces themselves are Graces.
53. Theocritus, who darkens what is fair—if he hates me,
hate him fourfold; but if he loves me, love him.
Yes, by fair-haired Ganymede, heavenly Zeus,
you too once loved—I say no more.
54. Again, Eileithyia, come at the call of Lycaenis,
bringing safe delivery from her pangs, with a good birth;
so that now, mistress, this offering for a girl, but next time
for a son, your fragrant temple may hold some other gift.
55. That you have your due, Asclepius, the debt that Aceson
owed by his vow for his wife Demodice,
know it; and if perchance you forget, and demand it again,
the tablet says it will furnish testimony.
56. To the Canopian god, Callistion, daughter of Critias,
dedicated me, a lamp rich with twenty nozzles,

having vowed it for her child Apellis; and looking into my light
you will say, "Hesperus, how have you fallen?"
57. Euaenetus, who set me up, says—for I myself
do not know it—that for his own victory
I am dedicated, a bronze cock, to the sons of Tyndareus.
I trust the son of Phaedrus, son of Philoxenides.
58. In the temple of Inachian Isis stands the child of Thales,
Aeschylis, by the vow of her mother Eirene.
59. "Who are you, shipwrecked stranger?" Leontichus found here
a corpse upon the shore, and heaped this tomb over it,
weeping for his own perilous life; for he himself
has no rest, but like a gull he travels the sea.
60. Happy that, mad in all else, the ancient Orestes
was not mad, Leucaretes, with my madness,
nor put the Phocian to the test that proves
a friend; but if he had made even one play,

he would soon have lost his comrade by doing this—
and I no longer have many Pyladeses such as those of old.
61. You who pass by the tomb of Cimon of Elis,
know, as you pass, that you pass the son of Hippaeus.
62. Aenian Menecrates, you too were here not for long;
what, best of strangers, brought you down?
Was it the same that took the Centaur? The sleep appointed
for me came on; and the poor wine bears the blame.
63. Cynthian goats, take heart; for the bow of Echemmas
the Cretan lies in Ortygia beside Artemis,
the bow with which he emptied your great mountain. But now he has ceased,
you goats, since the goddess has made a truce.
64. So may you sleep, Conopion, as you make me
lie down by these cold porches.
So may you sleep, most unjust one, as you lull your lover
to sleep, and have met not even pity in a dream.

1. A stranger from Atarneus once put this question to Pittacus
of Mytilene, the son of Hyrrhadius:
"Old father, two marriages are courting me. The one bride
matches my own rank in both wealth and birth;
the other is above me. Which is the better? Come, advise me,
which of the two shall I lead to the wedding?"
So he spoke; and the old man, lifting his staff, an elder's weapon,
said, "Look there—those children will tell you the whole tale."
Now those children, whipping their swift tops along,
were spinning them in the broad crossroads.
"Follow in their tracks," he said. And the man drew near
to where they stood; and they were saying, "Drive the one that matches you."
Hearing this, the stranger held back from grasping
at the greater house, taking to heart the children's omen.

And as that man led the lesser bride home to his dwelling,
so you too, Dion, drive the one that matches you.
2. Someone told me of your death, Heraclitus, and it brought
a tear to my eye; and I remembered how often
the two of us sank the sun in talk together. But you, I suppose,
my Halicarnassian friend, are long since ash;
yet your nightingales live on, and on them Hades,
who carries off all things, shall never lay his hand.
4. Timon—for you are no longer—which is hateful to you,
the dark or the light?
"The dark; for more of you are in Hades."
5. A shell am I, Lady of Zephyrium, a wonder of old; but now you,
Cypris, hold me, the first offering of Selenaea,
a nautilus that sailed upon the seas: if there were winds,
spreading my sail from my own forestays;
but if Calm, that gleaming goddess, then rowing hard with my feet—

so my name accords with my work—
until I fell beside the shores of Iulis, that I might become
your far-seen plaything, Arsinoe;
nor any longer in my chambers, as before—for I am breathless—
let the egg of the dewy halcyon be hatched within me.
But grant your grace to the daughter of Cleinias; for she knows
how to do noble things, and she is from Aeolian Smyrna.
6. I am the labour of the Samian, who once received in his house
the divine singer; I sing of Eurytus, all that he suffered,
and of golden-haired Iole; and I am called a Homeric
writing. For Creophylus, dear Zeus, this is a great thing.
7. Theaetetus walked a pure road. And if that path of his
does not lead to your ivy, Bacchus,
heralds shall sound the names of others for a brief season,
but of him Hellas shall proclaim the wisdom forever.

8. Small, Dionysus, is the speech allotted
to the poet whose work goes well; he says only, in his longest, "I win,"
but the one on whom you do not breathe with favour—if anyone asks
"How did you fare?"—says, "Things go hard."
May this be the word for him who broods on unjust things;
but for me, my Lord, the brief and few-syllabled.
9. Here Saon, son of Dicon, of Acanthus, sleeps
a sacred sleep. Do not say that the good are dead.
10. If you seek Timarchus in Hades, to learn
something about the soul, or how you yourself will be again,
seek the son, of the tribe of Ptolemais, whose father
was Pausanias; you will find him among the pious.
11. The stranger was brief; therefore this verse too, which will say no long thing:
"Theris, son of Aristaeus, a Cretan"—and to me even that is long.

12. If you come to Cyzicus, it is little trouble to find Hippacus
and Didyme; for their family is in no way obscure.
And you will tell them a grievous word, yet say
this all the same: that here I hold Critias, their son.
13. "Is it under you that Charidas rests?" "If you mean the son
of Arimmas of Cyrene, he is under me."
"O Charidas, what is below?" "Deep darkness." "And the ways up?"
"A lie." "And Pluto?" "A tale." "We are undone."
"This is my true word to you; but if you want
the pleasant kind: a great ox in Hades costs a Pellaean penny."
14. Who knows well the daemon of tomorrow? When even you,
Charmis—you who were before our eyes but yesterday—
we buried, weeping, on the next day. Nothing more grievous
than this did your father Diophon ever see.
15. "Timonoe." "Who are you? By the gods, I should not have known you,

had not the name of your father Timotheus stood
upon the stone, and Methymna, your city." "Truly, I declare,
your widowed husband Euthymenes grieves greatly."
16. Crethis, full of tales, who knew how to play sweetly,
the daughters of Samos often seek—
their sweetest fellow-worker, ever full of chatter; but she sleeps
here the sleep that is owed to all.
17. Would that swift ships had never been! For then we
should not be mourning Sopolis, son of Diocleides.
But now his corpse drifts somewhere on the sea, and in his place
we pass by a name and an empty tomb.
18. Lycus the Naxian died not on land but on the sea,
and saw his ship and his life perish together,
when he was sailing, a merchant, from Aegina. He, a corpse,
is in the waters; and I, a tomb that holds only his name,

proclaim this wholly true word: "Avoid, O sailor,
putting to sea with the Kids when they are setting."
19. Twelve years old, his father Philippus laid the boy
here—his great hope—Nicoteles.
20. At dawn we were burying Melanippus; and as the sun
was setting, the maiden Basilo died
by her own hand; for to live, having set her brother on the pyre,
she could not bear. And the house looked upon a twofold evil,
the house of their father Aristippus; and all Cyrene
bowed its head, seeing the home of fair children left desolate.
21. Whoever you are that carry your foot past my tomb, know
that I am the son and the father of Callimachus of Cyrene.
You would know them both: the one once led
his country's arms; the other sang songs stronger than envy.
No cause for resentment: those children whom the Muses have looked upon

with no sidelong eye, they do not, when grey, cast off as friends.
. . .
22. Astacides the Cretan, the goatherd, a Nymph carried off
from the mountain, and now Astacides is holy.
No more beneath the Dictaean oaks, no more of Daphnis
shall we shepherds sing, but ever of Astacides.
23. Saying "Farewell, O Sun," Cleombrotus of Ambracia
leapt from a high wall down into Hades,
having seen no evil worthy of death, but having read
one writing of Plato's, the one on the soul.
24. A hero, the warder of Aëtion of Amphipolis,
I am set up, small upon a small porch,
holding a coiled serpent and a single sword; angered
at a man of Epeus, he settled me here on foot as well.
25. Callignotus swore to Ionis that never would he
hold any friend, man or woman, dearer than her.

He swore; but they say truly that the oaths of lovers
do not enter the ears of the immortals.
And now he burns with love for a man; and of the poor
girl, as of the Megarians, there is no word nor reckoning.
26. I had from little means a scanty living, doing
nothing terrible, wronging no one. Dear Earth,
if I, Micylus, ever praised anything base, may you not lie
light upon me, nor you, kindly powers that hold me.
27. Hesiod's is the song and the manner; not the last of singers,
no—but I fear the man of Soli has milked off
the sweetest of his verses. Hail, you slender
discourses, the token of Aratus's vigil.
28. I hate the cyclic poem, nor do I take pleasure
in the road that carries many this way and that;
I loathe too the much-courted darling, nor do I drink
from the public fountain; I am sick of all common things.

Lysanias, you are indeed fair, fair—but before Echo
can say it clearly, someone else says, "He belongs to another."
29. Pour, and again say "To Diocles!" Not even Achelous
perceives those sacred ladlefuls.
The boy is fair, Achelous, exceedingly fair; and if anyone
says he is not—may I alone know what is fair.
30. Thessalian Cleonicus, wretched, wretched, no, by the keen
sun, I did not know you. Poor man, what has become of you?
Bones you are, and only hair still left. Has my own
daemon seized you? Have you met a harsh dispensation of the god?
I know it: Euxitheos has carried you off, and you too, coming,
gazed upon the fair one, poor wretch, with both your eyes.
31. The hunter, Epicydes, on the mountains tracks every hare
and the prints of every doe,
trudging, glad of the frost and snow; but if someone says,

"Here, this beast is struck down," he will not take it.
Such too is my love: it knows how to chase what flees,
but flies past what lies ready in its path.
32. I know that my hands are empty of wealth; but, Menippus,
do not, by the Graces, tell me my own dream.
I grieve, hearing this bitter word continually;
yes, dear friend, of all that comes from you, this is the least loving.
33. Artemis, to you Phileratis set up this image here;
do you accept it, lady, and keep her safe.
34. Me, lion-strangling, boar-slaying lord, a branch of oak—
who set me here? "Archinus." Which one? "The Cretan." "I accept it."
35. Past the tomb of the son of Battus you carry your feet—of one who knew
both song well, and well how to laugh in season over wine.
37. Lyctian Menoetas,
having spoken these words,

dedicated this bow:
"Here, I give you my horn
and quiver, Sarapis;
but the arrows the Hesperitae have."
38. Her gifts to Aphrodite,
Simon, who wanders the streets, set up—an image of herself,
and the girdle
that kissed her breasts, and the torch,
and the very thyrsus that the poor woman used to bear.
39. To Pylaean Demeter,
to whom that man of the Pelasgians,
Acrisius, built this temple—these gifts the man of Naucratis,
and to her daughter below,
Timodemus dedicated,
a tithe of his gains; for so indeed he had vowed.
40. Priestess of Demeter once was I, and again of the Cabiri,

sir, and thereafter of the Dindymene Mother;
I, the old woman, now dust, who . . .
was the patroness of many young wives.
And two sons were born to me, and I closed my eyes in their
arms in a fair old age. Go your way rejoicing.
41. Half of my soul still breathes; the other half I know not
whether Love or Hades has seized—only it is vanished.
Has it gone off again to one of the boys? And yet I forbade them
often: "Young men, do not receive the runaway."
Go, search there; for there, I know, that stone-worthy
and ill-loving thing of mine is somewhere turning about.
42. If of my own will, Archinus, I came reveling, blame me ten thousand times;
but if I come unwilling, let the rashness be.
Strong wine and Love compelled me; of these the one
dragged me, the other would not let me leave off my rashness.

And coming, I did not shout out who I was or whose, but kissed
the doorpost. If that is a wrong, I do wrong.
43. The stranger had a wound, and it went unnoticed. How painfully—
did you see?—his breath came through his chest. He drew it up
the third time as he drank, and the roses, shedding their leaves
from the man's garlands, all fell to the ground.
He is well roasted by something great; by the gods, it is no random
guess I make—a thief, I have learned the tracks of a thief.
44. There is something, yes by Pan, that is hidden; there is, yes
by Dionysus, here a fire beneath the ash.
I am not confident; do not embrace me. Often a quiet river,
unnoticed, gnaws away a wall;
so now too I fear, Menexenus, lest this silent creeper
slip in upon me and cast me into love.
45. "You will be caught; flee round about, Menecrates," I said

on the twentieth of Panemos; and "On what day of Loios?"—"the tenth"—
the ox came under the yoke of its own will. Well done, my Hermes,
well done, mine! I make no complaint over the twenty days.
46. What a good charm Polyphemus discovered
for the lovesick! Yes, by Earth, the Cyclops was no fool.
The Muses, Philippus, make love grow lean.
Truly, wisdom is an all-healing medicine for everything.
This, I think, is the one good that hunger too holds among hardships:
it cuts away the disease of love for boys.
And to me it is granted to say without stint to Love:
"Here, boy, your wings are clipped, little child,
and not a crumb do we fear you; for the charms,
both of them, are at home for the cruel wound."
47. The salt-cellar, on which, eating frugal salt,
Eudemus escaped great storms of debts,

he dedicated to the Samothracian gods, saying that this, according to his vow,
O great ones, having been saved from the sea, he set up thus.
48. Asking for good learning when he gave me, Simon, the son of Miccus,
to the Muses; and they, like Glaucus,
gave a great gift in return for a small one. And I lie here
gaping wide, the double Samian, the tragic
Dionysus, listening to the boys; and they say,
"The lock is sacred"—that is my dream to me.
49. Say, stranger, that I, Pamphilus, am dedicated here as the witness
of the truly comic victory of Agoranax the Rhodian;
not bitten by love, but half resembling
a roasted fig and the lamps of Isis.
50. The Phrygian Aeschra, good milk, in every good thing
Miccus, while she lived, tended in her old age;
and when she died he dedicated her to be seen by those to come—

how the old woman keeps the grace owed for her breasts.
51. Four are the Graces; for besides those three, one more
was lately fashioned, and still is moist with perfumes.
Blessed and conspicuous among all is Berenice,
without whom not even the Graces themselves are Graces.
52. Theocritus, who darkens what is fair—if he hates me,
hate him fourfold; but if he loves me, love him.
Yes, by fair-haired Ganymede, heavenly Zeus,
you too once loved—I say no more.
53. Again, Eileithyia, come at the call of Lycaenis,
bringing safe delivery from her pangs, with a good birth;
so that now, mistress, this offering for a girl, but next time
for a son, your fragrant temple may hold some other gift.
54. That you have your due, Asclepius, the debt that Aceson
owed by his vow for his wife Demodice,

know it; and if perchance you forget, and demand it again,
the tablet says it will furnish testimony.
55. To the Canopian god, Callistion, daughter of Critias,
dedicated me, a lamp rich with twenty nozzles,
having vowed it for her child Apellis; and looking into my light
you will say, "Hesperus, how have you fallen?"
56. Euaenetus, who set me up, says—for I myself
do not know it—that for his own victory
I am dedicated, a bronze cock, to the sons of Tyndareus.
I trust the son of Phaedrus, son of Philoxenides.
57. In the temple of Inachian Isis stands the child of Thales,
Aeschylis, by the vow of her mother Eirene.
58. "Who are you, shipwrecked stranger?" Leontichus found you here
a corpse upon the shore, and heaped this tomb over you,
weeping for his own perilous life; for he himself

has no rest, but like a gull he travels the sea.
59. Happy that, mad in all else, the ancient Orestes
was not mad, Leucaretes, with my madness,
nor put the Phocian to the test that proves
a friend; but had he taught even one play,
he would soon have lost his comrade by doing this—
and I no longer have many Pyladeses such as those of old.
60. You who pass by the tomb of Cimon of Elis,
know, as you pass, that you pass the son of Hippaeus.
61. Aenian Menecrates, you too were here not for long;
what, best of strangers, brought you down?
Was it the same that took the Centaur? The sleep appointed
for me came on; and the poor wine bears the blame.
62. Cynthian goats, take heart; for the bow of Echemmas
the Cretan lies in Ortygia beside Artemis,
the bow with which he emptied your great mountain. But now he has ceased,

you goats, since the goddess has made a truce.
63. So may you sleep, Conopion, as you make me
lie down by these cold porches.
So may you sleep, most unjust one, as you lull your lover
to sleep, and have met not even pity in a dream.
The neighbours pity me; but you—not even in a dream.
And soon the grey hair will remind you of all this.

How the laurel-branch of Apollo trembled!
How the whole shrine trembled! Away, away with whoever is sinful!
And now surely Phoebus knocks at the doors with his fair foot.
Do you not see? The Delian palm has nodded sweetly,
all at once, and the swan sings beautifully in the air.
Now of yourselves draw back, you bolts of the gates,
and you, the keys; for the god is no longer far off.
And you young men, make ready for the song and for the dance.
Apollo does not appear to all, but only to whoever is good;
whoever sees him, that man is great; whoever sees him not, that man is lowly.
We shall see you, Far-shooter, and we shall never be lowly.
Let not the children keep the lyre silent, nor their step soundless,
now that Phoebus has come to dwell among us,
if they mean to accomplish their marriage and to cut their grey hair,

and that the wall may stand upon its ancient foundations.
I marvel at the children, since the tortoise-shell is no longer idle.
Keep holy silence as you hear, at the song of Apollo.
Even the sea keeps silence, when the singers celebrate
either the lyre or the bow, the gear of Lycorean Phoebus.
Nor does Thetis, his mother, wail her dirges for Achilles,
whenever she hears the cry "Hië Paiëon, Hië Paiëon."
And even the weeping rock holds back its sorrows,
that wet stone set fast in Phrygia,
the marble in place of a woman, gaping in some lament.
Cry "Hië, hië"; it is an evil thing to strive with the blessed gods.
Whoever fights the blessed gods, let him fight my king;
whoever fights my king, let him fight Apollo too.
The chorus that sings to Apollo what is after his heart
he will honour; for he has the power, since he sits at the right of Zeus.

Nor will the chorus sing of Phoebus for one day only,
for he is rich in song; who would not readily sing of Phoebus?
Golden is Apollo's mantle and his clasp,
and his lyre, and his Lyctian bow, and his quiver;
golden too are his sandals; for Apollo is rich in gold.
And rich in possessions too: by Pytho you may judge it.
And he is ever beautiful and ever young; never upon Phoebus's
womanish cheeks has come so much as the down of youth.
His tresses drip fragrant oils upon the ground;
no common fat do Apollo's locks distil,
but very healing itself; and in whatever city those
drops fall to the earth, all things become free of harm.
None is so manifold in skill as Apollo;
to him belongs the archer, to him the singer
(for to Phoebus are entrusted both the bow and song),
his are the prophetic lots and the seers; and from Phoebus

the physicians have learned the postponement of death.
We call Phoebus also Nomios, ever since that time
when by the Amphrysus he tended the yoked mares,
fired with love for the youth Admetus.
Easily would the herd grow larger, nor would the she-goats
of the flock lack young, on whichever ones Apollo
turned his eye as they grazed; nor would the ewes be without milk
or barren, but all would have lambs at foot,
and she who bore one would soon bear twins.
Following Phoebus, men have measured out their cities;
for Phoebus ever delights in cities
being founded, and Phoebus himself weaves their foundations.
Four years old, Phoebus first laid the foundations
in fair Ortygia near the round lake.
Artemis, hunting, kept bringing the heads of Cynthian
goats continually, and Apollo plaited an altar.

He built the base of horns, and fixed the altar
of horns, and laid horn walls round about.
Thus first did Phoebus learn to raise foundations.
Phoebus too showed my deep-soiled city to Battus,
and as a raven led the people entering Libya,
favourable to the founder, and swore he would give walls
to our kings; and Apollo is ever true to his oath.
Apollo, many call you Boedromios,
and many Clarios, and everywhere your name is manifold;
but I call you Carneios; for so it is in my father's house.
Sparta, Carneios, was your first abode,
and second again Thera, but third the city of Cyrene.
From Sparta the sixth generation of the line of Oedipus
led you to be settled at Thera; and from Thera
sturdy Aristoteles set you in the Asbystian land,
and built you a very fair temple, and in the city

established a yearly rite, in which many
bulls fall for the last time upon their haunch, O lord.
Hië, hië, Carneios, much-besought, and your altars
bear flowers in spring, as many as the Hours
in their variety bring when the west wind breathes the dew,
and in winter the sweet crocus; and your fire is ever unfailing,
nor does the ash ever feed about yesterday's ember.
Truly Phoebus rejoiced greatly, when the men, the war-belted
warriors of Enyo, danced with the fair-haired Libyan women,
when for them the appointed Carnean seasons came.
But not yet had the Dorians come to the springs of Cyre;
they dwelt in Azilis, thick with glens.
The lord himself beheld them, and showed them to his nymph,
standing on horned Myrtussa, where Hypseis
slew the lion, the ravager of the oxen of Eurypylus.

No other dance more divine has Apollo seen than that,
nor to any city has he granted so many blessings as to Cyrene,
remembering his former rape. Nor have they themselves,
the sons of Battus, honoured any other god more than Phoebus.
Hië, hië, Paiëon we hear, because this
refrain the Delphic people first invented,
when you displayed the far-shooting of your golden bow.
At Pytho, as you came down, there met you a daemonic beast,
a dread serpent. Him you slew, casting shaft
upon shaft, your swift arrow, and the people cried aloud,
"Hië, hië, Paiëon, let fly the bolt." Straightway your mother
bore you a helper, and from that time it is sung.
Envy spoke secretly into Apollo's ears:
"I do not admire the singer who does not sing even as much as the sea."
Apollo spurned Envy with his foot, and spoke thus:

"Great is the stream of the Assyrian river, but it draws
much refuse of the earth and much rubbish upon its water.
And not from every source do the Bees carry water to Deo,
but only that which, pure and undefiled, creeps up
from a holy spring, a little drip, the choicest of all."
Hail, lord; and let Blame go where Envy is.

The holy nurse of Apollo's youth—when, my heart, or at what time
will you sing of her, of Delos? Indeed all
the Cyclades, which lie in the sea the holiest of islands,
are rich in song; but Delos wishes to bear away the first prize
from the Muses, because she washed and swaddled Phoebus,
the lord of song, and first praised him as a god.
As the Muses hate the singer who does not sing of Pimpleia,
so Phoebus hates whoever forgets Delos.
To Delos now I shall apportion a share of my song, that Apollo
of Cynthus may praise me for caring for his beloved nurse.
Windswept she is, and barren—such as, beaten by the sea,
she is the haunt of gulls rather than the run of horses—
fixed fast in the deep; and the sea, rolling much about her,
wipes off upon her the great foam of the Icarian water.

Therefore the fishers who roam the brine made their dwelling there.
But it is no cause for blame that she be named among the first,
when, toward Ocean and toward Titanian Tethys,
the islands gather, and she ever walks before them as their leader.
Behind, following in her tracks, comes Phoenician Cyrnus,
not to be despised, and Macris of the Abantes, home of the Ellopians,
and lovely Sardo, and the isle upon which Cypris first
swam up out of the water, and which she keeps safe in return for her landing.
Those islands are strong, fenced round with sheltering towers;
but Delos has Apollo. What stouter rampart is there?
Walls and stones may fall beneath the blast
of Strymonian Boreas; but a god is forever unshaken.
Delos, dear, such a helper stands around about you.
But if too many songs circle round you,

with what shall I entwine you? What is it that pleases you to hear?
Is it how at the very first the great god, smiting the mountains
with his three-pronged blade, which the Telchines wrought for him,
made the islands in the sea, and heaved them all
up from their lowest foundations and rolled them into the deep?
And these he rooted firm from below in the depths,
that they might forget the mainland; but you no constraint pressed—
you sailed free upon the open seas, and your name
was Asterie of old, since you leapt into the deep abyss
fleeing from heaven the marriage of Zeus, like a star.
So long as golden Leto did not yet draw near you,
so long you were still Asterie, and not yet called Delos.
Often did sailors, coming from the yellow town
of Troezen toward Ephyra within the Saronic gulf,

look upon you; and returning back from Ephyra
some no longer saw you there, while you had run
beside the swift, narrow strait of resounding Euripus,
and that same day, refusing the water of the Chalcidian sea,
swam onward as far as the headland of Athenian Sunium,
or Chios, or the isle's nipple dripping with water,
Parthenia (for it was not yet Samos), where the nymphs,
the neighbouring Mycalessian nymphs of Ancaeus, gave you welcome.
And when you gave Apollo a ground for his birth,
in return the seafarers laid this name upon you,
because no longer unseen did you sail, but in the deep
waves of the Aegean set the roots of your feet.
Nor did you tremble at angry Hera; she upon all
the women in childbed who bore sons to Zeus
roared terribly, but on Leto beyond all the rest,

because she alone was destined to bear to Zeus
a son dearer than Ares.
Therefore she herself kept watch within the upper air,
raging mightily and unspeakably, and she barred Leto
worn with her pangs; and two warders she set
to keep watch over the earth: the one, on the mainland's floor
seated upon the high crest of Thracian Haemus,
furious Ares kept guard with his armour, and his two horses
were stabled by the seven-chambered cave of Boreas;
the other, a watcher over the broad islands,
the daughter of Thaumas sat, swooping down upon Mimas.
There they remained, threatening those cities to which
Leto turned, and turning them aside from receiving her.
Arcadia fled, and the holy mountain of Auge
fled, Parthenion, and behind them fled old Pheneus.
Fled all the land of Pelops that lies along the Isthmus,

save Aegialus and Argos; for upon those
paths she did not tread, since Inachus fell by lot to Hera.
Aonia too fled the one road, and there followed
Dirce and Strophie, holding the hand
of their black-pebbled father Ismenus; and far behind followed
Asopus heavy-kneed, since he had been smitten by the thunderbolt.
And the earth-born nymph Melie, whirled in the dance,
ceased from it, and her cheek grew pale,
gasping for her coeval oak, when she saw the foliage
of Helicon shaken. My goddesses, tell me, Muses,
is it true that the oaks were born when the Nymphs were?
The Nymphs rejoice when the rain makes the oaks grow;
the Nymphs again weep when leaves are no more upon the oaks.
At them Apollo, still in the womb, was terribly enraged,
and uttered no idle thing, threatening against Thebe:

"Thebe, why, wretched one, do you put to the test your coming doom?
Do not yet, do not force me against my will to prophesy.
Not yet do I care for the tripod-seat at Pytho,
nor has the great serpent yet died, but still that
dread-jawed beast, creeping up from Pleistus,
wreathes snowy Parnassus with its nine coils;
yet all the same I shall speak something sharper than from the laurel.
Flee onward: swift shall I overtake you, washing my bow
in blood. You have got for offspring the children of an evil-tongued
woman. You shall not be my dear nurse, nor shall Cithaeron
be; but of the pure, and to the pure, may I be the care."
So he spoke. And Leto, turning back, again withdrew.
But when the Achaean cities refused her
as she came—Helice, the consort of Poseidon,
and Bura, the ox-stall of Dexamenus, son of Oeceus—

she turned her feet back toward Thessaly; and Anaurus fled,
and great Larissa, and the Chironian heights,
and Peneus too fled, winding through Tempe.
Hera, even then your heart lay pitiless,
nor were you broken, nor did you have mercy, when, stretching out
both her arms in vain, Leto cried such words:
"Nymphs of Thessaly, daughters of the river, tell your father
to lull his great stream. Twine yourselves about his beard,
beseeching that the children of Zeus be born in his water.
Phthiotian Peneus, why do you now strive with the winds?
O father, you are not mounted upon a prize-racing horse.
Are your feet thus always swift, or only over me
do they run light, and have you been made to fly
suddenly today?" But he was deaf. "O my burden,
where shall I carry you? For my poor sinews have given out.

Pelion, O bridal-chamber of Philyra, but you remain,
remain, since even the beasts upon your mountains often
have laid down their untimely birth-pangs, the lionesses."
And Peneus answered her, letting fall his tears:
"Leto, Necessity is a great goddess. For I,
lady, do not refuse your pangs; I know of others too
who washed themselves of childbirth from my waters. But Hera
has threatened me with abundance. Look, what a watcher
keeps watch from the topmost mountain, who would easily
drag me up from my depths. What shall I devise? Or is it
sweet to you that Peneus should perish? Let the appointed day come;
I shall endure for your sake, even if I must run forever
with a thirsting ebb, drained of my streams,
and be called, alone among rivers, the most dishonoured.
Behold me. What more? Only call upon Eileithyia."

He spoke, and checked his great stream. But Ares
was about to lift up the topmost peaks of Pangaeus
and hurl them into his eddies and hide his channels;
from on high he thundered and struck his shield with the point
of his spear; and it rang out warlike; and the mountains of Ossa
trembled, and the Crannonian plain and the ill-blown
edges of Pindus, and all Thessaly danced
with fear; such was the echo that roared from his shield.
And as when, the Etnaean mountain smouldering with fire,
all the recesses shake when the giant beneath the earth
shifts upon the other shoulder of Briareus,
and the furnaces roar beneath the tongs of Hephaestus
together with the works, and dreadfully the fire-wrought cauldrons
and tripods, falling upon one another, ring out—
such then was the clang of his well-rounded shield.

Yet Peneus did not give ground again, but stood as before,
steadfast as at the first, and stayed his swift eddies,
until the daughter of Coeus called to him: "Be saved, and rejoice,
be saved; do not for my sake suffer harm in return
for this compassion; your kindness shall have its recompense."
She spoke, and after many toils came to the islands
in the sea; but they did not receive her as she came—
not the Echinades, which hold a sheltered anchorage for ships,
nor Corcyra, the most hospitable of all,
since Iris, hastening upon them from the heights of lofty Mimas,
turned them all aside; and they at her rebuke
fled in a body down whatever stream each chanced upon.
Then to ancient Cos, the Meropian island,
she came, the holy haunt of the heroine Chalciope.
But this word of her son held her back: "Do not, mother,

bear me here. I neither blame nor begrudge
the island, since it is rich and good for pasture, if any other is;
but there is owed to it from the Fates another god,
the highest race of the Saviours; beneath whose crown
shall come, not unwilling to be ruled by a Macedonian,
both the inland regions and those that sit amid the seas,
as far as where the West is, and whence the swift horses
carry the sun; and he shall know the ways of his father.
And one day a common struggle shall come upon us
later, when the Titans of a later age, raising
against the Greeks a barbarian sword and Celtic war,
shall rush from the uttermost West, like snowflakes
or equal in number to the stars, when they most
graze across the sky; and the strongholds
and the Crissaean plains and the mainlands
shall be hemmed in on every side, and they shall see the thick smoke

of a burning neighbour, and no longer by report only,
but already beside my temple shall they catch sight of the phalanxes
of the enemy, and already beside my tripods
the swords and the shameless belts and the hated
shields, which for the Galatians, that senseless tribe,
shall set up an evil road; of these some shall be my prize,
and others, by the Nile, having seen those who bore them
breathe out their lives in fire, shall lie there
as the prizes of a king who has accomplished many labours.
O Ptolemy that art to be, these prophecies I reveal to you.
Greatly shall you praise the seer yet in the womb
hereafter, for all your days. But you, mother, consider this:
there is, dimly seen in the water, a slight island,
wandering over the seas; its feet are not in one place,
but it floats upon the tide like an asphodel-stalk,

now where the South wind, now the East, wherever the sea carries it.
Bear me thither; for to her you shall come, since she is willing."
As he spoke thus, the other islands ran away across the sea;
but you, Asterie, lover of song, were coming down from Euboea
to look upon the encircling Cyclades—not long ago,
but still behind you trailed the seaweed of Geraestus.
. . .
. . . burning, since you were scorched round about by fire,
seeing her, poor wretch, weighed down by her pangs:
"Hera, do to me this that is dear to you; for I have not
kept your threats. Come, come over to me, Leto."
You spoke; and she ceased from her grievous, longed-for wandering,
and sat beside the stream of Inopus, which deepest
the earth sends forth at that time, when with full flood
the Nile comes down from the Ethiopian crag;

and she loosed her girdle, and leaned back upon her shoulders
against a palm-trunk, worn out by grievous
helplessness; and down through her flesh ran the sweat of the South.
And she said, gasping: "Why, child, do you weigh down your mother?
Here, dear, is your island, floating upon the sea.
Be born, be born, child, and come gently from the womb."
Heavy-hearted bride of Zeus, you were not, after all, to remain
long unaware; such a messenger ran to you,
and spoke, still gasping, and her words were mingled with fear:
"Honoured Hera, far foremost of goddesses,
I am yours, and yours are all things, and you sit as queen,
the lawful mistress of Olympus, and we fear no other
hand of a woman; but you, mistress, shall know the cause of your wrath.
Leto is loosing her girdle within an island.

All the rest loathed her and would not receive her;
but Asterie called her by name as she passed by—
Asterie, the evil sweepings of the sea; you know it yourself.
But, dear lady—for you have the power—defend, mistress, your slaves
who tread your soil at your command."
So she spoke, and sat down beneath the golden throne like a hound
of Artemis, which, when it ceases from the swift chase,
sits, the huntress, beside her feet, its ears
held straight up, ever ready to receive the goddess's call;
like to her the daughter of Thaumas sat beneath the throne.
And she never forgets her seat,
not even when sleep lays its forgetful wing upon her,
but there, against the very corner of the great throne,
bending her head a little aside, she sleeps slantwise.
Nor ever does she loose her girdle or her swift

running-shoes, lest her mistress should say some sudden word to her.
And she, grievously vexed, spoke out:
"So now, you reproaches of Zeus, may you marry
in secret and bear in hiding, not even where the wretched
hard-labouring grinding-women toil, but where the seals
of the sea bring forth, upon desolate reefs.
Yet against Asterie I bear no grudge for this
offence, nor is there any way I would do her displeasure,
much as I should—for very wickedly she favoured Leto;
rather I revere her exceedingly, because she did not
tread my bed, but chose the sea instead of Zeus."
So she spoke; and the swans, the singers of the god,
left Maeonian Pactolus and circled
seven times about Delos, and sang over the birth-pangs,
the birds of the Muses, the most tuneful of winged things;
whence the child afterward bound just so many strings

upon his lyre, as often as the swans had sung over his pangs.
An eighth time they sang no more; he leapt forth, and over a long time
the Delian nymphs, offspring of an ancient river,
sang the holy song of Eileithyia, and at once the brazen
sky echoed back the piercing ululation,
nor was Hera angry, since Zeus had taken away her wrath.
Golden then, Delos, did all your foundations become,
and golden flowed the round lake all day long,
and golden grew the leafage of the natal olive-shoot,
and with gold brimmed deep Inopus, winding along.
And you yourself took up the child from the golden ground,
and laid him in your bosom, and spoke such a word:
"O great one, of many altars, of many cities, bearing much,
you fertile mainlands and you islands dwelling round about:
such am I, hard to plough; yet from me

shall Apollo be called Delian, nor shall any other
of lands be loved so much by another god—
not Cerchnis by lord Poseidon of Lechaeum,
not the Cyllenian hill by Hermes, not Crete by Zeus—
as I by Apollo; and I shall be no longer a wanderer."
So you spoke; and he drew the sweet breast.
Therefore from that day the holiest of islands
are you called, the nurse of Apollo's youth; nor does Enyo
nor Hades nor the horses of Ares trample you;
but to you year by year the tithe-bearing firstfruits
are ever sent, and all the cities lead up their dances—
those toward the dawn and those toward the evening and those in the middle
who have set up their lots, and those who above the northern
shore have their dwellings, a most long-lived blood.
These first bring the stalk and the sacred sheaves

of the corn-ears; which the Pelasgians at Dodona,
coming out from afar, are the very first to receive,
those servants who lie on the ground, of the unsilent cauldron.
Next they come to the Holy City and the mountains of the Malian land;
from there they sail across to the good
Lelantian plain of the Abantes; and no longer long
is the voyage from Euboea, since your harbours are near.
First did Oupis and Loxo and blessed Hecaerge,
the daughters of Boreas, bring these from the yellow Arimaspians,
and the noblest then of the young men;
nor did they come back home again,
but they were happy in their lot, and never were they without glory.
Indeed the Delian maidens, when the sweet-sounding wedding-song
frightens the spirits of the girls, offer their coeval hair
to the maidens, and the boys their first harvest of down,

the young men, offering it to those youths.
Fragrant Asterie, around you and about you the islands
have made a ring, and as a chorus surround you;
nor silent nor noiseless does Hesperus of thick locks
look down upon you, but ever loud-resounding.
Some sing the strain of the Lycian old man,
which the seer Olen brought you from Xanthus;
and the women of the chorus beat with their feet the firm ground.
Then too with garlands is weighed down the holy image,
that famous one of ancient Cypris, which once Theseus
set up with the youths, when he sailed up from Crete.
They, having escaped the harsh bellowing and the savage son
of Pasiphae and the winding lair of the crooked labyrinth,
lady, around your altar, as the harping rose,
danced in a circle, and Theseus led the chorus.
Thence the ever-living sacred things of the sacred ship

the children of Cecrops send to Phoebus, the rigging of that ship.
Asterie of many altars, of many prayers, what sailor,
what merchant of the Aegean, ever passed you by in his running ship?
Not even though strong winds blow upon him,
and need brings the swiftest voyage, but they furl
their sails quickly, and do not go on their way again,
before they have danced round your great altar, smitten
with blows, and bitten the holy trunk of the olive,
twisting their hands behind them; sports which the Delian nymph
devised, things for laughter to the young Apollo.
O hearth of the islands, well-hearthed one, hail yourself,
and hail Apollo, and her whom Leto bore.

title: The Declaration of Independence: A Study in the History of Political Ideas
author: Carl L. Becker

candidates.text: All are but parts of one stupendous whole, Whose body Nature is, and God the soul;. . . . All Nature is but art, unknown to thee; All chance, direction, which thou canst not see; All discord, harmony not understood; All partial evil, universal good: And, spite of pride, in erring reason’s spite, One truth is clear, whatever is, is right.

15.2. For consulting the Sibylline verses, they found written in them this very thing: "If the king of Egypt come needing some aid, do not refuse him friendship, yet do not aid him with any multitude; otherwise you will have both

Albert and Cecilia,
a Norman Tale.
Founded on Fact.
A FAIRER form than fiction ever feign'd;
A bloom surpassing far the opening rose;
Eyes where with softness animation reign'd;
A heart that sympathiz'd in others' woes:
Such was Cecilia — ere a father's pride
Clouded the noon-tide of a morn so bright;
Condemn'd each feeling nature sanctified,
And clos'd each beauty in eternal night.
The haughty Anselm, of his riches vain —
Vain of his ancestry and high estate —
View'd unassuming merit with disdain,
Or thought it only centred in the Great,
Each day, to win the young Cecilia's smiles,

" Whose lofty brow o'erlooks this ample plain,
"You bear the maid; nor rest a moment, till
" Ev'n to the top thy venturous steps attain. "
What mighty task will daring love refuse,
The object of its fond pursuits to gain?
Who in delusion's flattering mirror views
And grasps at shadows it can ne'er obtain.
The youth undaunted clasps the trembling fair,
Nor thinks the dangerous trial to decline:
"This happy hour," he cries, "ends all my care,
" And makes thee, dear Cecilia! ever mine. "
With eager haste he pass'd the level green,
And rapidly he climbs the steep ascent;
While numerous vassals throng'd to view the scene,
And prayers to Heaven for their deliverance sent.
Sadly prophetic of impending woe,

And flowery meadows fix the wandering sight —
Where pebbly streams in wild meanders flow,
And perfum'd winds o'er beds of roses blow —
Even there the love of fame mankind inspires,
And rustic breasts with rustic passions fires.
The 'Squire feels anguish more than words can tell,
If other hounds in swiftness his excel;
If other steeds, more forward in the race,
Outstrip his coursers in the devious chase.
The Country Justice, into years declin'd,
To more substantial honours turns his mind:
He glories in his barns with plenty stor'd,
And the luxuriance of his copious board;
Nor lets one care his placid mind molest —
Except some costlier dish should crown another's feast.
The rural Belle, impatient, seeks renown

The sober youth behind his counter sat:
His study was of stocks the rise and fall,
And his grand festival a Lord Mayor's ball.
When Fortune, careful of the fool and knave,
A large estate beyond his wishes gave,
He hastes to figure where the Great resort,
And quits th' Exchange to bustle through the Court.
To ape the courtly fop in vain he tries;
Now with Lord Trinket in his carriage vies;
Now games, now drinks, now swears — and all for fame,
Since more illustrious blockheads do the same. —
But hark! what knell, inspiring awful fear,
In broken sounds thus strikes my wounded ear?
That knell it calls Olivia to the tomb,
Fallen in gay youth, in beauty's brightest bloom,
Adorn'd with sentiment and sense refin'd,

Still powerful Virtue shall victorious prove,
And fix, where Beauty fails, a husband's love. —
Silius affects an absent careless mien,
Nothing by him is heard, and nothing seen;
Or, should his eyes a play or ball explore,
He listless yawns, and wishes it was o'er. —
His native England Lycidas disdains,

Run, drawing the thread, run, spindles! No house ever yet enclosed such loves, no love bound lovers with such pact, as abides with Thetis, as is the concord of Peleus. Run, drawing the thread, run, spindles! To you will Achilles be born, a stranger to fear, to his foes known not by his back, but by his strong breast, who, often the victor in the uncertain struggle of the foot-race, will outrun the fire-fleet footsteps of the speedy doe. Run, drawing the thread, run, spindles! None in war with him may compare as a hero, when the Phrygian streams trickle with Trojan blood, and when besieging the walls of Troy with a long, drawn-out warfare perjured Pelops’ third heir lays that city waste. Run, drawing the thread, run, spindles! Often will mothers attest over funeral-rites of their sons his glorious acts and illustrious deeds, when the white locks from their heads are unloosed amid ashes, and they bruise their discoloured breasts with feeble fists. Run, drawing the thread, run, spindles! For as the reaper, plucking off the dense wheat-ears before their time, mows the harvest yellowed beneath ardent sun, so will he cast prostrate the corpses of Troy’s sons with grim swords. Run, drawing the thread, run, spindles! His great valour will be attested by Scamander’s wave, which ever pours itself into the swift Hellespont, narrowing its course with slaughtered heaps of corpses he shall make tepid its deep stream by mingling warm blood with the water. Run, drawing the thread, run, spindles!
